title: 1-2-4-All
summary: A short Liberating Structure for generating ideas or answers in which everyone first reflects silently alone, then builds on ideas in pairs, then in groups of four, before a few groups share the strongest ideas with the whole room.
selfCheck: Was my invitation specific enough that someone could write concrete answers to it in one minute?
Did I protect the silent reflection, or did someone (including me) start talking before everyone had written?
In the all-group share, did I ask for new ideas from each group rather than letting the most confident group report everything?
Did I steer the content of the small-group conversations, or did I limit myself to running time and process?
steps: Write one open, specific invitation the group can act on, such as "What opportunities do you see to cut our release lead time?", and show it to everyone.
Give one minute of silent, individual reflection in which each person writes their own ideas; protect the silence and do not talk over it.
Have people pair up for two minutes to share and build on each other's ideas, keeping different ideas distinct rather than forcing agreement.
Merge pairs into groups of four for about five minutes to compare ideas and pick out the ones that stand out.
Bring everyone back and ask each group for one important idea that is not yet on the board, recording each one, until the strongest ideas are visible.
Close by naming what the group will do with the ideas - prioritise them, assign owners or feed them into a decision - and debrief briefly with a co-host on how the process went.

example.situation: A team lead runs a 30-minute retrospective with ten engineers, two of whom are senior and usually speak first, to find ways to reduce late-night production incidents.
example.before: So, what should we change to cut down on incidents? ... Good point, Priya [senior engineer], more alerting makes sense. Anyone else? No? Let's take that as the action.
example.after: Take one minute on your own and jot down every change you think would cut late-night incidents. Now share with the person next to you for two minutes, then join another pair for five. Each group of four, give me the one idea we haven't heard yet.
example.why: The open question lets the first senior voice set the answer and the quiet engineers never speak; reflecting alone and then in pairs means everyone has an idea and a low-risk audience before the whole room hears anything, so more and more varied options surface.

title: Acoustic speech-analysis coaching
summary: Practising spoken delivery with software that measures your voice (pitch range, speaking rate, pauses, fillers) and shows the result back to you, so you can widen a flat pitch range or steady a rushed pace against an objective reading rather than a hunch. Small controlled studies show measurable gains in pitch variation that carry over to a later presentation, but evidence that audiences notice is thin.
selfCheck: Am I training one parameter at a time, or chasing every number the tool shows?
Did I drill sentences from my real talk rather than generic exercises?
Did I check the recording by ear, or with a colleague, to confirm the change sounds natural and not exaggerated?
Is my extra pitch or volume landing on the words that carry the point?
steps: Record a baseline of three to five minutes of a real upcoming talk and note the tool's readings for pitch variation, pace and fillers.
Pick one parameter to train, such as a flat pitch range or a pace above the tool's recommended band, and ignore the rest for now.
Pull out five to ten sentences from your own talk that carry the key points, and decide which word in each should stand out.
Repeat each sentence aloud while glancing at the live meter, aiming to push the reading past your baseline without the sentence sounding forced.
Spread the drills over several short sessions across a few weeks rather than one long cram.
Deliver a full run-through, compare the readings with your baseline, and listen to the recording yourself or with a colleague to check it still sounds natural.

example.situation: An operations manager will present a quarterly results update to the leadership team; colleagues say she sounds flat.
example.before: She rehearses by reading her notes aloud twice. In the meeting every figure, including a 12% cost saving, sits on the same note and pace, and a director later asks whether the savings were mentioned.
example.after: She records a baseline in a speech-analysis tool, sees a narrow pitch range and a pace near the top of the band, then drills the six sentences carrying her figures over two weeks, watching the meter as she lifts the key numbers. In the meeting she slows down on the 12% saving and her voice rises on it.
example.why: An objective, in-the-moment reading shows a habit she could not hear in herself, and short targeted drills on her own sentences carried over to the real talk.

title: Active listening
summary: The learnable skill of listening to understand another person's full meaning - the content and the feeling behind it - and showing that understanding back to them, while holding off judgment, advice and persuasion until they confirm you have understood.
selfCheck: Could I state their point, and how they feel about it, well enough that they would say "yes, exactly"?
Did I hold back advice, reassurance and my own counter-argument until they confirmed I understood?
Was my attention on them, or was I rehearsing my reply or glancing at a screen?
Did I ask at least one question that drew out something they had not yet said?
Would they leave this conversation feeling heard, even if I did not agree with them?

title: Active voice
summary: Writing sentences so the person or organisation doing the action is the grammatical subject ("The team will send the report"), rather than the thing acted on ("The report will be sent"), so readers can see who does what.
selfCheck: Can the reader tell, sentence by sentence, who is responsible for each action?
Where I kept a passive, is the actor unknown, unimportant or obvious, or am I hiding who decided?
Did I mislabel any sentence as passive just because it uses "was" or describes the past?
steps: Find each sentence that has a form of "to be" plus a past participle (was sent, will be reviewed, has been approved).
Ask who does the action; if the sentence does not say, decide who should, and name them.
Rewrite with that actor as the subject and a strong verb right after it ("Finance will review the budget").
Address the reader as "you" when they are the one who must act.
Keep a passive only when the actor is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when the thing acted on is what the paragraph is about.

example.situation: A project manager tells a client team what happens before go-live.
example.before: The test results will be reviewed and any outstanding issues must be resolved before the release can be approved.
example.after: Our QA lead will review the test results by Tuesday. Your team needs to fix any open issues by Thursday, and then I will approve the release.
example.why: The original names no one, so each side can assume the other owns the work; the rewrite assigns every action to a person and a date.

title: Adam Galinsky
summary: Social psychologist and Columbia Business School professor whose 2001 experiments with Thomas Mussweiler established the first-offer advantage in negotiation, whose 2008 studies separated perspective-taking from empathy at the bargaining table, and who popularised the "range of acceptable behavior" idea for speaking up.

title: Alison Wood Brooks
summary: Harvard Business School behavioural scientist who studies conversation. Her lab's question-asking studies made follow-up questions - questions that build on what a partner just said - the best-known research-backed habit for being heard as responsive, and she introduced the "get excited" reappraisal of performance anxiety and the TALK maxims (topics, asking, levity, kindness) taught in her MBA course and 2025 book.

title: Alvin Toffler
summary: American writer and futurist (1928-2016) whose bestseller Future Shock (1970) brought the idea of information overload to a mass audience and coined "adhocracy"; his work is the reason most managers have a name for the feeling that messages arrive faster than anyone can process them.

title: Anchoring and adjustment
summary: The tendency for an estimate or judgment to stay too close to a starting value - a number someone mentioned first, last year's figure, or our own point of view - because people adjust away from that starting point only until the answer feels plausible.

title: Anxiety reappraisal
summary: Reinterpreting the racing heart and jitters before a talk, interview or other evaluated performance as useful energy or excitement - rather than trying to calm down - so that the arousal is treated as a resource for the task instead of a sign of threat.
selfCheck: Am I trying to force myself to feel calm, or accepting that being keyed up is normal before something that matters?
What is one thing that could go well in this talk, and have I pointed my energy at it?
Am I using the reframe as a substitute for preparing and rehearsing out loud?
After the talk, am I judging it by what the audience did, or by how nervous I felt?
steps: Expect your heart rate, breathing and alertness to rise before the talk, and stop treating that as proof that something is wrong.
Remind yourself, in a sentence, what the arousal is for - it moves oxygen and attention to where you need them for the task.
Just before you start, say "I am excited" (aloud or under your breath) instead of telling yourself to calm down.
Turn the excitement toward the opportunity - name one thing that could go well, such as the decision you want the audience to make.
Pair the reframe with preparation and rehearsal; it changes how the nerves feel, not whether you know your material.
Afterwards, judge the talk by what the audience understood or decided, not by how anxious you felt.

example.situation: A finance analyst is about to present a quarterly variance review to the leadership team for the first time and notices her hands shaking in the corridor.
example.before: Calm down, calm down. They'll see I'm nervous. Just get through the slides without messing up.
example.after: My heart's racing because this matters - that's energy I can use. I'm excited to show them why the logistics overspend is a one-off and get the forecast approved.
example.why: The first version fights the arousal, which rarely works, and keeps attention on what could go wrong. The second accepts the arousal, labels it as excitement and points it at a concrete opportunity - the shift the reappraisal studies tested.

title: Apology
summary: A message, spoken or written, in which a person or organization takes responsibility for a specific harm or mistake, expresses regret and commits to repair it, with the aim of restoring trust and the working relationship.
selfCheck: Have I said exactly what I did, in the first person, without "if", "but" or a passive construction?
Does my apology show that I understand what this cost the other person, not just how bad I feel?
Is my explanation short enough that it cannot be read as an excuse?
Have I offered a concrete repair and a change with a date, and will I actually follow through?
Is this a lapse of skill, where apologizing helps, or an accusation about my honesty that I believe is false, where admitting it could backfire?
steps: Apologize as soon as you know you caused the problem; do not wait until legal, political or face-saving worries have shaped the message.
Name the specific thing you did and say plainly that it was your responsibility, without "if anyone was offended" or a passive "mistakes were made".
State the concrete effect on the other person (lost time, rework, an embarrassing moment with their client) so they can see you understand the cost to them.
Give a short explanation of what went wrong only if it helps them trust the fix, and stop before it turns into an excuse.
Offer a specific repair for this instance and a change that prevents a repeat, with an owner and a date.
Leave out the demand for forgiveness; then listen to their reaction and follow through visibly on what you promised.

example.situation: A project analyst sent a client the wrong version of a cost model, and the client's finance director presented outdated numbers to her own leadership team.
example.before: Hi Priya, apologies for any confusion around the model - there were a few version-control issues on our side this week. Hope you can forgive the mix-up! Updated file attached.
example.after: Priya, I sent you last month's cost model instead of the final one, and that's on me - it meant you presented figures to your leadership that were about 8% too low. The correct file is attached with the changes highlighted, and I can join a 15-minute call with your CFO tomorrow to walk through the difference. From now on every client file will go out only from the release folder after a second-person check, starting today.
example.why: The rewrite names the specific error, takes responsibility in the first person and acknowledges the client's cost, then offers an immediate repair and a preventive change - the two components rated most effective - and drops the request for forgiveness, rated least effective.

title: Aristotle's Rhetoric
summary: Aristotle's fourth-century BCE treatise defining rhetoric as the ability to see the available means of persuasion in a given case; it introduced the three proofs of character, emotion and argument, and the first systematic analysis of how an audience shapes a speech.

title: Assertion-evidence slides
summary: A slide design in which each slide's headline is a full sentence stating the one point the slide makes, and the body is visual evidence for that point (a chart, diagram, photo or equation) instead of a topic phrase followed by bullet points.
selfCheck: If someone read only my slide headlines, would they get my argument and my conclusion?
Does each slide make exactly one point, and does the visual actually prove that point rather than decorate it?
Am I planning to explain each visual, or am I going to read the headline and bullets aloud?
Is the material complex enough to need visual evidence, or would a simple spoken point serve the audience better?
steps: Before opening the slide software, write the talk's main message, then list the three to six points the audience must accept to believe it.
Turn each point into one slide whose headline is a complete sentence of no more than two lines that states the point, not the topic.
Under each headline, place the visual that best proves the sentence - a chart, diagram, photo, table or equation - and delete decorative images.
Strip the body text down to short labels on the visual; move anything you would have bulleted into what you say aloud or into a handout.
Read only the headlines in order and check that they tell the whole argument; fix any slide whose headline could not stand on its own.
Rehearse explaining each visual in your own words rather than reading the headline back to the audience.

example.situation: An operations analyst is presenting the cause of a rise in late deliveries to the regional leadership team.
example.before: Headline: 'Q3 delivery performance'. Bullets: 'On-time rate down', 'Carrier changes in July', 'Warehouse B staffing', 'Weather events', 'Next steps'.
example.after: Headline: 'Late deliveries doubled after July because Warehouse B lost its night shift'. Body: a line chart of weekly on-time rate for each warehouse, with Warehouse B's drop marked at the week the night shift ended.
example.why: The first slide names a topic and leaves the audience to work out which bullet matters. The second states the conclusion in the headline and shows the one chart that proves it, so leaders who only glance at the slide still take away the cause.

title: Asynchronous communication
summary: Communication in which sender and receiver are not engaged at the same moment - email, chat threads, shared documents, recorded video - so each side can compose and respond in its own time; it suits conveying information and protecting focus, but needs complete, self-contained messages and a switch to live conversation when people must converge on a shared meaning.

title: Audience analysis
summary: The practice of working out, before you write or speak, who will receive a message, what they already know, what they care about and what they need to do with it, and then shaping the content, structure, tone and channel to fit them.
selfCheck: Who will read or hear this - including people copied or forwarded to - and which of them is the one who must act?
What does my primary audience already know, and which of my terms or steps would they not recognise?
What is in this for them, and do they see it in the first few lines?
Have I checked my picture of the audience against something they actually said or did, or am I only guessing?
steps: List every audience, not just the addressee - the decision maker, technical reviewers, people who are copied, people the message may be forwarded to and people affected by the outcome.
For the primary audience, write down what they already know, what they care about, what attitude they are likely to bring and what they must decide or do after reading.
Check your assumptions against evidence - the questions people actually ask you, past replies, usage data or a short conversation with a typical reader.
Choose content, order, vocabulary, tone and channel to fit the primary audience, putting what matters to them first.
Give secondary audiences their own clearly labelled section instead of mixing material for different readers.
Reread the draft as each audience in turn - including someone it might be forwarded to - and fix what would confuse or alienate them.

example.situation: An engineering lead emails a delay notice about a data-platform migration to a list that includes the client's finance director.
example.before: Heads up - the ETL refactor slipped because the CDC connector kept OOMing on the backfill. New ETA is sprint 14, assuming infra gets us the bigger nodes.
example.after: Subject: Data migration finishing three weeks later than planned (no change to cost). The move to the new reporting system will finish on 4 December instead of 13 November. Your month-end reports will run on the old system as usual until then. Technical details for your IT team are in the section below.
example.why: The finance director is the primary reader and needs the date, the impact on her work and the cost; the jargon and team shorthand move to a separate section for the technical secondary audience.

title: Avrim Fishkind
summary: Houston emergency psychiatrist and past president of the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry whose 2002 "10 commandments for safety" set out a short, teachable script for calming an agitated person with words, and became the basis of the 2012 Project BETA ten domains of verbal de-escalation now adapted for police, security and front-line staff.

title: BATNA
aliases: best alternative to a negotiated agreement
summary: Working out, before you negotiate, the best thing you will actually do if this negotiation fails - and using that alternative as the yardstick for every offer, the basis of your walk-away point and a source of leverage you can deliberately improve.
selfCheck: Do I know concretely what I will do tomorrow if this negotiation ends without a deal?
Have I compared my alternative with the offer on equivalent terms, or only on the headline price?
Is my opening ask set by my goal, or have I let a weak alternative drag it down?
Is everything I am about to say about my alternatives true?
steps: Before the first meeting, list every realistic thing you could do if no deal is reached - other vendors, other candidates, building it in-house, waiting, or doing nothing.
Translate each alternative into the same terms as the deal on the table (total cost, scope, risk, timing, effort to switch) so you are comparing like with like.
Pick the single best alternative - that is your BATNA - and from it set your reservation value, the worst deal you would still accept over walking away.
Spend some preparation time improving the BATNA itself (get a real competing quote, line up a second option) rather than only describing it.
Estimate the other side's BATNA too, and ask about their alternatives, so you know how much they need this deal.
Anchor your opening ask on your goal, not on your BATNA; keep a weak BATNA to yourself and never invent an alternative you do not have.
Re-check the BATNA whenever new information arrives during the talks, and walk away only when an offer is genuinely worse than it.

example.situation: An operations manager is renegotiating an annual software contract after the vendor proposes a 12% price rise.
example.before: We really can't move away from you, so please do what you can on the price. What's the best you can offer?
example.after: We've priced a comparable tool that would cost us about 8% less in year one, including migration. We'd rather stay - the team knows your product - so we're looking for a renewal at last year's rate with the new reporting module included. What would make that work on your side?
example.why: The manager did the BATNA homework first (a real, like-for-like competing quote), so the ask is anchored on a goal rather than on desperation, the alternative is mentioned truthfully without a threat, and the question invites the vendor to solve the problem with them.

title: Behavior modeling training
summary: A structured way to build interpersonal skills: learners get a few clear learning points, watch someone model them, rehearse in role-play, receive feedback and praise, and plan how to use the behaviour on the job. It is the best-studied method for turning communication advice into practised behaviour.
selfCheck: Can I state the learning points for this conversation as rules, not as a script I have memorised?
Have I actually practised this out loud with feedback, or only read about it?
What exact situation in the next two weeks will I use this in, and who will notice whether I did?
Is anything at work (my manager, our appraisal, team norms) rewarding the old way of handling this?
steps: Pick one recurring conversation (for example, raising a missed deadline) and write four to six learning points as rules that say what to do and why.
Show a model handling it, ideally more than one, including a version that goes wrong, and discuss the learning points before or after the demonstration rather than over it.
Have each learner picture themselves doing it, then role-play scenarios drawn from their own job, swapping roles.
Give specific feedback and praise on each learning point, then run the practice again.
End with a concrete goal for using the skill at work in the next two weeks, brief the learners' managers, and check back on it.

example.situation: A new team lead has to raise a late report with an experienced analyst. Before training she had only read an article on feedback; afterwards she had practised the conversation in a modeling session.
example.before: You missed the deadline again. This really can't keep happening, OK?
example.after: The board report was due Tuesday and came in Thursday, so I had to delay the pack. What got in the way? ... OK, so let's agree that you'll flag a slip by Monday noon. Can you do that?
example.why: She had watched the steps modeled, rehearsed them twice with feedback and set a goal to use them, so under pressure she named the specific behaviour and its impact, asked before judging and closed on an agreed action.

title: Bleyer's Newspaper Writing and Editing
summary: Willard G. Bleyer's 1913 university journalism textbook, which made the "lead" - the opening that gives the gist and the most important feature of a story - the centre of news writing, and told editors to dig out a point the writer had buried. It is an early, influential statement of the main-point-first rule behind "don't bury the lede".

title: Bottom line up front
summary: Opening a message with its conclusion, recommendation or request - the one thing the reader must know or do - and only then giving the background and supporting detail.
selfCheck: If my reader read only the subject line and first two sentences, would they know what I need from them and by when?
Have I stated my conclusion or recommendation, or only described the situation and left the reader to infer it?
Is this message an exception - serious bad news, or a reader who expects context first - and have I chosen the structure on purpose?
steps: Before drafting, write one sentence that states your conclusion, recommendation or request, including any decision and deadline you need.
Make that sentence (after a short purpose statement if the format calls for one) the opening of the message, and echo it in the subject line or title.
Add only the background the reader needs to act on it, most important first, and move history and method to the end or an attachment.
Put any secondary requests or audiences in clearly labelled sections below the main point.
Reread only the first two lines and ask whether a busy reader could act on them alone; if not, rewrite them.
Decide deliberately whether this message is an exception - serious bad news or a reader who expects context first - and if so use an indirect structure on purpose rather than by habit.

example.situation: A project analyst emails her director about a vendor problem that needs a decision.
example.before: Hi Sam, I wanted to give you some background on the reporting vendor. Over the last two months we have seen several late deliveries, and after a call with their account team on Tuesday it looks like their new platform will not support our quarterly export. I have looked at a few options...
example.after: Subject: Decision needed by Thursday - switch reporting vendor for Q1. Sam, I recommend we move the Q1 reports to our backup vendor; it adds about two weeks of setup but keeps the March board deadline. Please approve or decline by Thursday. Background: our current vendor's new platform cannot produce the quarterly export (confirmed on Tuesday's call), and deliveries have been late twice since September.
example.why: The recommendation, the decision asked for and the deadline appear in the subject line and first two sentences, so the director can act without reading the history, which is still there for anyone who wants it.

title: Brainstorming
summary: A group idea-generation method, introduced by advertising executive Alex Osborn, in which people produce as many ideas as possible on one question while deferring criticism; research shows the classic talk-it-out version yields fewer ideas than the same people working alone, so effective practice mixes solo or written idea generation with group building and later evaluation.
selfCheck: Did everyone generate ideas on their own before hearing anyone else's?
Could more than one person contribute at the same moment, or did ideas wait in a speaking queue?
Did I keep evaluation - including my own reactions - out of the generation phase?
Did I separate choosing ideas from producing them, with criteria agreed in advance?
steps: Frame one specific question in writing before the session, for example "What could cut our customer onboarding time from ten days to five?", and send it to participants a day ahead.
Open with five to ten minutes of silent, individual writing so everyone lists their own ideas before hearing anyone else's.
Pool the ideas in writing - sticky notes, a shared doc or passed cards - rather than having people call them out one at a time.
Give the group a short review round to read the pooled list and build on, combine or extend others' ideas, then send people back for another brief solo round.
State and enforce the ground rules - aim for quantity, welcome unusual ideas, build on others, and hold all criticism until the generation phase is over.
Evaluate and shortlist in a separate step - ideally after a break - using agreed criteria and a private or simultaneous vote.

example.situation: A product manager gathers seven colleagues, including a vice president, for an hour to find ways to reduce customer churn.
example.before: Let's just throw ideas out - no bad ideas! ... [VP] I think it's pricing. ... Good point. Anyone want to build on pricing?
example.after: Spend eight minutes writing every churn idea you can, one per sticky note. We'll post them all, read them silently, add new notes that build on what you see, and only then cluster and vote with dots.
example.why: Calling ideas out lets only one person speak at a time and lets the most senior voice anchor the room; writing first and pooling in parallel removes the queue and gets every person's ideas on the wall before status shapes the discussion.

title: Bulleted and numbered lists
summary: Setting a series of parallel items, requirements or steps on separate lines under a lead-in sentence, with numbers when order matters and bullets when it does not, so readers can find, remember and act on each item.
selfCheck: Does my list have a lead-in that tells the reader what the items are and what to do with them?
Do all items start with the same kind of word, and does each one read correctly after the lead-in?
Have I used numbers only where order or reference matters?
Did turning prose into bullets strip out a reason, condition or caveat the reader needs to judge the point?
steps: Spot any sentence or paragraph that strings together three or more requirements, options, conditions or steps.
Write a lead-in sentence that says what the list is and who must do what with it.
Put each item on its own line, starting every item with the same grammatical form (all verbs, or all nouns) so each one completes the lead-in.
Number the items if the order matters or readers will refer back to them; otherwise use plain round or square bullets.
Keep the list short, roughly six to eight items at most, and split or group longer lists under subheadings.
Keep reasons, caveats and trade-offs in sentences around the list rather than shrinking them into fragments inside it.

example.situation: An operations lead emails twelve site managers about what they must send before a system migration.
example.before: Ahead of the migration on the 14th, we will need you to confirm your local admin contacts, and also it would help to have the inventory spreadsheet updated, plus please make sure any scheduled jobs are paused and the backup report is sent to IT by the 12th.
example.after: By Thursday the 12th, please send IT these four items so your site can migrate on the 14th: 1. Your local admin contacts. 2. The updated inventory spreadsheet. 3. Confirmation that scheduled jobs are paused. 4. Last week's backup report.
example.why: The lead-in states the deadline and purpose, the numbers let managers reply "done 1-3, 4 by Friday", and no request is lost in the middle of a long sentence.

title: Burying the lede
summary: Placing the most important point of a message - the decision, request, risk or news - after background, history or lesser details, so readers who skim or stop early miss it or misread what the message is about.
selfCheck: If my reader stopped after the first two sentences, would they know what I need, by when, and why it matters?
Is anything in my opening paragraph there only because it happened first, rather than because the reader needs it first?
Does my subject line or first slide name the decision, risk or news itself, not just the topic?
If I am delivering bad news, have I stated it plainly before the explanation instead of after it?

example.situation: An engineering manager emails a vice president after a vendor slip and needs a go/no-go decision on paying for weekend overtime by Wednesday noon.
example.before: Hi Sam, quick update on the payments integration. As you know we kicked off with the vendor in July and the first two milestones went well. Over the last few weeks we have been working through some API changes on their side, and the team has done a great job adapting. Last Thursday the vendor told us their sandbox will be down until the 18th. We looked at a few options, including stubbing the service, and think weekend overtime is the most realistic way to protect the launch date, which would cost about $9K. Let me know what you think.
example.after:
Subject: Decision by Wed noon - approve $9K overtime to keep the 1 Dec launch?

Sam, I need a yes/no by Wednesday noon on about $9K of weekend overtime. Without it, the 1 December launch slips about two weeks.

Why: the vendor's sandbox is down until the 18th, which removes our last test window.
Option we rejected: stubbing the service - faster to build, but it leaves the riskiest calls untested.

Background on the integration is below if useful.
example.why: In the original the cost, the decision and the deadline arrive in the last two sentences and the deadline is never stated, so a reader skimming the opening reads it as a routine progress note; the rewrite states the decision, amount, deadline and consequence in the subject line and first sentence and moves the history to the end.

title: Business report
summary: A document, usually longer than a page and shorter than a book, that records findings for a specific audience and purpose: informational reports present facts without judgement, while analytical reports add analysis and recommendations. Effective reports are built for selective reading, with the main messages and recommendations up front and the detail layered behind them.

title: Camera-level gaze on video calls
summary: Setting up your webcam and screen so that your gaze reads as eye contact on a video call, by raising the camera to eye level, placing the other person's video just below the lens, and looking into the lens at the moments that matter most.
selfCheck: Is my camera at or slightly above eye level, and is the other person's window right under it?
When I made my main point or my request, was I looking into the lens?
Was I watching the other person's face while they spoke, rather than my own self-view or another screen?
Am I forcing myself to stare at the lens so hard that I am losing track of what people are saying?
steps: Raise the camera to your eye level or slightly above, propping a laptop on books if you need to.
Sit about an arm's length back so you are framed from the chest up with your eyes roughly a third of the way down the frame.
Drag the video window of the person you are talking to up to the top centre of your screen, directly under the lens, rather than off to one side.
Look into the lens when you state your main point, make a request or ask a question, using a small sticker beside the lens as a reminder.
While the other person is talking, watch their face in the window under the lens so you can read their reaction.
If you need to glance at notes, keep them just below the camera so you look down briefly rather than sideways.

example.situation: A project manager presents a schedule change to a client on a video call.
example.before: The laptop sits flat on the desk, the client's video is on a second monitor to the right, and the manager reads from notes on that monitor; the client sees someone looking down and away while asking for a two-week extension.
example.after: The laptop is raised to eye level, the client's window sits just under the lens with brief notes beneath it, and the manager looks into the lens to say: we need two more weeks, and here is what you get for it. Then the manager watches the client's face while the client responds.
example.why: Gaze below the lens is barely noticed while sideways gaze reads as looking away, and looking into the camera makes a speaker seem more sociable, so the request lands as direct and attentive.

title: Camera-optional norm
summary: An explicit team agreement that webcams are a choice rather than a requirement in video meetings, set per meeting type and modelled by the person running the meeting, so people can rest from being on camera without being judged for it.
selfCheck: Have I said out loud, or written in the invite, whether cameras are expected in this meeting and why?
Would a new team member feel safe turning their camera off here, and have I told them so?
Am I modelling the norm, or does my own always-on camera quietly signal that video is required?
When cameras are off, do I still give everyone a clear way to contribute?
steps: List your recurring video meetings and decide for each whether faces add value - small working sessions, sensitive one-to-ones and first meetings with new people usually benefit; large updates, webinars and long all-hands rarely do.
Agree the camera expectation for each meeting type with the team, write it in the invite or team charter, and say plainly that cameras-off is fine wherever video is not needed.
Tell newer colleagues directly, in person or one-to-one, that turning the camera off will not count against them.
Model it as the organiser - switch your own camera off for part of a long meeting or for audio-only segments, because people follow what they see others doing.
Keep participation visible without video - ask people by name, use chat, reactions or a shared document, and agree that cameras-off still means no multitasking.
When video is used, suggest hiding self-view once framing is set, and build in short audio-only breaks in meetings longer than about 45 minutes.

example.situation: A team lead runs a daily 30-minute stand-up and two weekly hour-long planning calls for eight people, several of whom joined in the last three months.
example.before: Invite text - 'Cameras on please, it helps us stay connected.' The lead keeps a full gallery view, comments when a tile is dark, and the newest analysts never switch off even on their fourth call of the day.
example.after: Team charter line - 'Stand-up: cameras optional. Planning: cameras on for the first 10 minutes of check-in, optional after. 1:1s: your call.' The lead turns their own camera off after the check-in, calls on people by name, and tells new joiners in their first 1:1 that cameras-off is normal here.
example.why: The expectation is explicit and tied to the purpose of each meeting, the lead's behaviour shows the norm is real, and the people under the most self-presentation pressure hear it said to them directly, while the check-in keeps the group connection that buffers fatigue.

title: Carl Hovland
summary: Yale psychologist (1912-1961) who led the Army's wartime film-evaluation experiments and then the Yale Communication and Attitude Change Program, which turned persuasion into an experimental science and gave communicators the modern idea of source credibility (expertise plus trustworthiness) and the sleeper effect.

title: Channel selection
summary: Deliberately choosing the medium for a message - in person, video, phone, chat, email or a document - according to whether the job is to transmit information or to build shared understanding, how much tone and feedback matter, and what the receiver needs to do with it.
selfCheck: Am I mainly passing information on, or do we need to reach agreement - and does my channel fit that job?
If my reader misread the tone of this text, what is the worst plausible interpretation, and would a call prevent it?
Am I choosing email or chat because it suits the message, or because it lets me avoid an awkward conversation?
After a live discussion, have I put the decision, owners and dates in writing?
steps: Name the job of the message in one line - is it mainly to pass on information the receiver can absorb alone (conveyance), or to agree on meaning, resolve disagreement or decide something together (convergence)?
For conveyance - updates, data, instructions, reference material - default to a written, asynchronous channel the receiver can reread and process in their own time.

For convergence - an ambiguous problem, a disagreement, a sensitive or emotional message, or a request you need someone to say yes to - default to a live channel with voice and fast feedback, such as a call, video or a face-to-face conversation.

If tone, sarcasm or humour carries part of the meaning, either move to voice or rewrite the text so the meaning survives without your tone of voice; read it aloud in a deliberately flat or opposite tone before sending.
Combine channels when the task needs both - send the facts in writing first, discuss live, then confirm the decision and owners in writing.
Check the receiver's side - their familiarity with you and the topic, time zone, norms and access - and adjust the default; a lean channel works better between people who already share context.

example.situation: A project manager needs a client's sign-off to cut a feature so the release can stay on date, and the client sponsor is known to be attached to that feature.
example.before: Email, sent at 6 pm - Subject: Scope change. Hi Priya, given the integration issues we will need to drop the reporting module from the March release. Let me know if that works. Thanks.
example.after: Short email first - Subject: Decision needed Thursday - reporting module vs. March date. Priya, I'd like 20 minutes Wednesday to talk through a trade-off: keep the March date by moving the reporting module to April, or keep the module and slip to mid-April. One-page options summary attached. Then a 20-minute call to discuss, followed the same day by a written recap of the decision, owner and new dates.
example.why: The facts travel in writing where they can be reread, the contested decision happens live where questions and concerns surface immediately, and the written recap locks in the shared understanding the call produced.

title: Charismatic leadership tactics
summary: A trainable set of nine verbal tactics (metaphors, stories, contrasts, three-part lists, rhetorical questions, moral conviction, shared sentiment, high expectations and expressed confidence) and three nonverbal ones (gestures, facial expression, animated voice) that make a speaker's message more vivid and are rated by listeners as more charismatic and leader-like.
selfCheck: Is every story, number and promise in my message true and something I would stand behind afterwards?
Did I use the tactics to clarify a substantive point, or did they replace one?
If I watched a recording of this, would the gestures and metaphors look natural or like self-parody?
Is this message going out by video or email, where the evidence for these tactics is weakest, and should I also send a clear written summary?
Have I followed the vision with the operational detail - who does what by when?
steps: Write the one decision or goal your talk is about, and check that you believe it and can back it with facts.
Frame it with a contrast (what we will do and not do, or where we are versus where we are going) and a three-part list of reasons or steps.
Add one short, true story or anecdote and at most one metaphor that makes the abstract point concrete.
State the shared stake and the values involved, set a high but credible expectation, and say plainly that you are confident the group can meet it.
Use one rhetorical question to bring the audience into the problem, then answer it.
Rehearse aloud on video with open gestures, varied facial expression and an animated voice; count the tactics you used and cut any that sound forced.
Get feedback from a colleague on whether it sounded like you, and repeat over several weeks rather than cramming before one talk.

example.situation: A team lead tells her group, at an all-hands, that the release date is moving up by three weeks.
example.before: So, leadership has asked us to pull the release forward to the 3rd. I know it's tight. Please update your estimates and let me know about any blockers.
example.after: We can keep shipping late fixes, or we can ship the thing customers keep asking for three weeks sooner - I'd rather we did the second. Last month a client told me she'd delayed her own launch waiting on us. Three things make this doable: the test suite is green, scope is frozen, and the platform team is lending us two engineers. It's a stretch, and I'm confident this team can do it. What would you need from me to make the 3rd?
example.why: The second version uses a contrast, a short true story, a three-part list, shared stakes, a high expectation, expressed confidence and a question - the same facts, but listeners can see why it matters and that the leader believes in it.

title: Charles E. Osgood
summary: University of Illinois social psychologist who devised the semantic differential for measuring what words mean to people and, in his 1962 book An Alternative to War or Surrender, proposed GRIT - small, announced, reversible conciliatory steps that invite reciprocation - an early model of graduated concession making.

title: Chat etiquette
summary: A small set of shared habits for workplace chat tools such as Slack or Teams - complete self-contained messages, threads, sparing use of group alerts, honest status, and explicit response expectations - that keep chat fast without turning it into a stream of interruptions.
selfCheck: Could the recipient act on this message without asking me a single follow-up question?
Does this belong in a shared channel or thread rather than a direct message?
Am I about to alert more people than actually need to see this right now?
Have I said when I need a reply, and that it can wait if it can?
steps: Put the whole request in one message - who it is for, what you need, the context or link, and by when - instead of sending "hi" and waiting for a reply.
Choose the place deliberately - a team or project channel for work others may need to find later, a direct message only for genuinely private or one-person matters.
Reply in the thread of the original post so the discussion stays together and the main channel stays readable.
Mention a named person only when you need that person, and reserve channel-wide alerts such as @channel or @here for urgent items the team has agreed qualify.
Keep your status honest - set away, focus or out-of-office, and set notification hours - and respect other people's status rather than pinging through it.
Say how soon you need an answer, and state plainly that nobody is expected to reply outside their working hours.
Move to a call when a thread passes a few back-and-forths without agreement or the topic turns sensitive, then post the outcome back in the thread.

example.situation: A product manager needs the data engineer's estimate for a dashboard change before Thursday's planning meeting.
example.before: Direct message at 4:55pm: 'Hey, you around?' - then nothing until the engineer replies 'yes?' twenty minutes later.
example.after: In #dashboards thread: @Priya - could you estimate the effort to add region filters to the sales dashboard (spec linked)? A rough range is fine. Needed by Wed noon for Thursday planning; no need to look tonight.
example.why: The rewrite carries the whole request, the link, the deadline and an explicit no-rush note in one interruption, posts it where teammates can see the answer later, and mentions only the person who must act.

title: Checking understanding
summary: The habit of testing, rather than assuming, that a message was understood as intended - in both directions - by asking for a read-back, a restatement or a next step, restating what you heard before acting on it, and closing the loop on anything that must be exact.
selfCheck: Which one or two details in this exchange would cause real damage if they were misunderstood, and did I check those specifically?
Did I accept a nod, a "makes sense" or a thumbs-up as proof, or did I hear the point back in the other person's words?
Before acting on a request, did I restate what I think was asked and get a "yes, that's it"?
Did I invite questions with an open phrase that assumes they exist, rather than a yes/no "any questions"?
For anything sent in writing, did I ask for a reply that shows understanding, not just receipt?

title: Leveraging the Asymmetric Sensitivity of Eye Contact for Videoconferencing
summary: Milton Chen's 2002 CHI paper reporting that viewers barely notice when someone on video looks slightly below their eyes, and turning that finding into the design rule of placing the camera just above the other person's on-screen eyes, the basis of today's camera-level gaze advice.

title: Clarity
summary: The quality of a message that lets its intended audience grasp what the sender means, and what (if anything) they are expected to do, quickly, accurately and without having to guess.

title: Client communication
aliases: communication with clients in professional services
summary: The ongoing exchange between a professional (consultant, adviser, agency, lawyer, internal service team) and the client who pays for or depends on their work. Because clients often cannot judge the quality of expert work directly, how expectations are set and how progress, problems and results are explained shapes satisfaction, trust and whether the relationship lasts.

title: Closed-loop communication
summary: A three-part exchange for messages that must be exact: the sender directs a call-out to a named person, the receiver repeats back what they heard, and the sender confirms it is correct or fixes it - and, for tasks, the receiver reports back when the action is done.
selfCheck: Which details in this message would cause damage if misheard, and did I hear each one repeated back?
Did I direct the instruction to one named person, or did I say it to the room?
When I heard the repeat-back, did I actually confirm or correct it, or did I let the loop stay open?
Was my call-out short enough to repeat accurately, or did I pack in several topics at once?
For a task, do I know it is done because someone told me, or because I assumed it?
steps: Decide which messages need a closed loop - instructions, numbers, names, deadlines or decisions where a mishearing would cause real harm - and use the full exchange only for those.
Address one named person ("Priya, ...") so someone owns the message, and keep each call-out short, with one to three items.
Ask the receiver to repeat back the critical details in full (the figure, the identifier, the deadline), not just "got it".
Listen to the repeat-back and close the loop out loud - "Correct" - or correct the wrong part and hear it repeated again.
For tasks, agree that the receiver reports back when the action is done ("Rollback complete"), so the sender is not left assuming.
In email or chat, ask for a reply that restates the key detail or next step, and confirm or correct it in the thread.

example.situation: During a production-incident video call, an incident lead asks an on-call engineer to roll back a recent release while four other people are talking.
example.before: Lead - 'Can someone roll back payments?' Engineer - 'On it.' (Twenty minutes later the team finds the engineer rolled back the wrong region, and the lead had assumed it was finished.)
example.after: Lead - 'Sam, roll back payments-api in us-east to version 4.2.' Sam - 'Rolling back payments-api, us-east, to 4.2.' Lead - 'Correct.' ... Sam - 'Rollback of payments-api us-east to 4.2 is complete.' Lead - 'Thanks, noted.'
example.why: Naming one owner removes the "someone" ambiguity, the repeat-back exposes a wrong region or version before anyone acts, and the completion report replaces an assumption with a fact the lead can log.

title: Coaching
summary: The learnable skill of helping someone improve their own performance mainly by asking, listening and supporting rather than telling - drawing out their goal, view of the situation, options and commitment, and adding your own expertise only when it helps. Meta-analyses find moderate positive effects of workplace coaching, though most studies are small and rely on self-report.
selfCheck: Did I ask what they had already thought of before offering my own answer?
Had I decided the answer in advance and then steered them towards it with leading questions?
Who did most of the talking - and who owns the next step now, me or them?
Was this a moment for coaching at all, or did they simply need information, a decision or to be left alone?

title: Cognitive bias
summary: A systematic, predictable error in judgment that comes from the mental shortcuts (heuristics) people use to estimate, interpret and decide quickly; in communication, biases shape what we assume others know, how we read their messages and which evidence we notice.

title: Cognitive load theory
summary: John Sweller's theory that new information must pass through a small, short-lived working memory, so a message is understood best when its design removes avoidable mental effort (extraneous load) and leaves room for the genuine complexity of the content (intrinsic load).

title: Common ground and grounding theory
summary: Herbert Clark's account of conversation as joint action: people communicate by drawing on common ground (the knowledge, beliefs and assumptions they mutually take to be shared) and by grounding, the collaborative work of presenting a message and getting evidence it was understood well enough for the current purpose.

title: Communicating across languages
summary: Adjusting how you speak and write when colleagues are working in their second or third language: slower, clearer delivery, fewer idioms and phrasal verbs, consistent plain terms, regular comprehension checks and deliberate sharing of airtime, so that meaning and trust survive a shared working language that is not everyone's first.
selfCheck: Did I use any idiom, sports metaphor or phrasal verb that a careful second-language speaker could take literally?
Did I check understanding by asking someone to restate the point, or only ask whether it was clear?
Who spoke least in that conversation, and was that because of their ideas or their fluency?
Have I put the key numbers, dates and decisions in writing as well as saying them?
steps: Before the meeting or message, find out which participants are working in a second language and how fluent they are, rather than guessing from accent or job title.
Speak a little slower than feels natural, articulate word endings and pause between ideas; do not raise your volume.
Swap idioms, sports metaphors, slang and phrasal verbs for plain single words ("cancel", not "call off"; "start", not "kick off").
Pick one term for each key thing and keep using it, spell out acronyms on first use, and put numbers, dates and decisions in writing as well as saying them.
Check understanding by inviting people to restate the next step or decision in their own words, not by asking "Does that make sense?".
Manage airtime - leave pauses after questions, invite quieter second-language speakers by name or in the chat, and judge contributions on substance rather than fluency.
For important written content, test it with a reader who has limited English or run it through a translation tool and back to spot phrases that break.

example.situation: A UK-based project lead updates a video call of engineers in Brazil, Poland and Japan about a vendor delay.
example.before: Quick heads-up - the vendor's dropped the ball again, so we'll have to push back the go-live and play it by ear. Let's touch base Thursday and circle back once we've ironed out the kinks. Make sense?
example.after: The vendor delivered the test server late. So we will move the launch from 3 March to 17 March. I will put both dates in the chat. On Thursday we will meet again to fix the remaining problems. Ana, could you say back what changes for your team?
example.why: The rewrite removes five idioms and phrasal verbs, states the new date in writing, uses short active sentences, and replaces a yes/no check with a restatement that would expose any misunderstanding.

title: Communicating uncertainty to decision makers
aliases: conveying what is and is not known
summary: The skill of telling the people who must decide what you know, how precisely you know it, how solid the evidence is and what you are doing to learn more - stated as specifically as your knowledge allows rather than hidden, hedged into vagueness or inflated into false certainty.
selfCheck: Have I given a number or range where I have one, instead of a word like "probably" or "should be fine"?
Have I said separately how good the evidence behind my estimate is?
Have I told them what we do not yet know, what we are doing to find out and when we will know?
Am I presenting real disagreement among experts or data as such, rather than smoothing it over or overplaying it?
Is the uncertainty in the sentence that carries the estimate, not in a footnote or a later slide?

example.situation: A product lead tells the leadership team how many customers a pricing change will cost.
example.before: Churn should be fine - we don't expect much impact, though obviously nobody can be sure.
example.after: Our best estimate is that 3% of accounts cancel in the first quarter, with a plausible range of 1-6%. The estimate rests on a four-week pilot in one region, so confidence is moderate. We will know much more after the second region's renewals on 15 March; until then I'd budget for 6%.
example.why: The before version mixes false reassurance with a blanket hedge, so leaders can neither plan nor challenge it; the after version gives a point estimate, a range, the quality of the evidence and when it will improve, which is what a decision needs.

title: Communication apprehension
summary: The fear or anxiety a person feels about real or expected communication with others - in one-to-one talk, group discussions, meetings or public speaking - which leads many people to stay quiet, avoid speaking roles and under-contribute, even when they have something worth saying.
selfCheck: Am I staying quiet because I have nothing to add, or because speaking up here makes me anxious?
Which setting is hardest for me - one-to-one, group discussion, meetings or presenting - and am I quietly steering my work away from it?
What is the one point I will say in this meeting, and have I said it out loud beforehand?
Is someone on my team silent because they disagree or lack input, or because the format itself is hard for them?
Have I given quieter colleagues a written or small-group route to contribute, not only the open floor?

title: Communication competence
summary: The degree to which your communication is judged both appropriate (it fits the norms and relationship of the situation) and effective (it achieves what you set out to do). It rests on motivation, knowledge and skill, and it is an impression held by others in a context rather than a trait you own once and for all.
selfCheck: In this conversation, what exactly counts as effective for me, and what would the other person count as appropriate?
If I get my outcome, will I have damaged the relationship or broken a norm that matters to them?
Is my problem here motivation (I am avoiding it), knowledge (I do not know what fits) or skill (I know but cannot yet do it)?
Whose view of how this went have I actually asked for, beyond my own?

title: Communication studies
summary: The academic discipline that studies how people use messages to create meaning across contexts, forms and media, drawing on both humanistic and social-scientific methods; it grew from the teaching of rhetoric and public speaking into a broad field whose subfields include interpersonal, organizational, intercultural and digital communication.

title: Concession strategy
summary: Deciding in advance how much you will give up in a negotiation, in what size steps, at what pace and in exchange for what - then labelling each move and asking for something in return rather than conceding one-sidedly.
selfCheck: Do I know my total concession budget and walk-away point before I make the first move?
For the concession I am about to make, what exactly am I asking for in return?
Have I said clearly what this move costs me, without exaggerating it?
Are my steps getting smaller as I get closer to my limit, or am I making one big jump under pressure?
Have I acknowledged and reciprocated the concessions the other side has already made?
steps: Before the meeting, write down your opening position, your target and your walk-away point, and the total amount you are prepared to concede between them.
List what you want back for each possible concession - a longer term, faster payment, a reference, reduced scope - so you never give without a matching ask ready.
Plan the moves as a sequence of real steps that get smaller as you approach your limit, rather than one large jump, and hold some of the concession budget back.
When you concede, name it - say what it costs you and what it gives them - and state exactly what you need in return, or make it explicitly conditional ("we can do X if you can do Y").
Answer the other side's concessions in kind and on time; acknowledge them and move a proportionate amount, rather than pocketing them in silence.
Keep every statement about your costs and limits true; stop conceding when the next step would cross your walk-away point.

example.situation: A software vendor's account manager is renewing a contract with a client who has asked for a 15% discount.
example.before: OK, we can do 15% off. Hopefully that works for your budget - shall I send the paperwork?
example.after: I can't get to 15%, but I can offer 6% off the renewal, which comes out of our services margin. To make that work, we'd need a two-year term instead of one. If the two-year term is a problem, tell me what matters most and we can look at the payment schedule instead.
example.why: The first reply gives away the whole concession budget at once, labels nothing and asks for nothing, so the client learns the price was soft and has no reason to give back. The second makes a smaller, named move tied to a specific return, leaves room for later steps, and invites the client to reveal what they value.

title: Concise writing
summary: The skill of saying what the reader needs in the fewest strong words, by cutting words, sentences and whole ideas that do not help that reader understand or act.
selfCheck: If my reader stopped after the first two sentences, would they know what I need and by when?
Which sentence, paragraph or side point could I delete without the reader losing anything they need to act?
Did my last edit make this shorter, or did I only add caveats and background?
Have I cut so far that a reader new to the topic would now be missing context or find the tone curt?

title: Conflict resolution
summary: The multidisciplinary field of research and practice that studies how disputes between people, groups and organizations can be conducted constructively, with less antagonism and with outcomes the parties can accept; it took shape in the 1950s and 1960s and grew into mediation, negotiation and alternative dispute resolution practice.

title: Considering others' contributions first
summary: Before judging or describing your own share of a team's work, deliberately listing each collaborator and what they did, which curbs the habit of over-claiming credit that comes from remembering your own work best.
selfCheck: Before I describe what I did on this project, have I named everyone else and what they did?
If each person on the team wrote down their share, would our numbers add up to more than 100%?
Whose work am I least likely to remember because it happened out of my sight?
If the list shows I carried more than others, am I raising the workload split for next time instead of keeping score?
steps: Before anyone states or estimates their own share of a piece of team work, write down the name of every person who contributed, including people outside the core team.
Next to each name, note one or two concrete things that person did, such as drafts written, analysis run, approvals chased or customers handled.
Only after the list is done, write your own contributions in the same concrete terms and estimate your share.
If people give percentages, add them up; a total well above 100% is a signal that someone's work is being overlooked, not that someone is lying.
In large teams, split the review by sub-team or workstream and make assignments explicit, so each person has fewer colleagues' contributions to recall.
When the list shows an uneven split, talk about how work will be divided next time rather than letting the person who carried more quietly resent it.

example.situation: A project lead is drafting the end-of-quarter update to a director about a launch that five people worked on.
example.before: I drove the launch end to end: I built the rollout plan, fixed the pricing page and got legal sign-off. Shipped on time.
example.after: The launch shipped on time. Ana built the analytics dashboard, Raj rewrote the pricing page, Mei ran the legal review, and Tom handled the support handoff. I owned the rollout plan and coordinated the go/no-go calls.
example.why: Listing colleagues first surfaces work the lead had half forgotten, gives the director an accurate picture of who to recognise, and still states the lead's real role plainly.

title: Conversational narcissism
summary: The habit of repeatedly steering a conversation back to yourself - your experiences, opinions and achievements - instead of following the other person's topic; studies find partners rate self-focused talkers as less socially attractive, sincere and likeable.
selfCheck: In the last conversation, how many of my replies kept the focus on the other person, and how many moved it to me?
When someone shared a problem, did I tell a story about my similar experience before asking anything about theirs?
Did I ask a question only so that I could give my own answer to it?
Can I name one specific thing the other person said that I followed up on?

example.situation: In a Monday one-on-one, a team member tells her manager that the client workshop on Friday went badly because the client's finance lead challenged every number.
example.before: Manager: 'Oh, finance people always do that. When I ran the Henley account I had a CFO who tore apart my whole deck - I ended up rebuilding it overnight and we still won the renewal. Anyway, what's next on your list?'
example.after: Manager: 'That sounds draining. Which numbers did he push on, and was it the figures themselves or how we got to them?' [listens] 'So the cost baseline is the sticking point. What would help you go back in with it?'
example.why: The first reply is a shift response - it takes her topic and turns it into the manager's war story, then closes the subject, so he learns nothing about the problem. The second is a support response that keeps her at the centre and uses follow-up questions, which surfaces the real issue and leaves her feeling heard.

title: Conversational receptiveness
summary: Using specific word choices - hedging, naming agreement, acknowledging the other view and phrasing things positively - to show a person who disagrees with you that you are willing to engage thoughtfully with their view, without giving up your own.
selfCheck: Could the other person read my opening line and recognise their own view in it?
Have I named anything we agree on, even just the goal?
How many times did I write "no", "not", "can't" or "the reason is" - and could any become a positive proposal?
Am I hedging where I am genuinely unsure, or only to sound agreeable?
Would I mean every acknowledgement if they asked me to expand on it?
steps: Before replying to someone you disagree with, restate their main point in a sentence of your own and check it is one they would accept.
Open by acknowledging that view explicitly ("So your concern is...", "I understand that you see...").
Name at least one real point of agreement or shared goal before you give your own position.
Hedge your claims where you are genuinely less than certain ("I think", "it's possible that", "in my experience").
Replace flat negations and "no, because" rebuttals with positive, forward-looking phrasing about what you would do instead.
Reread the message and cut any line that only proves the other person wrong without moving the work forward.

example.situation: In a project channel, an operations lead argues that a new release should be delayed two weeks for more testing; the product manager thinks the release should ship on schedule.
example.before: No, delaying makes no sense. The reason is that the testing we've done is enough, and two weeks costs us the launch window. We can't keep moving dates.
example.after: So your worry is that we haven't tested the failover path enough to be safe in production - I understand that, and I agree we can't ship something that pages on-call every night. I think it's possible we can cover that risk without losing the launch window: what if we run the failover test this week and hold the go/no-go on Friday based on what it shows?
example.why: The rewrite acknowledges the other view, names the shared goal, hedges the claim and frames a positive next step, replacing the negations and "the reason is" rebuttal that research found readers judged harshly - the position is unchanged, but the other person is far more likely to engage with it.

title: Conversational turn-taking
summary: The near-universal way people in conversation pass the floor back and forth, mostly one speaker at a time, with brief overlaps and gaps of roughly a fifth of a second, governed by implicit rules about who speaks next and when a turn can end.

title: Cooling-off period
summary: Deliberately putting time between a provoking message or moment and your reply or decision, and spending that time on something other than replaying the grievance, so that you respond from a calmer state than the one the provocation put you in.
selfCheck: Would I be comfortable with this reply being forwarded to my manager and read tomorrow morning?
Am I replying now because the situation needs it, or because my anger wants it?
During the pause, was I distracting myself or replaying the grievance over and over?
Did I tell the other person when they will hear back, so the delay doesn't read as silence or avoidance?
steps: Notice the trigger - a racing pulse, clenched jaw, or an urge to reply right now - and rate your anger from 1 to 10.
Say or send a short holding line ("Thanks, I want to give this proper thought and will reply by 3 pm") instead of your full reaction.
If you must write, draft the reply with the recipient field empty, or save it unsent.
Spend the gap on an unrelated task, a walk or other work, not on rereading the message or rehearsing comebacks to colleagues.
Before you return, ask what outcome you actually want from this exchange and what the other person may have meant.
Come back when your rating has dropped to a 3 or 4, reread the original and your draft, then cut anything written to wound and send or say the considered version.

example.situation: A project lead gets a terse message from a peer in another department, copied to both their managers, saying her team "missed the handover again" when the delay was caused by the peer's late inputs.
example.before: Reply-all within two minutes: 'For the record, we only missed it because YOUR team sent the data three days late, as usual. Maybe check your own process before blaming mine.'
example.after: Reply to the peer only: 'Got it - I'll come back to you by 2 pm.' After lunch and an hour on other work: 'Hi Sam, I want to fix the handover too. On our side, we received the inputs on Tuesday rather than Friday, which pushed us back. Could we agree a cut-off date for inputs and a quick check-in the day before? Happy to talk it through.'
example.why: The holding line meets the need to respond without committing to a hot-state reply, and the delay spent on other work let the anger fade, so the final message fixes the process instead of starting a public feud in front of both managers.

title: Credibility
summary: The audience's judgement of whether a speaker or writer is worth believing, usually broken into perceived competence, trustworthiness and goodwill; it belongs to the listener's perception, not the speaker, and it shapes how much the same message persuades.
selfCheck: If I asked two trusted colleagues how credible I am on this topic, would their answer match mine?
Does this audience doubt my expertise, my motives, or whether I care about their interests, and which one am I addressing?
Where I lack a track record, have I borrowed one through data, a pilot or a respected expert?
Have I met the key people one-on-one to listen before asking them for anything?
Am I stating limits and uncertainty plainly, or overselling in a way that will cost me trust later?

title: Cultural intelligence
summary: The capability to function and communicate effectively in culturally diverse settings, usually described as four linked capabilities: motivation (drive), knowledge, metacognitive strategy and behavioural flexibility. At work it shows up as noticing when a colleague's norms differ from yours, checking your assumptions, and adapting how you speak, write and decide without losing your purpose.
selfCheck: Before this conversation, have I asked myself which of my assumptions about directness, hierarchy or timing might not be shared?
Did I check my reading of their reaction (a silence, a "maybe", a blunt reply) with a question instead of judging it?
Did I adapt something concrete, such as pace, wording, the channel or who speaks first, rather than only intending to be sensitive?
After the exchange, what did I learn about this person or group that I should test next time instead of generalising?

title: Culture assimilator
summary: A self-paced training method built from short, real critical incidents of cross-cultural misunderstanding: for each one the learner picks the most likely explanation from several options and gets feedback on why each is right or wrong, so they learn to interpret colleagues' behaviour the way people from that culture would.
selfCheck: When a colleague's behaviour surprised me, did I list more than one explanation before settling on mine?
Would someone from their culture pick the same explanation I picked?
Is the lesson I took from an incident a tested hypothesis about this team or a stereotype about a whole country?
steps: Collect real incidents from people who have worked across the two cultures, choosing moments that surprised, annoyed or confused someone.
Write each incident as a short scene that describes who did what and how people reacted, without giving the reason.
Draft three or four plausible explanations for each scene, including the ones your own culture would reach for first.
Ask colleagues from the other culture which explanation best fits, and keep only incidents where they broadly agree.
Write feedback for every option that explains why it is or is not likely, naming the underlying norm or value.
Have learners work through the incidents alone or in pairs, then debrief what surprised them and test the lessons in real exchanges.

example.situation: A project manager onboarding to a supplier team in another country after a tense first week.
example.before: Their engineers never push back in our calls, then miss dates. I'll tell them plainly that silence means agreement and they need to speak up.
example.after: I worked through the team's incident pack. One scene matched ours: silence in a group call often signals a problem the speaker can't raise in front of seniors. I'll ask for risks in writing before each call and check in one-to-one.
example.why: The manager swapped a first-instinct explanation (they are passive or careless) for one locals would give, and changed the channel to fit it instead of lecturing the team.

title: Curse of knowledge
summary: The difficulty of imagining what it is like not to know something you know, which leads informed people to overestimate what their audience already understands and to communicate in shorthand, abstractions and skipped steps.
selfCheck: Which terms, acronyms or steps in this message did I learn on the job rather than expect my reader to know?
If my reader had only this message and none of my background, what would they do next?
Have I asked someone outside the work to restate my point in their own words, or am I only judging clarity myself?

title: David Maister
summary: London-born management adviser and former Harvard Business School professor (born 1947) whose books on professional service firms, from Managing the Professional Service Firm (1993) to The Trusted Advisor (2000), helped turn client communication - listening, explaining, keeping clients informed and managing expectations - into a practical discipline for consultants, lawyers, accountants and other advisers.

title: De-escalation
summary: Using calm, deliberate talk, listening and body language to bring an agitated or angry person's arousal down so that the conversation can continue safely, without force, threats or humiliation - and recognising when to stop and get help instead.
selfCheck: Is it actually safe to keep talking, or should I be stepping back and calling for help?
Is my own voice slower and quieter than theirs right now?
Have I told them what I heard them want or feel before I explained the rules?
Did I state the limit as a boundary with a choice, or as a threat?
Have I promised anything I can't actually deliver?
steps: Check safety first - yours and others' - and if a threat or hostile act looks imminent, step away and call security or emergency services instead of talking.
Regulate yourself before you speak - slow your breathing, lower your volume and pace, and keep a neutral, attentive face.
Give physical room - stay about two arm's lengths away, do not block the exit, and keep your hands visible, open and low.
Have one person do the talking; introduce yourself and say plainly that you want to help sort it out.
Keep sentences short and simple, and repeat the key message calmly rather than escalating your wording.
Ask what they want and how they feel, listen closely, and name the feeling or need you hear before you explain anything.
Agree with whatever you honestly can (the facts, the principle, that it is frustrating), or agree to disagree.
State any limit matter-of-factly as a boundary on behaviour, not a threat, and offer realistic choices about what happens next.
Afterwards, write down what was said and done factually, report through the proper channel, and debrief with the person and your team.

example.situation: A supplier's account manager arrives unannounced at a reception desk, raising their voice because an invoice is 60 days overdue, and a facilities coordinator is first to respond.
example.before: Sir, you need to calm down right now. Shouting won't get you paid any faster, and if you keep this up I'll have security walk you out.
example.after: I'm Sam, I coordinate this site. Sixty days unpaid is a real problem, and I want to help get it moving. Would you sit with me over here so I can take down the invoice number? I can't change payments myself, but I can get it to someone who can by this afternoon.
example.why: The rewrite drops the command to calm down and the threat, gives a name and a purpose, agrees with the legitimate grievance, offers a choice of setting, and is honest about limits - so the visitor has a face-saving route to lower their voice.

title: De Ira
summary: Seneca the Younger's three-book Latin treatise on anger, addressed to his brother Novatus in the first century AD.
