It treats anger as a judgment the mind can withhold, and its practical advice - wait before acting, check the report before believing it, never punish while angry, review your day each evening - is the oldest well-known statement of the cooling-off period used in workplace conflict today.

title: Deaf effect
aliases: turning a deaf ear to bad news
summary: The tendency of a decision maker - a project owner, sponsor or executive - not to hear, to ignore or to overrule a report of bad news or a risk warning, and to carry on with a failing course of action. It is the receiver-side counterpart of the MUM effect.
selfCheck: When someone last warned me about a project I sponsor, did I change anything - or did I mainly question their credibility or their timing?
Am I dismissing this warning because of what it says, or because of who is saying it and whether I see them as being on my side?
How much does my confidence that "I have this under control" depend on reports from people whose own work would look bad if they disagreed?
Is there a warning I have parked in a follow-up meeting, a procedure or a request for more data, without ever giving the messenger a decision?

title: Death by PowerPoint
summary: A presentation in which dense, bullet-heavy slides take over from the speaker and the argument: the audience reads crowded text while the presenter reads it aloud, and the main point gets lost in fragments, nested bullets and irrelevant detail.
selfCheck: Could someone read only my slide titles and know my conclusion and what I need from them?
Am I planning to read any slide aloud word for word, and if so, why does that text need to be on screen?
Is there any slide with more than about four bullets, or bullets nested more than two levels deep?
Is this material really a document that should be sent and read, rather than a talk that needs slides?

example.situation: A team lead presents a quarterly operations review to the leadership team and needs approval to hire two support engineers.
example.before: Slide title: 'Q3 Support Update'. Nine bullets in 16-point type - 'Ticket volume up', 'New product launch in August', 'Tier 2 backlog', 'Response-time SLA - see appendix', 'Staffing considerations', and four more - which the lead reads aloud line by line before moving to the next identical-looking slide.
example.after: Slide title: 'Missed response-time targets doubled after the August launch - two hires would restore them'. Body: one chart of weekly SLA misses with the launch week marked. The lead explains the chart in their own words, then asks for the hiring decision; the detailed ticket data goes in a one-page handout sent before the meeting.
example.why: The first version leaves leaders to dig the problem and the request out of fragments while competing with the speaker's voice. The second states the conclusion and the ask in the headline, shows the one piece of evidence that proves it, and moves the detail to a document that can be read at the reader's pace.

title: Defensiveness
summary: A self-protective reaction to perceived or anticipated threat in a conversation, in which a person spends energy guarding their image instead of taking in the message - and in which the listener's distorted hearing tends to make the speaker defensive in turn.
selfCheck: Am I about to describe what happened, or to deliver a verdict on the person who did it?
Have I signalled that the outcome is still open, or does my message sound like the decision is already made?
When I felt criticised just now, did I restate their point before I explained or justified myself?
Is the other person reacting to my content, or to a tone of superiority, certainty or hidden agenda they are picking up?

title: Delivering bad news
summary: The recurring situation of telling someone about an outcome that will disappoint, worry or cost them - a cancelled project, a rejected proposal, a missed deadline, a layoff, a price rise. It goes best when the messenger prepares, states the news early and plainly, makes room for the reaction, and ends with what happens next.

title: Describe-analyze-evaluate
summary: A three-step habit for unfamiliar or puzzling behaviour: first describe only what you observed, then list several possible explanations, and only then notice your own evaluation, so that a culture-bound judgement does not masquerade as a fact.
selfCheck: Could someone who disagrees with me still accept my description of what happened as accurate?
Have I written down more than one explanation, including one that would make this behaviour sensible where they come from?
Which of my own norms am I using to judge this, and where did I learn it?
Am I about to give feedback that starts with my verdict instead of what I observed?
steps: When a colleague's behaviour surprises or irritates you, pause before replying and write down only what you saw or heard, in words a camera could confirm.
List at least two or three different explanations for that behaviour, including at least one that would make it reasonable in the other person's context.
Name your own evaluation and its source - what you feel about the behaviour and which norm you are measuring it against.
Check the most important explanation with the person or a cultural informant using a neutral question built on your description.
Only then decide how to respond, and if you give feedback, lead with the description rather than the evaluation.

example.situation: A team lead in a global project notices that a newly transferred engineer never raises objections in design reviews and later sends concerns privately by email.
example.before: You're not engaging in reviews. If you disagree, say it in the room - sending emails afterwards looks like you're going around the team.
example.after: In the last three reviews you didn't comment during the meeting, then emailed me concerns afterwards - and they were good ones. I can think of a few reasons that might happen. How do design disagreements usually get raised on teams you've worked on?
example.why: The first version presents an evaluation ("not engaging", "going around the team") as fact; the second states the observable pattern, admits several possible explanations and asks before judging, so the engineer can explain a norm the lead may not share.

title: Devil's advocacy
summary: A structured way to bring constructive challenge into a group decision by assigning a person or sub-team to critique the leading proposal - its assumptions, evidence and logic - before the group commits. It beats unchallenged expert recommendations in experiments, but role-played dissent is weaker than a colleague who sincerely disagrees.
selfCheck: Did I state the proposal and its key assumptions clearly enough that someone could attack them?
Did everyone know the advocate was playing an assigned role, so the critique was not taken personally?
Did we actually change, test or caveat anything in response to the critique, or just listen and proceed?
Is anyone in the room sincerely unconvinced, and have I given them a real chance to say so?
steps: Write down the leading proposal in one or two sentences, with the key assumptions and evidence it rests on, and share it with the group.
Name the devil's advocate (a person or small sub-team) openly, explain that the role is assigned, and rotate it so it never sticks to one person.
Give the advocate time before the meeting to pick the assumptions most open to challenge and to look for weak evidence, gaps and facts that point elsewhere.
Have the advocate present the critique to the group, and ask the proposal's owner to respond to each point on the merits rather than defend the plan as a whole.
Record which objections change the plan, which need more analysis, and which are answered, then decide, and label any written critique as a devil's-advocate exercise.
Invite anyone who genuinely disagrees to say so in their own name, because sincere dissent is more valuable than the assigned role.

example.situation: A product team of six is about to approve moving its customer-support tool to a new vendor; the head of support proposed it and everyone in the meeting has nodded along.
example.before: Sounds like we're all aligned on the switch. Any objections? No? Great, let's sign the contract this week.
example.after: Before we sign, Priya will play devil's advocate - that's an assigned role, not her personal view. Priya, take the three assumptions you think are weakest and make the best case against the switch on Thursday. Then Sam, as the owner, answers each point, and we decide.
example.why: An open call for objections in a room that already seems agreed rarely surfaces doubts; assigning and labelling the critic role makes challenge expected rather than disloyal, and forces the owner to answer specific weaknesses before the commitment is made.

title: Difficult conversation
summary: A conversation you are tempted to avoid because the topic threatens the relationship, the other person's or your own self-image, or strong feelings on either side - raising a performance problem, disagreeing with a decision, delivering bad news or repairing a falling-out. It goes best when approached as a shared attempt to learn what happened, not a contest over who is right.

title: Digital communication
summary: Communication that travels through networked technology (email, chat, video calls, shared documents) rather than shared physical space, and the research area, usually called computer-mediated communication, that studies how stripping out or reshaping social cues changes what people say, how they relate and how well they understand each other at work.

title: Direct vs. indirect feedback
summary: The contrast between stating criticism plainly, often intensified with "upgraders" such as "totally", and softening it with "downgraders", understatement or omission so the listener infers the problem; norms differ across cultures, but research shows the gap shifts with setting, status and urgency rather than following nationality alone.
selfCheck: If I strip out the softeners or intensifiers, what is the core message I am sending - and would this listener decode it the same way?
Am I about to deliver criticism in front of people who do not need to hear it?
Have I checked what the person understood, rather than assuming my politeness or bluntness landed as intended?

title: Distributive negotiation
summary: Negotiating over how to divide a fixed amount of value, usually a single number such as price, rate or budget, where every unit one side gains the other gives up; done well, it means claiming a fair share through preparation, ambitious but defensible offers and reciprocated concessions rather than bluffs.
selfCheck: Have I checked that there is truly only one issue, or am I treating a multi-issue deal as a single number?
Do I have an estimate of the other side's walk-away point, and what is it based on?
Is every concession I am about to make tied to something the other side gives in return?
Did I just make a second move before they responded to my first?
Could I defend every statement I made about my limits if it were later checked?
steps: Confirm the issue really is fixed-sum - one number with nothing else worth trading - before you treat the talk as a pure split.
Write down your BATNA and reservation value, then improve the BATNA by opening talks with other parties where you can.
Research the counterpart's likely alternatives and walk-away point, and estimate the zone of possible agreement from both bottom lines.
Set a target that is ambitious but defensible, and prepare the market data or reasoning that makes it look reasonable.
If you know the market value well, make the first offer near your target and explain the basis for it.
Concede only in exchange for movement from the other side, name what each concession costs you, and tie it to something specific you get back.
After you make or receive an offer, stop talking and let the other side respond instead of sweetening your own number.
When asked for your bottom line, decline to disclose it rather than inventing a figure, and walk away if the best offer is worse than your BATNA.

example.situation: A team lead is renewing an external contractor whose day rate is the only open term; the contractor has asked for a rise from 600 to 750.
example.before: 750 is a lot more than we budgeted. Could you do 700? Actually, if that's hard, I could probably get approval for 720.
example.after: Thanks for the proposal. Three comparable contractors quoted us between 580 and 640 this quarter, and we're offering a twelve-month term with guaranteed volume. On that basis we can do 630. If you can confirm the full twelve months, I can move to 645 - that's the top of what those quotes justify.
example.why: The first version concedes twice without getting anything back and signals that the budget is soft; the second anchors on evidence, labels the one concession and makes it contingent on a commitment, and never misstates the actual limit.

title: Eduardo Salas
summary: Industrial-organizational psychologist and team scientist, first with the U.S. Navy and later at the University of Central Florida and Rice University, whose 2005 "Big Five in teamwork" model made closed-loop communication a named coordinating mechanism of teams and whose team-training research shaped how aviation, health care and defence teach people to communicate under pressure.

title: Edward R. Tufte
summary: Statistician and political scientist, professor emeritus at Yale, whose self-published books on information design - beginning with The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983) - and whose 2003 essay The Cognitive Style of PowerPoint popularised the critique of bullet-heavy slide presentations and the case for dense, evidence-first technical reports.

title: Effective Writing for Army Leaders
summary: A 1986 U.S. Department of the Army pamphlet (DA Pam 600-67) that told leaders how to enforce the Army Writing Standard - writing understood in one rapid reading - by putting the "bottom line" first, using active voice and short sentences, and coaching writers with a quick-screen edit.

title: Egocentric bias
summary: The tendency to use our own knowledge, intentions and experience as the default for judging what other people know, notice, think or contributed, so that we overestimate how clear our messages are and how central our role was.
selfCheck: If someone outside my team read this message cold, what would they need that I am carrying only in my head?
Have I asked the other person what they think, or am I just imagining their view and trusting my guess?
Before I say how much I did on this project, have I listed what each other person contributed?
Am I assuming my tone is obvious in this email because I can hear it in my own head?

title: Elaboration likelihood model
aliases: central and peripheral routes to persuasion
summary: Petty and Cacioppo's dual-process theory that people are persuaded either by thinking carefully about a message's arguments (the central route) or by reacting to simple cues such as who is speaking (the peripheral route), depending on how motivated and able they are to think about it.

title: Elevator pitch
summary: A spoken summary of an idea, project, venture or of yourself, short enough to deliver in a minute or two, whose job is not to close a deal but to earn a follow-up conversation. Field studies of investor pitches show that delivery and visible preparation shape how listeners judge the substance, but polish cannot rescue a weak idea in front of an experienced listener.
selfCheck: Could the listener repeat back what I want and why it matters to them after hearing it once?
Is my request specific and small enough to agree to in the moment?
Have I replaced every adjective about myself with a concrete result?
If this listener knows the field better than I do, does the substance still hold up without the delivery?
steps: Write down the one thing you want the listener to do next (a meeting, an introduction, a pilot slot) before you write anything else.
State the problem in the listener's terms, then what you propose or offer and the single strongest piece of evidence that it works.
Say why you are the person to do it, in one concrete accomplishment rather than adjectives.
End with a specific, small request the listener can say yes to on the spot.
Cut it to 90 seconds or less, then rehearse it aloud until it sounds conversational rather than memorised.
Stop and invite a question; treat what they ask as the start of the real conversation.

example.situation: An operations analyst has two minutes with a regional vice president before a town hall and wants to propose a pilot that would cut invoice-processing time.
example.before: Hi, I'm in finance ops. I've been doing a lot of analysis on our AP process, looking at the ERP data, vendor categories and approval chains, and there are a lot of interesting patterns, and I think there might be some opportunities with automation if we looked at it more closely at some point.
example.after: Invoices in our region take 19 days to pay, and we lost early-payment discounts on about a third of them last quarter. I tested auto-matching on one vendor group for a month and cut that to 6 days with no extra headcount. I'd like a 20-minute slot with your team next week to propose a three-month pilot across all vendors. Would that work?
example.why: The rewrite leads with a cost the VP cares about, offers one piece of evidence, shows the speaker has already done the work, and ends with a small, specific ask, so the listener can decide in seconds whether to continue.

title: Email
summary: The asynchronous, text-based channel most organisations use for requests, updates, decisions and records; it suits messages the reader can absorb and act on alone, and works best when each message is scannable, answer-first and explicit about what is needed and by when.

title: You don't need to answer right away! (Giurge & Bohns, 2021)
summary: Laura Giurge and Vanessa Bohns's 2021 Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes paper, whose eight preregistered experiments (N = 4,004) found that receivers of non-urgent work emails, especially off-hours ones, think senders want replies sooner than senders do, and that a one-line sender note closed the gap.

title: Emoji and tone in text
summary: Deliberately signalling the intended tone of a written work message - first in the words themselves and, where the relationship and channel suit it, with a sparing, unambiguous emoji - because text strips out the voice and facial cues that normally carry tone, and emoji can either clarify or cost credibility depending on context.
selfCheck: If the recipient read this in their worst mood, which tone would they hear?
Have I put the tone in words, or am I relying on an emoji or punctuation to carry it?
Is this a first contact, an external or formal message, or bad news - where an emoji is likely to cost more than it adds?
Would the emoji I chose look and mean the same thing on the recipient's device?
steps: Before sending anything that could be read two ways (a short reply, a joke, a critique, a "can we talk?"), reread it as a stressed recipient who does not know your mood.
Put the tone into words first - say "no rush", "happy to help", "this is a small fix, not a problem" - rather than relying on punctuation or an emoji to carry it.

Decide whether an emoji fits by context - informal internal chat with people who already know you, yes; first contact, external clients, formal requests and anything about performance, money or bad news, leave it out.
If you use one, pick a single common positive face or symbol whose meaning is hard to misread, put it at the end of the sentence, and never let it replace words.
Match the other person's level once a relationship exists - if they never use emoji, keep to plain text; if the team uses reactions, a thumbs-up can acknowledge a message without another reply.
When a thread turns tense or ambiguous, stop adjusting the emoji and switch to a call.

example.situation: A team lead replies in chat to a new analyst who has asked whether a draft report is ready to send to a client.
example.before: Not yet. Needs work 😬
example.after: Not quite yet - the analysis is solid, but the summary needs tightening before the client sees it. I've left three comments; happy to walk through them at 2pm if useful.
example.why: The original leaves the new analyst to decode a terse line and a grimace face whose meaning varies by reader and platform; the rewrite carries the reassurance and the next step in plain words, which is safer with someone who does not yet know the lead's style and in a message about the quality of their work.

title: Emotional contagion
summary: The tendency for one person's emotions to spread to the people they interact with, often without anyone noticing, so that a speaker's or leader's mood shapes how a conversation, meeting or team feels and behaves; the effect is well documented in groups but small in text-only channels, and its mimicry mechanism is debated.

title: Hot-cold empathy gap
summary: The tendency to misjudge how strongly an emotional or physical state shapes feelings and behaviour when you are not in that state yourself, so a calm communicator underestimates a stressed, excluded or anxious colleague's experience and pitches the message wrong.
selfCheck: Am I judging how much this news, workload or exclusion hurts from my calm state rather than from theirs?
Have I asked how they are actually experiencing this, instead of assuming it matches what I remember from my own similar experience?
If I am angry, anxious or exhausted right now, is this the moment to send that message, or should it wait until I am calmer?
Am I explaining a tired or stressed colleague's slip as a character flaw when the situation may account for it?

title: Employee silence
summary: Employees' choice to hold back ideas, concerns, problems or disagreement from people who could act on them - usually managers - out of fear, a sense that speaking up is futile, or taken-for-granted rules about hierarchy. It starves leaders of bad news and good ideas alike.
selfCheck: Is there something I know about this work - a risk, a mistake, a better idea - that the person who could fix it has not heard from me?
Am I staying quiet because I have weighed the risk, or because "you just don't say that here" without ever testing it?
If others on the team see the same problem, who is going to raise it, and when?
As a manager, when did someone last bring me unwelcome news, and what did my reaction teach them?

title: Erving Goffman
summary: Canadian-American sociologist (1922-1982) who made face-to-face interaction a field of study in its own right, which he called the interaction order. He introduced the ideas of face and face-work and a dramaturgical account of how people manage the impressions they give.

title: Escalating a problem
summary: Deliberately taking a problem, risk or disagreement that cannot be resolved at your level to the person with the authority to decide - early, with the facts, the options and a specific ask, and with the other parties informed rather than bypassed - so that escalation works as a normal decision route instead of a complaint or an act of blame.
selfCheck: Have I genuinely tried to resolve this directly, and does it really exceed my authority or tolerance?
Does the other party know I am escalating, and would they agree my summary states their position fairly?
Could the decision maker act on my first two sentences alone - the decision, the deadline and the cost of waiting?
steps: Check the trigger - the issue exceeds your authority or agreed tolerance on cost, time, scope or risk, or a disagreement has stalled after a genuine attempt to resolve it directly.
Decide within a couple of working days and book time with the decision maker, rather than waiting for the next scheduled report.
Tell your own manager, and tell the other party that you are escalating and why; invite them to escalate jointly with you.
Write the escalation answer-first - the decision needed, by when, and the cost of delay - then the facts, the options with trade-offs, and your recommendation.
Describe the problem, not the people; state each side's position in terms its owner would recognise.
Keep working the current plan until a decision is made, then confirm the decision in writing to everyone affected.

example.situation: A product team lead's launch depends on a platform team that has just moved the shared release date by three weeks, and two conversations between the leads have not resolved it.
example.before: Hi Priya (VP), I need to flag that the platform team has blown up our launch again. They won't commit to anything and we're going to miss the date because of them. Can you please sort this out?
example.after: Priya, Sam (platform) and I need a decision from you by Thursday: hold the 3 March launch with a reduced feature set, or move it to 24 March for the full release. Platform has to take three weeks for a security fix; we agree on the facts but not the priority. Options, costs and our two recommendations are in the attached one-pager. We are continuing to the current plan until you decide.
example.why: The rewrite is a joint escalation with the other party copied and their position fairly stated, leads with the decision and deadline, offers options instead of blame, and confirms work continues - the moves practitioner guidance recommends - rather than asking a senior leader to take a side on a one-sided account.

title: Ethnocentrism
summary: Treating your own culture's habits, values and ways of communicating as the normal, correct standard and judging other people's messages and behaviour against it; in workplace research it goes with lower willingness to talk across cultures and harsher judgements of out-group colleagues' competence and credibility.
selfCheck: When I called a colleague's message rude, vague or odd, was I measuring it against how people communicate where I learned to work?
Would I rate this candidate's or manager's competence the same if their accent, style and background matched mine?
Have I asked what this behaviour means in the other person's context before deciding what it means?
Who on this team have I quietly been avoiding or routing around, and is the real reason a difference in style?

title: Executive briefing
summary: A short, scheduled session (or paper) in which you give a senior decision maker what they need to understand an issue or make a decision, usually in far less time than the subject deserves. It works when the purpose and recommendation come first, detail is held in reserve, and questions are expected.

title: Executive presence
summary: The impression that a person can be trusted with high-stakes leadership work - built from how they carry themselves under pressure (gravitas), how they speak and listen, and how they show up - which research treats as an audience's judgement that forms quickly but is revised over time by integrity and results.
selfCheck: If someone asked "what exactly should I do differently?", could I turn the presence feedback I received into two or three observable behaviours?
In the last tense meeting, did I stay composed and make a clear call, or did I hedge, over-explain or go quiet?
Did I listen and draw others in, or did I mistake talking most for presence?
Am I copying a style that is not mine, when the goal is to show my own judgement and values more clearly?
Is the standard I am being held to applied the same way to colleagues who look and sound different from me?

title: Executive summary
summary: A short, stand-alone section at the front of a report or proposal that gives a busy decision maker the problem, the key findings and the recommended action, so they can decide without reading the rest. Unlike an academic abstract, it leads with conclusions and recommendations, keeps methods to a line or two, and is written in the reader's terms.
selfCheck: If my reader stops after the first paragraph, do they know what I recommend and why?
Could someone who never opens the report make a sound decision from this summary alone?
Have I put methods and background where they belong, after the findings, or cut them?
steps: Finish the report first, then name the one decision or action you want from the reader.
Open with the recommendation or main finding in one or two sentences, before any background.
State the problem and what is at stake for this reader in concrete terms such as cost, risk, time or customers.
Give the three to five findings that justify the recommendation, with the specific numbers.
Mention limitations and open risks honestly, and cut methods to a line unless they change how far the result can be trusted.
Check that it stands alone, uses the report's terms consistently and stays within roughly 5-10% of the report's length.

example.situation: An operations analyst summarises a 30-page review of a regional warehouse for the chief operating officer.
example.before: This report examines the performance of the Northfield warehouse over the past four quarters. The project team collected data from the warehouse management system, interviewed 14 staff and benchmarked three peer sites. Section 2 describes the methodology...
example.after: Recommendation: consolidate Northfield into the Easton site by Q3, saving about $1.4M a year. Northfield ships 22% fewer orders per labour hour than our other sites, its lease renews in March at a 30% increase, and Easton has the spare capacity. Main risk: two large customers need next-day delivery from Easton; the transport plan in Section 4 covers this. Decision needed by 15 January to give notice on the lease.
example.why: The first version describes the report; the second gives the decision, the reasons, the risk and the deadline, so the COO can act from the first paragraph alone.

title: Gaze and eye contact
summary: The skill of using where and how long you look at someone to signal attention, manage turn-taking and build connection in conversation; research suggests moderate, well-timed eye contact helps, while more eye contact is not always better and its meaning varies by culture and situation.
selfCheck: Was I looking at the other person mostly while they were speaking, and letting my gaze move while I was thinking?
Did I hold anyone's gaze long enough that it might have felt like a stare or a challenge?
Did I share my eye contact around the room, or did I keep looking only at the most senior person?
Is this person's comfort with direct gaze likely to differ from mine, and did I adjust to what they did?

title: Face and facework
summary: Face is the public self-image a person claims in an interaction and expects others to honour; facework is everything speakers do, in words and behaviour, to protect, restore or challenge their own and others' face. Introduced by Erving Goffman and developed in politeness theory and face-negotiation theory, it explains why requests, criticism and disagreement are so often softened, and why that softening varies across cultures.

title: Face-to-face conversation
summary: Talking with someone while physically together, so words, voice, face and body arrive at once and each side can respond instantly; it is the richest workplace channel and the most effective for requests, ambiguous problems and sensitive messages, but it is costly to arrange, leaves no record and is easily crowded out by email and chat.
selfCheck: Is this a request, a disagreement, an ambiguous problem or sensitive news - the kinds of message that land better in person?
Am I choosing email because it suits the message, or because it spares me an awkward conversation?
Have I picked a private place and enough time, rather than catching the person in a corridor or open-plan area?
Before we part, have we said the decision and next steps out loud, and will I confirm them in writing?

title: Facial expressions
summary: The movements of the face (smiles, frowns, raised brows, scowls) that people produce and read in conversation; they carry real social signal, but research shows a given expression maps to a given emotion far less reliably than popular "read the face" advice claims, so context and checking matter more than decoding.

title: Facilitation
summary: Guiding how a group works through a discussion - agreeing the goal and ground rules, managing turns, keeping the conversation on track, summarising and closing - while leaving the content and the decisions to the group.
selfCheck: Before we started, did the group agree the goal, the agenda and how we would take turns, or did I assume everyone knew?
Who got cut off or stayed silent, and did I hand the floor back to them by name?
Did I summarise where we had landed before moving to the next item, and check that the summary was right?
Did I keep my own opinions out of the content, or did I steer the group toward the answer I wanted?
Did the meeting end with named owners and next steps for each decision?

title: Facilitator's Guide to Participatory Decision-Making
summary: Sam Kaner and colleagues' practitioner handbook (first edition 1996, third edition 2014) that set out the facilitator's role in participatory groups and introduced the Diamond of Participatory Decision-Making, with its divergent zone, groan zone and convergent zone.

title: Feedback
summary: Information given to a person about their performance or understanding, relative to a goal, so they can close the gap; on average it improves performance, but a sizeable share of feedback makes things worse, depending mainly on what it draws attention to and how much usable information it carries.

title: Feedback sandwich
summary: A widely taught way of delivering criticism by placing one piece of corrective feedback between two pieces of praise (positive, corrective, positive); popular in medicine, education and management, but controlled studies find it mostly changes how feedback feels rather than how people perform.
selfCheck: Is my praise specific and sincere, or am I using it only to cushion the criticism?
If the person repeated back only one sentence from this conversation, would it be the correction?
Am I sandwiching because the feedback needs it, or because I am uncomfortable saying it?
Do the people I manage now brace for a "but" whenever I praise them?
steps: Decide whether a sandwich is needed at all - routine corrections in a healthy working relationship can be given on their own, and praise can be given separately when it is earned.
Pick one specific, important correction; if there are several, the issue is bigger than a sandwich and needs a fuller conversation.
Open with sincere praise for a specific behaviour you want the person to keep, ideally related to the same piece of work.
State the correction plainly as an observable behaviour, not a judgement of the person, and offer a concrete alternative.
Close with genuine, specific encouragement - not a generic compliment - and invite the person to respond, then paraphrase what they say.
Afterwards, check that the correction was heard by asking what they will do differently next time.

example.situation: A team lead reviewing an analyst's first client slide deck, which is well researched but hides the recommendation on slide 14.
example.before: Great job overall, really nice work! Just one tiny thing, maybe think about the order a bit? But honestly it's great, the client will love it.
example.after: Your market-sizing section is the strongest I've seen from a new analyst - the sources are solid. The main fix: the recommendation is on slide 14, so the client won't see it until the end; move it to slide 2 and let the rest support it. Your data work makes that recommendation easy to defend. What do you think of moving it?
example.why: The first version wraps a vague correction in generic praise, so the analyst may hear only "great job"; the rewrite keeps the positive-corrective-positive shape but makes every part specific, states the fix as an action, and checks it landed.

title: Feedforward
summary: A development technique popularised by executive coach Marshall Goldsmith: instead of reviewing what someone did wrong, you name one behaviour you want to improve and ask others for a couple of concrete suggestions for the future, which you listen to and thank them for without debate.
selfCheck: Have I named one behaviour I want to improve in the future, rather than asking for a verdict on the past?
When a suggestion arrived, did I say "thank you" - or did I explain why it would not work?
Am I using feedforward to avoid a conversation about a real problem that still needs to be discussed?
Which of the suggestions will I actually try, and have I told the people who gave them?
steps: Pick one specific behaviour you want to get better at, phrased as a future goal ("run tighter project kick-offs"), not a past failure.
Describe that goal briefly to a colleague who has seen you work or who knows the subject - they do not need to be your manager.
Ask for two concrete suggestions for the future, and make clear you are not asking for a review of anything that already happened.
Listen and write the suggestions down without judging, explaining or defending - the only permitted reply is "thank you".
Offer to return the favour - ask what they want to improve and give them two forward-looking suggestions in turn.
Repeat with a few different people, then choose the suggestions you will actually try and tell those colleagues what you changed.

example.situation: A project manager whose kick-off meetings regularly overrun wants to improve before the next quarter's projects start.
example.before: Can you give me some feedback on last week's kick-off? I know it ran 40 minutes over, but the client kept raising scope questions, so honestly I'm not sure what I could have done differently.
example.after: I'm working on running kick-offs that finish on time. Could you give me two ideas I could try at the next one? I'll just note them down - no need to go back over last week.
example.why: The first version invites a debate about a past meeting and opens with a defence, so the colleague has to argue to be helpful; the rewrite names a future goal, asks for a bounded number of ideas and promises not to argue, which makes it easy to offer useful suggestions.

title: Filled pauses
summary: Sounds and words such as "um", "uh", "like" and "so" that a speaker uses to fill a gap while planning what to say next. A few are normal and even useful to listeners; a high rate in a presentation or briefing makes the speaker sound less prepared and less effective.
selfCheck: In my last recorded talk, how many "ums" and "uhs" did I use per minute - closer to two or to twelve?
Do my fillers cluster at the start of answers to questions, where a planned first sentence would remove them?
When I lose my place, can I let two seconds of silence pass instead of filling it?
Am I trying to remove every single filler, when a few are normal and cost me little?

example.situation: A product manager gives a two-minute status update to a leadership meeting and is asked why the launch slipped.
example.before: So, um, basically the, uh, launch is, like, moving out a bit, um, because of, uh, the vendor thing, so, um, yeah, we're, uh, looking at maybe the 20th.
example.after: The launch moves to the 20th. [pause] The cause is a late security review from our vendor. [pause] It finished yesterday, so the 20th is firm.
example.why: The speaker replaces each filler with a short silent pause and plans one sentence at a time, so the answer is shorter, the date comes first, and the hesitation that suggested doubt is gone.

title: First offer
summary: Deliberately naming the opening number or package in a negotiation so that it anchors the other side's expectations, and deciding - based on who knows more about the zone of possible agreement - whether to move first at all and how ambitious to be.
selfCheck: Do I know the likely range of agreement better than, as well as, or worse than the other side?
Is my opening based on my target and a reason I can say out loud, rather than on my walk-away point?
Is it ambitious enough to leave room to move but not so extreme that it could offend or end the talks?
Am I about to reveal a preference we probably share, which they could trade back to me as a concession?
If they opened first, have I re-anchored on my own numbers before replying?
steps: Before the conversation, research the market and estimate the zone of possible agreement - your walk-away point, the other side's likely walk-away point, and what comparable deals settled at.
Decide whether to move first - do so when you know the range at least as well as the other side; if they clearly know more, ask questions and let them open.
Set the offer from your ambitious target, not from your walk-away point, and make sure it is one you can justify with a real reason.
Limit the opening to the issues where your interests conflict; hold back terms you suspect both sides want anyway until you have learned their preferences.
State the number precisely and confidently, give the reason in one or two sentences, then stop talking and listen.

If they open first, do not respond to their number straight away - restate your own target, their likely limits and your alternatives to yourself, then counter from your plan rather than from their anchor.

example.situation: A marketing team lead is buying a six-month analytics retainer from a small agency she has researched; similar retainers she found ranged from $8K to $11K a month.
example.before: We don't have a fixed budget yet - what would you normally charge for something like this?
example.after: Based on the three proposals we reviewed for similar scope, we'd like to propose $8,500 a month for six months, with the weekly dashboard and quarterly review included. That reflects the market and a six-month commitment from us. How does that sit with you?
example.why: She knows the market range at least as well as the agency, so moving first lets her set the reference point near the low end with a stated rationale, instead of inviting the agency to anchor at the top of the range.

title: Army Field Manual 6-0
aliases: FM 6-0, Commander and Staff Organization and Operations
Commander and Staff Organization and Operations
summary: The U.S. Army field manual on how commanders and staffs organise and work (2014 edition, amended 2015-16), whose chapter on military briefings codifies the four briefing types - information, decision, mission and staff - and a plan-prepare-execute-assess routine that underlies much civilian advice on briefing executives.

title: Follow-up questions
summary: Questions that build directly on what the other person has just said - asking them to expand, clarify or give an example - rather than switching to a new topic. They show you were listening, draw out detail a first answer leaves out, and in conversation research are the question type most consistently linked to being seen as responsive and likeable.
selfCheck: Did my last question build on something they actually said, or on my own list?
Which detail in their answer did I let pass that I still do not understand?
Was my probe neutral, or did it hint at the answer I wanted to hear?
Have I asked several questions in a row without sharing anything myself?
steps: Listen to the whole answer and note one specific word, claim or detail in it that you want to understand better.
Ask about that detail in their terms ("You said the handover was messy - what happened there?") instead of moving to your next prepared question.
Keep the probe neutral - "how did you decide?", "what did that look like?" - rather than suggesting the answer you expect.
Go one or two layers deeper on what matters, then summarise what you heard before switching topic.
Offer something of your own between questions so the exchange feels like a conversation, not an interrogation.
In formal settings such as structured interviews or reviews, plan the likely probes in advance and use the same ones for everyone.

example.situation: A manager's one-to-one with a team member who mentions the client launch "went okay, apart from the data issue".
example.before: Good to hear. Next thing - how are you getting on with the Q3 planning doc?
example.after: What was the data issue, and how did the client react when it came up?
example.why: The first reply jumps to the manager's own agenda and loses the one signal of trouble; the follow-up picks up the speaker's own words, shows they were heard, and surfaces a risk while it is still small.

title: George Loewenstein
summary: Carnegie Mellon behavioural economist and psychologist who, with Colin Camerer and Martin Weber, put the "curse of knowledge" on the research map in 1989 and later proposed the information-gap theory of curiosity; both ideas explain why experts misjudge audiences and how to hold attention.

title: Gesturing while speaking
summary: The skill of using hand and arm movements alongside speech to show size, shape, sequence and emphasis; meta-analyses find gestures that add information moderately improve listeners' understanding, while claims that gesturing always makes speakers sharper or more persuasive rest on smaller and mixed evidence.
selfCheck: Did my hands show something my words did not, such as a size, a sequence or a comparison?
When I watch a recording, do I see fidgeting with my pen, hair or laptop that could read as nerves?
Did I use any hand sign whose meaning might differ for someone from another culture in the room?
Was I relying on gestures to carry a point that people on audio or reading the slides afterwards would miss?

title: The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states
summary: Thomas Gilovich, Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Husted Medvec's 1998 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology paper, whose lying, disgust-tasting and bystander experiments showed that people overestimate how readable their inner states are to others, and which named that bias.

title: Ginny Redish
summary: Harvard-trained linguist who directed the Document Design Project and Document Design Center at the American Institutes for Research from 1978-79, co-wrote the 1981 Guidelines for Document Designers (which taught writers to break parallel items into bulleted or numbered lists), and carried reader testing from government forms into software usability and writing for the web.

title: Graded assertiveness
summary: A set of scripted, escalating ways to voice a concern to someone with more authority - from a probing question, through a plain statement of concern and a proposed fix, to an explicit call to stop - taken from team-safety training in aviation and healthcare (AHRQ's TeamSTEPPS assertive statement, CUS words and two-challenge rule; the PACE mnemonic).
selfCheck: Have I said the concern out loud in words the other person cannot mistake for small talk, or only hinted at it?
Did I name the specific fact and the consequence, and offer a fix?
Did I ask for and get an explicit answer, or did the point just fade?
If I was ignored, did I raise it a second time before deciding whether to escalate?
Am I matching the level of challenge to the real size of the risk, rather than to my nerves or my frustration?
steps: Decide in advance which level the situation warrants - a question, a stated concern, a request to pause, or a stop - based on how serious and how imminent the harm is.
Open by getting the person's attention and using their name: "Priya, can I flag something before this goes out?"
State your concern in the first person and name the problem as you see it, with the specific fact behind it ("I'm concerned - the Q3 figure on slide 4 doesn't match the ledger").
Offer a concrete fix or next step rather than only the objection.
Ask for an explicit decision or agreement, and wait for an answer instead of letting the point drop.
If you are not acknowledged, say it a second time, more plainly, naming the consequence you expect.
If the concern is still unresolved and the risk is serious, escalate in the open - ask for a pause, bring in a colleague, or go to the next level - and say that you are doing so.

example.situation: A finance analyst notices, ten minutes before a board call, that the revenue figure in the VP's deck is from the unaudited draft. The VP is busy and has already said the deck is final.
example.before: Um, sorry, this is probably nothing, but did anyone double-check slide 4? Maybe it's fine.
example.after: Dana, I'm concerned about slide 4 - the revenue is the draft number, $2.1M higher than the audited one. I can swap in the audited figure in two minutes. Can we hold the deck until I do?
example.why: The rewrite gets attention by name, states the concern and the evidence, offers a fix and asks for a decision, so the VP can act in seconds; the hedged version invites a quick "it's fine" and leaves the analyst no clear second step.

title: Grice's cooperative principle
summary: Philosopher Paul Grice's account of how conversation works: listeners assume a speaker is trying to contribute what the exchange needs, and expect contributions to be true (Quality), as informative as needed and no more (Quantity), relevant (Relation) and clear (Manner); departures from these expectations are read as signals of unstated meaning.
selfCheck: If my reader took every word literally and also read between the lines, what would they conclude that I did not intend?
Did I use a weaker word such as "some", "most" or "should" where a stronger one was true, and so imply the stronger one is false?
Does every sentence I am about to send answer the question that was actually asked?
Have I stated anything I believe but cannot back up, without flagging it as a belief?
Is there detail here the reader does not need to act, and detail they need that I left out?

title: Group decision making
summary: The recurring situation in which a team, committee or board must pool what its members know and commit to one choice. Groups can outperform their best member, but usually only when the decision owner and rule are clear, members state their views independently before discussing, and the discussion deliberately surfaces what only one person knows.

title: GROW model
summary: A four-stage structure for coaching conversations - Goal, Reality, Options, Will (or Way forward) - in which the coach mainly asks questions so the other person sets their own goal, sizes up the current situation, generates choices and commits to a next step. Developed by Graham Alexander and popularised by John Whitmore, it is the most widely taught coaching sequence but has little direct testing of its own.
selfCheck: Did the other person state the goal in their own words, or did I set it for them?
How much of the time did I spend asking versus telling?
Did we leave with a specific first step, an owner, a date and a review point?
Did I spend so long on what is going wrong that we ran out of time for options and commitment?
Did I follow the letters mechanically when the conversation needed to go back a stage?
steps: Goal: ask what the person wants from this conversation and what success would look like, and agree a goal they own ("What would good look like by the end of the quarter?").
Reality: ask what is happening now, what they have already tried and what helps or gets in the way; keep it factual and brief rather than digging into blame.
Options: ask for several possible routes before judging any ("What else could you try?"), and offer your own idea only after theirs, labelled as one option.
Will / Way forward: ask which option they will start with, what the first step is, by when, and how you will both know it is working.
Summarise the commitment in their words and agree when you will review it, then open the next conversation by checking progress against the goal.
Loop back to an earlier stage whenever the conversation shows the goal or the facts were wrong; do not march through the letters in order for its own sake.

example.situation: A team lead's direct report says in a one-on-one that she is drowning in ad-hoc requests from another department and keeps missing her own project milestones.
example.before: OK, just tell them no. Send me the requests and I'll talk to their manager - and block out Friday mornings for the project.
example.after: What would a good week look like for you a month from now? ... Roughly how many requests came in last week, and which ones did you take on? ... What could you do about the ones that aren't urgent? Anything else? I'd add one option - routing them through a shared intake form. ... Which will you try first, and shall we look at how it went next Tuesday?
example.why: The first reply solves the problem for her, so she learns nothing and the lead now owns it; the GROW version gets her to set the target, size the problem, pick an option and commit to a review date, while still letting the lead contribute an idea as one option among several.

title: Habit reversal training
summary: A behavioural method for breaking an unwanted speaking habit, such as "um" and "uh": learn to notice each occurrence as it happens, then replace it with an incompatible response, usually a brief silent pause. Short versions of it cut filler rates in public speaking studies.
selfCheck: Do I know my actual filler rate from a recording, or am I guessing?
Can I name the exact sound or word I am trying to replace, and where it usually appears?
When I felt a filler coming in that talk, did I pause silently instead?
Have I tested the new habit in front of a real audience, not just alone with a recorder?
steps: Record two or three short practice talks and count your fillers per minute to get a baseline.
Write a one-line description of the habit you are targeting, such as "um" or "uh" at the start of a sentence.
Replay a recording and mark every filler the moment you hear it, until you catch nearly all of them.
Practise the competing response - close your mouth and take a brief silent pause - each time you feel a filler coming.
Give a new practice talk, ideally with a colleague tapping the table when you miss one, and recount your rate.
Repeat a short booster session before high-stakes talks if your rate drifts back up.

example.situation: A team lead must present quarterly results to a department of 40 and has noticed she says "um" constantly in rehearsals.
example.before: Um, so revenue was, uh, up this quarter, um, about 8%, and, uh, the main driver was, um, the renewals.
example.after: Revenue was up 8% this quarter. [brief pause] The main driver was renewals.
example.why: After three 15-minute sessions of spotting her fillers on recordings and practising a silent pause instead, she catches the urge before it becomes a sound, so each sentence starts clean and the number lands first.

title: Handling audience questions
summary: Preparing for, listening to and answering the questions an audience asks during or after a talk or briefing - restating each question, answering it briefly and directly, and saying plainly when you cannot answer and why.
selfCheck: Did I answer the question that was asked, or a nearby question I found easier?
Could someone at the back of the room tell what the question was?
Did I stop talking once I had given my position and one piece of support?
When I could not answer, did I give the real reason and a follow-up date?
Did the questions I took come from across the room, or only from the first hands up?
steps: Before the talk, list the ten questions you most expect - including the ones you would rather not get - and rehearse a two- or three-sentence answer to each out loud.
Decide in advance which questions you cannot answer (legal, confidential, not yet decided) and write down the honest reason and the principle you can share instead.
When a question comes, let the asker finish, pause, and check you have the real question rather than the first sentence of it.
Restate the question in one short sentence so the whole room hears it and the asker can correct you.
Answer the question that was asked - position first, one piece of evidence, then stop - and offer to follow up offline if it needs more detail.
If you do not know, say so, say how you will find out, and give a date for the follow-up.
For a hostile or emotional question, keep your own tone level, acknowledge the concern, and answer the substance underneath it.
Spread the questions around the room rather than taking hands in order, and close the session with a one-sentence restatement of your key message.

example.situation: An operations lead presents a warehouse automation plan to forty staff; a supervisor asks whether the change means job cuts, and the decision on headcount has not been made.
example.before: "That's a great question. So, the automation roadmap has three phases, and phase one is really about throughput, which, as I showed on slide four, improves by around twenty percent, and the vendor has a strong track record..." She talks for two minutes about throughput and never mentions jobs.
example.after: "The question is whether this plan means job cuts. The honest answer is that headcount hasn't been decided - the board reviews it in March. What I can tell you is the principle we're using: retraining first, and no changes without 90 days' notice. I'll share the March decision with this group the same week."
example.why: The rewrite restates the actual question, admits what is not yet known and why, shares the principle that is known, and commits to a follow-up date. The original answers an easier question, which listeners may not catch in the moment but which erodes trust once they notice.

title: Hattie and Timperley's feedback model
aliases: model of feedback to enhance learning
feed up feed back feed forward
summary: A model from John Hattie and Helen Timperley (2007) that judges feedback by whether it answers three questions - where am I going, how am I going, where to next - and by the level it is aimed at: the task, the process, self-regulation, or the self, with comments about the person as a whole judged least useful.
selfCheck: Could the other person state the goal of this work in one sentence after my feedback?
Did I say what to do next, or only what was wrong?
Is most of what I said about the approach and how to check it, rather than about this one output or about the person?
Did any praise I gave carry information about the work, or was it a general compliment?
steps: Before the conversation, write the goal in one line - what good looks like for this piece of work - and check the other person would describe it the same way (where am I going?).
Compare the work with that goal using specific observations, saying what is already on target and what is not (how am I going?).
Name one or two concrete next actions, a stretch or a resource that will close the gap (where to next?).
Aim most comments at the process - the approach, method or strategy that produced the result - rather than only at whether this output is right.
Where the person is experienced, add a self-regulation prompt that helps them check their own work next time, such as a question they can ask before sending.
Drop or separate praise of the person ("you're a star") from the information about the work, so it does not crowd out the useful part.

example.situation: A team lead reviews a junior analyst's first draft of a client status report, which ran long and buried a schedule risk.
example.before: Great effort, you're a natural! A few things to tidy - see my edits. Section 3 is wrong, and it's too long.
example.after: The goal is a one-page report the client can act on in two minutes. Your data is accurate and the budget table is clear. Right now the slip on the testing milestone sits on page 3, so the client could miss it. Next draft, open with the top risk and our proposed fix, and before sending, ask yourself: what is the one thing the client must decide this week?
example.why: The first version mixes person-level praise with a bare verdict and tracked changes, so the analyst learns neither the goal nor how to avoid the problem; the rewrite answers all three questions, explains the process behind the issue, and leaves a self-check the analyst can reuse without the lead.

title: High- and low-context cultures
summary: Edward T. Hall's contrast between communication in which most meaning sits in shared context, relationships and nonverbal cues (high-context) and communication in which meaning is carried mainly by explicit words (low-context); widely taught for intercultural work, but its country rankings have weak empirical support.

title: Hofstede's dimensions of national culture
summary: Geert Hofstede's model that compares national cultures on six value dimensions - power distance, uncertainty avoidance, individualism-collectivism, masculinity-femininity, long- vs. short-term orientation and indulgence-restraint - built from country-average survey scores; useful for anticipating group-level tendencies but weak at predicting any one colleague.

title: Humble inquiry
summary: Edgar Schein's practice of drawing another person out by asking questions you do not already know the answer to, out of real curiosity about them, instead of opening with your own diagnosis, advice or instructions - especially when you hold the higher status.
selfCheck: Did I ask at least one question I did not already know the answer to?
Was my question a real question, or a suggestion or a test dressed up as one?
Who talked more in that conversation, and did I learn anything that changed my view?
Did I acknowledge what they said before telling them what I think?
steps: Before the conversation, write down what you are assuming about the situation and the person, and mark which parts you have not actually checked.
Open with a question you do not know the answer to ("Walk me through how you approached this") instead of your verdict or fix.
Stop after the question and let the other person talk; resist filling the first silence with your own view.
Ask one genuine follow-up that builds on what they just said, rather than steering back to your agenda.
Acknowledge what you heard in your own words before you add any opinion, request or decision.
Only then tell - share your view or ask for what you need - and invite them to correct or add to it.

example.situation: A team lead notices a direct report delivered a client analysis in an unexpected format, a day before the client review.
example.before: This isn't the template we use. Please redo it in the standard deck format tonight so we're ready for tomorrow.
example.after: You built this differently from our usual deck - I'd like to understand why. Can you walk me through what you were going for and what you know about this client that I might not?
example.why: The first version assumes the lead already knows everything relevant and shuts the report down; the second surfaces their reasoning (perhaps the client asked for it), keeps them engaged, and still leaves time to agree a format together.

title: Hybrid meetings
summary: Meetings in which some participants share a room while others join remotely by video or audio; the two groups hear, see, take turns and wield influence unequally, so the organizer has to choose the format deliberately and run the meeting to offset the room's built-in advantage.
selfCheck: Does this meeting need some people in the same room, or would an all-remote call put everyone on equal footing?
Can every remote attendee hear every speaker in the room and see what is being written or shown?
Who is watching the screen and the chat, and how will remote people get the floor without having to interrupt?
Did I invite a remote participant to speak first on at least one item?
Did anything get decided in a side conversation or after the call ended that remote attendees still have not heard?

title: I-statements
summary: Raising a problem by describing the other person's specific behaviour, its concrete effect on you and how you feel about it, phrased from your own point of view ("I…") rather than as an accusation or verdict about them ("You always…").
selfCheck: Have I described a specific behaviour I could point to, or slipped in a label, a motive or an "always"?
Is my "I feel…" a real feeling, or a disguised accusation such as "I feel that you don't care"?
Have I said anything that shows I understand the other person's side of the situation?
After I speak, am I ready to listen to their reaction rather than repeat my point louder?
steps: Before speaking, name one specific, observable behaviour (what was said or done, and when) instead of a trait or a pattern word like "always" or "never".
Work out the concrete, tangible effect that behaviour has on you or your work - time lost, rework, a missed commitment.
Identify the feeling underneath, and check whether anger is masking something more precise such as worry or frustration.
Say it in the first person in roughly this order - behaviour, effect, feeling - and, if useful, a request for what you would like instead.
Add one sentence that shows you see the other person's side (their constraints, intentions or pressures) before or after your own view.
Stop and listen; expect some defensiveness, reflect back what you hear, and send a clearer second I-statement only if the first one was not understood.

example.situation: A project lead raises a recurring problem with a colleague who sends status updates late on the morning of the weekly client call.
example.before: You never get your updates in on time. You're making the whole team look unprepared in front of the client.
example.after: I know Mondays are packed for you with the support queue. When the status update reaches me after 9 a.m. on call days, I can't check the numbers before we present them, and I get anxious that we'll give the client something wrong. Could we agree on Friday afternoon as the cut-off?
example.why: The rewrite replaces a character verdict ("never", "you're making") with one observable behaviour, its concrete effect and the speaker's own feeling, acknowledges the colleague's constraint, and ends with a specific request - the combination the 2018 rating study found least likely to provoke defensiveness.

title: Illusion of transparency
summary: The tendency to overestimate how clearly other people can see our internal states - our nerves, feelings and intentions - and, by extension, how plainly our messages convey what we meant, so we under-signal and fail to check understanding.
selfCheck: Have I actually said the thing I am assuming they already picked up from my tone or face?
In this email, would a reader who could not hear my voice know whether I was joking, annoyed or serious?
Did I check what they understood, or did I take their nod as proof?
Before this presentation, am I treating my racing heart as something the audience can see?

title: Impression management
summary: The theory that people, consciously or not, shape the impressions others form of them - deciding both how much image matters in a situation and which image to project - and that common workplace tactics such as self-promotion and ingratiation shift interview and performance ratings, but can backfire when they read as insincere.

title: Influence without authority
summary: Getting help from colleagues, other teams, bosses or clients you cannot direct by treating them as potential allies, learning what they care about and offering something they value in return - the reciprocity-based "influence model" of Allan R. Cohen and David L. Bradford.
selfCheck: Do I know what this person is measured on and worried about right now, or am I guessing?
What can I offer that they would value, and is it something I can genuinely deliver?
Have I separated what I must have from what would merely be nice?
Would I be comfortable if they saw exactly how I planned this request, or does it rely on spin?
steps: Treat the person whose help you need as a potential ally, even if past dealings were tense, and drop any story that they are simply difficult.
Write down exactly what you need from them, which parts are essential and which are nice to have, and check that the request serves the work rather than only your own ambitions.
Diagnose their world - how they are measured and rewarded, what their boss expects, what their workload and pressures are this quarter.

List the currencies they are likely to value (resources, information, help, recognition, visibility, a link to a larger purpose) and the ones you can actually offer, including cheap ones you control yourself.
Assess the relationship; if trust is low, repair it first, and adapt to how they prefer to work (data or story, email or a quick call).
Make a concrete, honest offer that trades something they value for what you need, then deliver on it and keep in touch afterwards so the relationship exists before you need it again.

example.situation: A product analyst needs an engineer on another team to add tracking events before a launch, but has no authority over the engineer's priorities.
example.before: Hi, I need these six tracking events added before Thursday's release. It's important for the launch, so please prioritise it. Thanks!
example.after: Hi - I know your team is measured on the release shipping cleanly, so I don't want to add risk. Of the six events, two are essential for the launch review (sign-up and first purchase); the rest can wait a sprint. I've written the event specs and test cases so it should be about an hour of work, and I'll credit your team in the launch metrics readout to the VP. Would Wednesday morning work, or is there a better slot?
example.why: The rewrite shows an understanding of the engineer's goals, cuts the ask to what is essential, lowers the cost by doing the preparatory work, and offers currencies the engineer may value (less effort, visibility with leadership) instead of borrowing urgency the analyst has no standing to impose.

title: Information overload
summary: The state in which the volume, pace or complexity of incoming messages and information exceeds what a person can process in the time available, so decisions get slower and worse, important messages are skimmed or missed, and people feel stressed and behind.
selfCheck: Does every person on this distribution list need to act on or know this, or am I copying them to cover myself?
Could the reader act on my first two lines without opening the attachment?
Am I adding a fifth channel or thread for something that already has a home?
Have I told my team when I do and do not expect replies, so nobody feels they must watch the inbox all day?
When I feel swamped, is it the volume of messages, or a lack of clear priorities behind them?

title: Informative headings
summary: Writing headings that tell the reader what a section says or answers, such as "Costs rise 12% if we wait", instead of bare labels such as "Costs" or "Discussion", so a reader can skim the headings alone, find what they need and grasp the document's main points.
selfCheck: If my reader read only the headings, would they know my main findings and what I need from them?
Could any of my headings sit unchanged on top of a different report, and if so, what specific point should it state instead?
Does the first sentence under each heading deliver what the heading promises?
steps: List the questions your reader will bring to the document, and draft one heading for each main answer before you write the body.
Turn every label heading into a statement or question that carries the section's point, starting with the most informative words.
Keep each heading to about one line, use parallel wording within a level and stop at three levels.
Make sure the first sentence under each heading delivers what the heading promises.
Read the headings alone, as a table of contents, and check that they tell the main story and match your executive summary.

example.situation: A finance analyst sends a six-page review of a software licence renewal to a director who will skim it before a budget meeting.
example.before: Headings: 1. Background  2. Analysis  3. Options  4. Discussion  5. Next steps
example.after: Headings: 1. Renewal costs rise 18% on 1 April  2. A third of our licences are unused  3. Cutting to 400 seats saves $90K a year  4. Main risk: peak-season demand in Q4  5. Approve the reduced order by 15 March
example.why: The labels only say what kind of content each section holds; the rewritten headings carry the findings, the recommendation and the deadline, so the director can grasp the case and the decision from the headings alone.

title: Integrative negotiation
summary: Negotiating to enlarge the total value available before dividing it: uncovering each side's interests and priorities across several issues, then trading what matters less to you for what matters more, so both parties end up better off than a split-the-difference compromise.
selfCheck: Have I put more than one issue on the table, or am I haggling over a single number?
Do I know which issues matter most to the other side, or am I assuming their interests are the opposite of mine?
Am I trading low-priority terms for high-priority ones, rather than conceding issue by issue?
Am I sharing information step by step and checking that it is reciprocated?
Is there a package that would leave both of us better off than the one we are about to sign?
steps: Before the conversation, list every issue that could be on the table - not only price, but timing, scope, payment terms, staffing, risk sharing, duration - and add issues if there is only one.
Rank those issues by how much each matters to you, and note your BATNA so you know the point below which no package is worth taking.
Open by asking why, not what - ask what the other side needs to achieve, what constraints they face and which terms matter most to them - and listen for differences in priority.
Share some of your own priorities in return, a piece at a time, watching whether the other side reciprocates before you disclose more.
Propose trades across issues - give ground on what you value less in exchange for movement on what you value more - instead of meeting in the middle on each issue separately.
Bundle the trades into complete packages and test them with "what if" questions, using objective criteria such as market rates to settle the remaining distributive pieces.
Before closing, ask whether any other arrangement would leave both sides better off than the one on the table.

example.situation: An IT manager is negotiating a software renewal with a vendor account executive who has proposed an 8% price increase.
example.before: An 8% increase isn't going to work for us. Can you meet us halfway at 4%?
example.after: Help me understand what's driving the 8% - is it a revenue target for this year, or the cost of supporting us? On our side, budget certainty matters more than anything, and we're flexible on contract length. If we signed for three years instead of one, and agreed to be a reference customer, could you hold this year's price flat with a capped increase after that?
example.why: Splitting the difference treats the renewal as a single fixed pie; asking about the vendor's interests and offering terms that are cheap for the buyer but valuable to the vendor (a longer commitment, a reference) lets both sides gain more than a 4% compromise would give them.

title: Intercultural communication
summary: The study and practice of communication between people whose cultural backgrounds lead them to different interpretations and expectations about what competent communication looks like; at work it supplies the concepts, barriers and training methods used to collaborate across national, regional, occupational and other cultural lines.

title: Intercultural competence
aliases: Deardorff process model of intercultural competence
summary: The ability to communicate and behave effectively and appropriately with people whose cultural backgrounds differ from yours, built from attitudes (respect, openness, curiosity), knowledge (including cultural self-awareness) and skills (listening, observing, interpreting) that develop over a working life rather than being completed by one course.
selfCheck: Before this exchange, which of my own norms (how direct to be, who speaks first, what silence means) am I assuming the other person shares?
Did I describe what I actually observed before deciding what it meant?
Is my goal here both effective (I got what we needed) and appropriate (they would see how I behaved as acceptable)?
What did I learn in this conversation that I will test, rather than generalise, next time?

title: Interests vs. positions
summary: The negotiation principle of looking past each side's stated demand (its position) to the needs, concerns and goals that produced it (its interests), because several different agreements can usually satisfy the same interests even when the positions look incompatible.
selfCheck: Can I say in one sentence why I want what I am asking for, separately from the number or term itself?
What do I think the other side's demand is protecting, and have I asked them rather than assumed it?
Have I put at least two different options on the table that would meet the same interests?
Which parts of this deal are genuinely fixed-sum, so I still need a fair standard to divide them?

title: Interpersonal communication
summary: The study and practice of communication between people whose lives mutually influence one another, usually two people or a small group, and of how that talk gets things done, builds or strains relationships and shapes identity; as an academic field it grew out of speech communication and social psychology in the 1960s and 1970s.

title: Interrupting
summary: Taking the floor before another speaker has finished their point, especially to change the topic, disagree or redirect; observers read the interrupter as higher in status but less likeable, and in groups early interruptions snowball into lasting unequal airtime.
selfCheck: Did I start talking before the other person had finished their sentence or their point?
When I came in over someone, was it to agree and build on what they said, or to change the subject or win the argument?
In this meeting, who got cut off early, and did anyone, including me, hand the floor back to them?
If I was interrupted, did I calmly reclaim the turn ("Let me finish this point, then I'd like your view")?

example.situation: In a weekly project meeting, a junior analyst starts explaining why the vendor data looks wrong, and the team lead jumps in.
example.before: Analyst: 'The Q3 numbers don't reconcile because the vendor changed—' Lead: 'Yeah, vendors always do that, let's just use last quarter's file. Next item.'
example.after: Analyst: 'The Q3 numbers don't reconcile because the vendor changed—' Lead: [waits until she stops] 'So the vendor changed something in the feed. What changed, and what does it mean for the forecast?'
example.why: In the first version the lead takes the floor mid-sentence and closes the topic, so the analyst loses both the point and the standing to raise it again; in the second he lets her finish, summarises, and hands the floor back, so the actual cause surfaces.

title: Irving Janis
