summary: Yale social psychologist (1918-1990) who co-wrote the Yale programme's Communication and Persuasion (1953) and coined "groupthink" in Victims of Groupthink (1972), the case-study account of how cohesive teams silence doubts - and whose prevention advice made the assigned devil's advocate, the impartial leader and the second-chance meeting standard parts of group decision practice.

title: Selling issues to leadership
aliases: getting the boss to buy in
summary: Deliberately getting senior leaders to notice, understand and act on an issue, idea or risk you see from below - by framing it in terms of goals they already own, involving allies, and choosing the timing and channel - as described in Jane E. Dutton and Susan J. Ashford's research on issue selling.
selfCheck: Can I state in one sentence which of leadership's existing goals this issue helps, and is that link honest?
Am I bringing a proposed solution and the evidence my leaders usually ask for, or only a complaint?
Who else have I involved, and would any of them be surprised to hear me raise it?
Is this the right moment and forum, or am I raising it because I am frustrated right now?
If they say no, what will I do next - and am I prepared to accept that answer?
steps: Write the issue in one sentence and link it to a goal, metric or priority your leaders already own, framed as an opportunity where honestly possible.
Find out how the decision maker likes to receive proposals - data or story, a written pre-read or a conversation - and what evidence counts in your organisation.
Build a short business case - cost, benefit, risk and what happens if nothing changes - and bring at least one concrete proposed solution, not only the problem.
Test the idea with peers and one or two respected senior people first; fold in their objections and ask who should be involved or informed.
Read the context before you raise it - is leadership listening, under pressure, or recently burned by a similar idea? - and pick a moment and channel that fit.
Raise it calmly, acknowledge any past decision you are revisiting without blaming whoever made it, and ask for one specific next step.
Follow up, report what happened, and decide deliberately whether to persist, re-bundle the issue with another priority, or let it go for now.

example.situation: A support team lead wants leadership to fund a fix for a confusing billing page that drives a large share of tickets.
example.before: Hi all, I wanted to flag (again) that the billing page is a mess. My team is drowning in tickets and nobody seems to care. Can we please prioritise this?
example.after: Proposal for Thursday's ops review: about a third of last month's support tickets trace to the billing page. A two-sprint redesign, already scoped with product, would cut handling costs and supports this year's customer-retention goal. I'd like a decision on adding it to Q1. One-page case attached; finance has checked the numbers.
example.why: The rewrite ties the issue to a goal leaders own, brings data and a solution, shows peers are already involved, and uses a scheduled forum - the packaging, involvement and process moves the research links to success - instead of venting frustration.

title: Job interview
summary: The conversation in which an employer questions a job applicant to judge fit for a role; it is a high-stakes exchange where the interviewer's question design and the candidate's answers both shape how accurate the hiring decision turns out to be.

title: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance
summary: Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi's 1996 Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes, which found that feedback raises performance on average (d = 0.41) yet lowers it in more than a third of cases, and proposed feedback intervention theory to explain why.

title: Checking email less frequently reduces stress
summary: Kostadin Kushlev and Elizabeth Dunn's 2015 Computers in Human Behavior field experiment, in which 124 heavy email users spent one week checking email three times a day and one week checking at will, and reported moderately lower daily stress in the limited week.

title: Labeling emotions
summary: Putting a short, tentative name to the emotion someone seems to be feeling ("it sounds like this deadline has you worried"), then pausing so they can confirm or correct it, as a way of lowering the emotional temperature before you deal with the problem itself.
selfCheck: Did I name the feeling as a guess ("it sounds like...") rather than telling them what they feel?
Did I pick a word no stronger than the emotion they actually showed?
Could my label be heard as a criticism of them, and if so, did I reword it as a neutral observation?
After the label, did I stay quiet long enough for them to correct me?
steps: Listen until you have a reasonable read of the feeling - from their words, pace, tone and what they keep returning to - rather than labeling the first sign of emotion.
Name the emotion and, if you can, its trigger in one short sentence that starts with "It sounds like..." or "It seems like...", choosing a milder word than your first instinct.
Phrase the label as a neutral observation about them, not a verdict on their behaviour or motives.
Stop talking and let the label land; give them time to agree, refine or reject it.
If they correct you, accept the correction, restate it in their terms and do not argue for your original read.
Once they confirm the feeling, move to the substance - their facts, priorities and what happens next.

example.situation: A finance analyst learns in a team call that the month-end close has been pulled forward two days, and replies tersely that the new date "is fine, I guess".
example.before: Great, so we're all aligned on the new date. Let's move on to the forecast.
example.after: It sounds like the new date has you pretty stretched, with the reconciliations still open. ... What would make it workable?
example.why: The rewrite names the likely feeling and its cause tentatively, then pauses, so the analyst can confirm the pressure or correct the read; the manager learns about the open reconciliations now instead of after the close slips.

title: Listening styles
aliases: relational analytical task-oriented and critical listening
summary: A framework that sorts the goals people bring to listening (relational, analytical, task-oriented and critical in the revised model; people, content, action and time in the original) so a listener can notice their default and shift to the one the conversation needs.

title: The Illusion of Transparency and Normative Beliefs About Anxiety During Public Speaking
summary: A 2010 Current Research in Social Psychology paper in which students in a public-speaking course believed their audience saw far more nervousness than it reported, and a second survey showed that people expect high speaking anxiety to be normal.

title: Hesitation phenomena in spontaneous English speech
summary: Howard Maclay and Charles E. Osgood's 1959 paper in the journal Word, which counted filled pauses, silent pauses, repeats and false starts in the unscripted speech of about a dozen conference participants and set the four-way taxonomy of disfluency that speech research still uses.

title: Managing up
summary: The learnable skill of deliberately building a working relationship with your manager (or a senior client) that gets the best results for both of you and the organisation - by understanding their goals, pressures and preferred style, agreeing expectations, keeping them informed and being dependable - as framed by John J. Gabarro and John P. Kotter.
selfCheck: Can I name my manager's top two goals and the pressure they are under this quarter, from what they have told me rather than my guess?
Do I know whether my manager would rather read this in writing first or hear it live, and am I using that format?
Have we explicitly agreed what "done" looks like and when they want to hear from me, or am I assuming?
Is there a problem or slipping date I have not told them about yet, and why am I waiting?
Am I spending their time and goodwill on something that truly needs them, and have I brought a proposed solution?
Would I be comfortable if my manager saw exactly how I prepared for this conversation, or does it rely on flattery or spin?

title: Erie Railroad Superintendent's Report (1856)
summary: Daniel C. McCallum's report as general superintendent of the New York and Erie Railroad (covering 1855, dated March 1856), which set out six principles of administration and a system of hourly, daily and monthly reports flowing up the hierarchy. Business historians treat it as an early blueprint for routine upward reporting, the practice from which the modern internal business report grew.

title: Mea Culpa: A Sociology of Apology and Reconciliation
summary: Nicholas Tavuchis's 1991 Stanford University Press book, a landmark sociological account of apology, which treats it as a two-party moral exchange of admitted fault and regret, separates it from excuses and justifications, and compares interpersonal, institutional and cross-cultural forms.

title: Media richness theory
aliases: Daft and Lengel's media richness model
summary: Daft and Lengel's 1980s theory that communication media differ in their capacity to change understanding quickly ("richness") and that work goes best when ambiguous, equivocal messages travel through rich media and routine, unambiguous ones through lean media.

title: Media synchronicity theory
summary: Dennis and Valacich's theory that a medium's fit depends on the communication process at hand, not on the task as a whole: low-synchronicity media such as email and documents suit conveying information, while high-synchronicity media such as calls and meetings suit converging on a shared meaning, so most team tasks go best with a deliberate mix of channels.

title: Meeting agendas
summary: Planning and circulating, before a meeting, a short written list of the questions the group must answer, with the purpose, owner and time for each, so attendees can prepare and the meeting can be steered and ended against it.
selfCheck: Could each attendee tell from the agenda alone what the meeting must decide and what they should prepare?
Is every item phrased as a question that needs this whole group, or could some be handled by email?
Did the agenda reach people early enough for them to actually prepare?
At the end, can I point to an answer for each question on the agenda?
steps: Ask the people who will attend what they need the meeting to settle, and include only items that need this whole group.
Write each item as a question the group must answer, not a topic label.
Mark each item as share, seek input or decide, and name who leads it and how many minutes it gets.
Use the questions to set the invite list - invite only the people needed to answer them - and cancel if you cannot write any questions.
Circulate the written agenda, with any pre-reading, far enough ahead for people to prepare.
Open the meeting by restating its purpose, follow the agenda, and end when the questions are answered.

example.situation: A team lead schedules a 45-minute meeting with six colleagues about next quarter's office move.
example.before: Agenda: 1. Office move update 2. Desk allocation 3. AOB
example.after: Purpose: agree the move plan. 1. (Decide, Priya, 15 min) Which two weeks in March should we move? 2. (Seek input, Tom, 20 min) Under what conditions should we reallocate desks to hybrid staff? 3. (Share, me, 5 min) What changes for parking? Please read the floor plan before Tuesday.
example.why: Questions show what counts as done, the labels tell people whether they are deciding or just listening, and the named owners and pre-reading let them arrive prepared instead of reacting cold.

title: Meeting recaps
summary: Sending, soon after a meeting, a short written record of what was decided, who will do what by when, and what remains open, so attendees and absentees share one account of the outcome and can act on it.
selfCheck: Could someone who missed the meeting tell from my recap alone what was decided and what they need to do?
Does every action have exactly one named owner and a date, or did I write "we will" or "the team"?
Did each owner agree to their task out loud before we left, rather than discovering it in my email?
Have I separated firm decisions from open questions so nobody mistakes a suggestion for a commitment?
steps: Before the meeting ends, read the decisions and action items aloud and get each owner to confirm their task and date in the room.
Within 24 hours, send the recap to everyone who attended and everyone affected who was absent.
Put the decisions first, each as one plain sentence stating what was agreed.
List each action as owner, verb-first task and due date - one named person per action, not a team.
Add a short "open questions" list naming who will resolve each one and where it lands next (a later agenda, a subgroup).
Ask readers to reply with corrections by a stated time, then treat the uncorrected recap as the record.
Start the next meeting by checking the previous recap's actions before new business.

example.situation: A product manager follows up a 40-minute cross-team meeting about a delayed release.
example.before: Thanks all for a great discussion today! Lots of good ideas about the release. Let's keep the momentum going and circle back next week.
example.after: Decided: release moves to 18 March; the export feature ships in the April update. Actions: Ana - tell the three pilot customers about the new date by Thu 5 Mar. Raj - rebuild the test plan without export by Mon 9 Mar. Me - update the public roadmap by Fri 6 Mar. Open: whether support needs extra training (Lee to decide by our 12 Mar meeting). Reply by noon tomorrow if I've got anything wrong.
example.why: The first version records a mood, not an outcome; the second lets anyone - including people who missed the meeting - see what changed, who owns each next step and when to expect it, and gives a deadline for correcting the record.

title: Mehrabian's 7-38-55 rule
summary: The popular claim that only 7% of a message's meaning comes from words, 38% from tone of voice and 55% from facial expression and body language; it overgeneralises two narrow 1967 lab studies about inconsistent cues for liking, and Mehrabian himself says it does not apply to communication in general.

title: Message Equivocality, Media Selection, and Manager Performance
summary: A 1987 MIS Quarterly article by Richard Daft, Robert Lengel and Linda Klebe Trevino that turned media richness theory into a claim about managerial skill: managers tend to send ambiguous messages through rich media and clear ones through lean media, and higher performers match the two more closely.

title: Message structure
summary: The order and grouping of the points in a message, document or talk: what comes first, how ideas are grouped and sequenced, and how that arrangement is signalled to the audience. Good structure follows what the reader needs and how they are likely to react, not the order in which the writer worked things out.

title: Michael Argyle
summary: Oxford social psychologist (1925-2002) who made gaze and other nonverbal signals a mainstream research topic, proposed with Janet Dean the equilibrium (affiliative conflict) theory of eye contact and distance, and treated everyday social interaction as a learnable skill, an idea behind modern communication-skills training.

title: Michael Ross
summary: University of Waterloo social psychologist who, with Fiore Sicoly, named and demonstrated egocentric bias in shared work (people claim more credit for joint outcomes than partners grant them), and who co-authored the landmark studies of the planning fallacy behind today's advice on realistic estimates.

title: Mirroring
summary: Deliberately repeating a few of the other person's own words (and, more loosely, matching their phrasing or posture) to signal attention and invite them to say more; lab studies link early, subtle mimicry to more trust and better negotiation outcomes, but the rapport effect does not always replicate.
selfCheck: Did I repeat their words with curiosity, or did it sound like an accusation or a parrot?
Did I stay quiet long enough after the mirror for them to add something?
Have I mirrored so many times in a row that it is becoming noticeable?
Am I mirroring to understand them, or only to steer them toward a position I already hold?
steps: Let the other person finish their point before you respond, and notice the one to three words that carry the most weight or the most ambiguity.
Repeat those words back as a short question, in a calm and curious tone ("Under-resourced?").
Stop talking for a few seconds so they can expand, rather than filling the silence with your own view.
Use what they add to ask a follow-up or summarise, and switch to paraphrasing or labeling if a second mirror would start to sound mechanical.
In writing, mirror sparingly and early - reuse their terms and framing in your first replies instead of substituting your own jargon.

example.situation: In a project check-in, a vendor account manager says the delivery date "should be fine, assuming the integration piece doesn't get messy."
example.before: Great, so we're on track for the 14th. Next item.
example.after: Gets messy? ... (pause)
example.why: The two-word mirror targets the hedge, and the pause lets the vendor explain the open API dependency now, while there is still time to plan around it, instead of after the date slips.

title: Mixed messages
summary: A message whose words say one thing while the voice, face or posture says another, such as "I'm fine" in a flat, clipped tone. Listeners resolve the conflict in ways the speaker cannot control, usually by trusting the tone when the topic is feelings, so the intended point is lost.
selfCheck: If someone heard only my tone and saw only my face, would they reach the same conclusion as from my words?
Am I saying "it's fine" or "no problem" about something I am actually unhappy with?
When someone's words and manner just disagreed, did I ask, or did I silently pick one and act on it?
Would this listener's culture lead them to weigh my tone more, or my words more, than I expect?

title: Monroe's motivated sequence
summary: A five-step pattern for persuasive speaking - attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action - devised by Purdue speech professor Alan H. Monroe in the 1930s and still taught as the standard outline for proposals that ask an audience to act. It is a useful planning checklist, but the one controlled test found it made a message no more persuasive than the same content in another order.

title: Morton Deutsch
summary: Social psychologist (1920-2017) at Teachers College, Columbia University, regarded as one of the founders of the conflict resolution field; his theory of cooperation and competition explains why shared goals open up communication and trust while win-lose goals close them down, and why conflicts tend to spiral in whichever direction they start.

title: Multicultural team
summary: A work team whose members bring different national or cultural backgrounds - and often different first languages - to a shared task. Its communication challenges are predictable (direct vs. indirect styles, fluency gaps, attitudes to hierarchy, decision norms), and how the team handles them decides whether diversity shows up as extra creativity or extra conflict.

title: Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers
summary: Opening or moving a multi-issue negotiation by putting two or three complete packages on the table at the same time, each worth about the same to you but built differently, and asking the other side which one works best for them.
selfCheck: Are my packages really equivalent in value to me, or have I hidden a preferred option among decoys?
Is every package above my walk-away point and more ambitious than my target?
Have I kept it to two or three options so the other side can compare them?
Am I ready to respond to cherry-picking with new packages instead of single concessions?
Is everything I say about the packages - including that I would accept any of them - true?
steps: List every issue that is genuinely negotiable (price, scope, timing, payment terms, support, duration) and give each a weight that reflects how much it matters to you.
For each issue, write the realistic range of options and score them so that options you prefer earn more points.

Build two or three complete packages that score about the same in total for you but trade the issues off differently - for example, higher price with faster delivery versus lower price with a longer commitment.
Check every package against your BATNA and make all of them more ambitious than your target, so there is still room to move.
Present the packages together, say you would be comfortable with any of them, and ask which one fits the other side best - or, if none does, which is closest and why.
Treat their choice as information about their priorities; if they combine the best parts of different packages, reply with a fresh set of equivalent packages rather than conceding piece by piece.

example.situation: A consulting manager is proposing terms for a follow-on analytics engagement to a client's procurement lead.
example.before: Our proposal is a 12-week engagement at $240K, paid monthly, with two analysts on site. Let us know if that works.
example.after: We've put together three options we'd be glad to do. A: 12 weeks, $240K, two analysts on site, monthly billing. B: 16 weeks, $255K, one analyst on site plus remote support, quarterly billing. C: 10 weeks, $215K, two analysts, with your team owning the dashboard build. Which of these fits your budget cycle and team best - or which is closest?
example.why: Each package is worth roughly the same to the firm, so any choice is acceptable; the client gets a real choice instead of a take-it-or-counter offer, and their pick reveals whether they care most about price, duration or internal capacity.

title: MUM effect
summary: The reluctance people feel about passing on unwelcome information, which leads them to delay, soften, distort or withhold bad news - especially upward, to a boss or client - so problems surface late, when they are more expensive to fix.
selfCheck: Is there something I know about this project that my manager or client would want to hear today, and that I am waiting to "get more certainty" on?
In this update, have I said the bad news plainly in the first lines, or hidden it under progress and qualifiers?
Am I staying quiet mainly to spare them distress, to avoid blame, or because I think nothing will change - and would they agree with that trade-off?
As the person receiving reports, what happened the last time someone brought me bad news early?

title: Murray Turoff
summary: Computer scientist (died 2022) at the New Jersey Institute of Technology who built EMISARI (1971) and EIES, early computer conferencing systems that let groups discuss and decide in writing without meeting at the same place or time, and who co-wrote The Network Nation (1978), the standard early reference on computer-mediated communication.

title: Mythical fixed-pie bias
summary: The default assumption, often held before a negotiation even starts, that the other side's interests are directly opposed to yours, so that anything they gain you must lose. It hides trades that would leave both sides better off.
selfCheck: Have I listed every issue in this deal, or am I treating it as one number to fight over?
Do I actually know which issues matter most to the other side, or am I assuming they want the opposite of what I want?
Is there an issue where we might want the same outcome that I have not checked out loud?
Am I discounting their proposal because of who made it rather than what it gives each of us?

title: Narrative persuasion
summary: Making a case through a true, representative story - a particular character facing a problem, with causes and consequences unfolding over time - so that the audience is absorbed in it, rather than through argument or statistics alone; it works mainly through narrative transportation.
selfCheck: Is this story true, and is it typical of the problem rather than the most extreme case I could find?
Does the story lead directly to my request, or is it just a warm-up anecdote?
Have I given the numbers that show how often this happens, so the audience can judge how far the story generalises?
Would I be comfortable if the person in the story, or a sceptical colleague, heard how I told it?
steps: Decide what you want the listener to think, feel or do at the end, and where they start from today.
Pick one true case that is typical of the problem, not the most dramatic one you can find, and check you may share it (anonymise people and clients).
Build it around a specific character with a goal, an obstacle, what happened and why, and the stakes - concrete enough that the listener can picture it.
Open with the story or a hook from it, keep it short, and cut details that do not move the cause-and-effect chain forward.
Put the numbers right after it to show the story is representative, and say so explicitly ("this happened to roughly one in five new customers last quarter").
Close by linking the story to your specific request, then test it on a colleague and ask what stuck and what felt unconvincing.

example.situation: A product manager asks the leadership team to fund a redesign of the customer onboarding flow.
example.before: Onboarding completion is 61%, down 7 points year on year. Support tickets in the first 30 days are up 18%. I'd like two sprints to redesign the flow.
example.after: Last month a 40-person logistics firm signed with us on a Monday. By Thursday their admin had opened four tickets, still couldn't import their driver list, and asked about cancelling. That isn't unusual: completion is down to 61% and early tickets are up 18%. Two sprints on the import and setup steps would fix the exact place she got stuck. Can we add it to Q1?
example.why: The rewrite gives leaders one concrete, typical customer to picture and follow from cause to consequence, then uses the figures to show the case is representative and ends with the ask - pairing the story's pull on intentions with the statistics' pull on beliefs.

title: Negotiation
summary: The recurring situation in which two or more people who need each other's cooperation to reach their goals talk their way to an agreement that leaves them better off than the status quo - from a job offer or a vendor contract to a deadline, a budget or a share of a colleague's time.

title: Negotiation preparation
summary: The planning work done before and between negotiation sessions - clarifying issues, interests, alternatives, walk-away and target points, the other side's likely position, and the logistics of the talks - so that you can create and claim value and adapt when the conversation surprises you.

title: Neil Rackham
summary: British behavioural researcher and founder of the Huthwaite research group whose direct observation of real negotiations and sales calls - notably the 1978 skilled-negotiator study with John Carlisle and the SPIN selling research - turned habits such as testing understanding, summarizing and asking questions into named, countable behaviours that can be trained.

title: Nicholas Epley
summary: University of Chicago Booth behavioural scientist whose experiments on how people read other minds produced two practical correctives for egocentric communication: considering others' contributions before claiming credit, and getting someone's perspective by asking rather than imagining it.

title: Nominal group technique
summary: A structured meeting method for generating and prioritising ideas in which people first write ideas silently and alone, then share them one at a time in a round robin, clarify them, and finally rank them privately so the group's priorities come from pooled individual votes.
selfCheck: Is my question specific enough that people could write concrete answers to it on their own?
Did I protect the silent-writing and round-robin phases from early debate or evaluation, including my own?
Did each person rank privately, so seniors' preferences were not visible before others voted?
Is this really a single-question, prioritise-and-decide meeting, or does the topic need open exploration first?
steps: Write one specific, open question on the board or shared screen and read it aloud, for example "What are the biggest obstacles to closing month-end two days faster?"
Give everyone 10-20 minutes of silent, individual writing to list as many answers as they can, with no talking.
Run a round robin - each person reads out one idea per turn, which you record verbatim and number - and keep going until the lists are exhausted; allow no debate yet.
Walk through the numbered list for clarification only, letting anyone explain an item, and merge true duplicates with the agreement of the people who raised them.
Ask each person to privately pick and rank their top five items (5 points for the most important down to 1), then tally the scores in front of the group.
Discuss the top-ranked items and the surprises in the tally, and, if the scores are close, run a second private vote before you commit to next steps.

example.situation: An operations manager runs a one-hour meeting with eight team members, including two senior leads, to decide which process problems to fix first next quarter.
example.before: Okay, open floor - what should we fix first? ... Great point, Sam [senior lead], the ticketing tool is a mess. Anyone disagree? No? Let's go with that.
example.after: Take ten minutes and write down, on your own, every process problem that slows you down. Then we'll go round the table one idea at a time, I'll number them, and everyone ranks their top five privately before we talk priorities.
example.why: The open floor lets the first senior voice anchor the room and blocks quieter people from offering ideas; silent writing and private ranking let every member contribute and weigh in equally before status and conversation shape the outcome.

title: Nonverbal communication
summary: Creating and reading meaning through behaviour other than words, such as facial movement, gesture, posture, gaze, voice, touch, space and time; it shapes impressions and relationships at work, but single cues are ambiguous and people are far worse at reading lies or exact emotions from them than popular "body language" advice claims.

title: Nonviolent Communication
summary: Marshall Rosenberg's four-part model for saying hard things and hearing them: describe what you observed without evaluation, name the feeling it stirs, link that feeling to an underlying need, and make a concrete, doable request rather than a demand - and listen for the same four elements in the other person.
selfCheck: Could the other person agree my observation is accurate, or have I slipped in an evaluation?
Is my "feeling" an emotion, or a hidden accusation about what they did to me?
Have I named the need behind my position, separately from the one solution I want?
If they decline my request, am I ready to explore other ways to meet the need - or was it really a demand?
steps: Write down what happened as a camera would record it - who did what, when - and strike out every label, motive or "always".
Name the feeling it stirs in you using an emotion word (worried, frustrated, relieved), not a thought dressed as a feeling ("I feel ignored", "I feel that you...").
Identify the need or value behind the feeling (predictability, fairness, being able to do good work) and keep it separate from your preferred solution.
Turn your preferred solution into one concrete, doable request for now, phrased as what you do want, and be ready to hear "no".
If they say no or react strongly, listen for their observation, feeling, need and request, and reflect those back before restating yours.

example.situation: A team lead's colleague has twice changed a shared project plan the night before a client review without telling anyone.
example.before: You keep going rogue on the plan. It's disrespectful, and if it happens again I'm escalating it.
example.after: The plan changed on Monday night and again last night, and I found out in the client call. I was rattled, because I need to be able to stand behind what we show the client. Would you be willing to post changes in the channel by 5 p.m. the day before a review, starting this week? And what's been pushing those late changes?
example.why: The rewrite swaps a judgement ("going rogue", "disrespectful") and a threat for a checkable observation, a feeling, the need behind it and a specific request that the colleague can accept or renegotiate, then invites their side instead of assuming a motive.

title: Norbert Wiener
summary: MIT mathematician (1894-1964) who founded cybernetics, the study of control and communication in animals and machines, and carried the engineering idea of feedback - correcting action by the gap between actual result and goal - into the behavioural and social sciences.

title: Note-taking while listening
summary: Writing brief, selective notes in your own words while someone speaks, so you can recall what they said, check it back with them and follow through on what was agreed, without letting the notes replace attention.
selfCheck: Was I looking at the person more than at my notes?
Could I read my notes back as a short summary in my own words rather than a transcript?
Have I marked every commitment I made, and when will I act on each one?
steps: Before the conversation, write the two or three questions you need answered so your notes have a structure to hang on.
While the other person speaks, keep your eyes on them and jot only keywords, numbers, names and their exact phrasing of anything contentious.
Mark commitments, decisions and open questions with a symbol (for example a box for actions) so they stand out later.
At natural pauses, read the key points back in your own words and ask whether you have them right.
Within a day, review the notes, turn marked items into a written recap and act on what you promised.

example.situation: A team lead holds a one-on-one with an engineer who is worried about an upcoming release.
example.before: The lead types steadily on a laptop throughout, capturing nearly every sentence, rarely looks up, ends with 'Thanks, I've got it all down,' and never mentions the notes again.
example.after: The lead jots a few words on paper while keeping eye contact, then says: 'Let me check I have this: the two integrations are untested, and you want the risk flagged to the director before Friday. I'll do that by Thursday and copy you.' The lead sends that recap the same afternoon.
example.why: Selective notes in the lead's own words kept attention on the speaker, allowed an accurate read-back, and turned the conversation into a visible follow-up, which is often what makes people feel heard.

title: Manager one-on-one meetings
summary: Recurring, scheduled conversations between a manager and one direct report, held live and focused mainly on the direct report's needs - priorities, roadblocks, feedback, wellbeing and development - rather than on the manager's status updates.

title: One remote, all remote
summary: A meeting norm under which, if any attendee is remote, everyone joins individually from their own device, camera and microphone, even colleagues sitting in the same office, so no shared conference room becomes a privileged hub and all participants meet on the same screen.
selfCheck: Is anyone joining remotely, and if so, have I asked everyone else to join from their own device?
Can every attendee see the same agenda, slides and notes on their own screen?
Does this meeting gain enough from being in one room to justify the cost to remote colleagues?
Will people in the office be adding more video hours than they can sustain this week?
steps: Before sending the invite, check whether anyone will be remote; if even one person is, make the meeting all-online and say so in the invite.
Ask in-office attendees to join from their own laptop at their desk or in separate small rooms, each with a camera and a headset.
If several people must share one physical room, have them join with their laptop microphones and speakers off and only one room audio device live, so the call does not echo.
Put the agenda, slides and notes in one shared document everyone opens on their own screen, rather than on a wall display or whiteboard only the room can see.
Run turn-taking through the platform for everyone, using hand-raise, chat and an explicit speaking order, and post decisions and actions in a written recap afterwards.

Review the norm for meetings where nobody is remote or where the room's benefits are large, such as hands-on workshops or relationship-building sessions, and choose in person or hybrid there on purpose.

example.situation: A product team of eight holds its weekly planning meeting; five sit in the office and three, including a new hire, work from home.
example.before: The five in the office gather in a conference room around one speakerphone and room camera, sketch the plan on the whiteboard and talk over each other, while the three remote colleagues see a wide shot of the room, miss side remarks and are asked "anything from the people online?" at the end.
example.after: The organizer's invite says "One remote, all remote: please join from your own laptop." The five in the office join from their desks with headsets, everyone edits the same planning document, the facilitator takes updates in screen order and invites the new hire to go first, and the decisions are posted in the team channel.
example.why: Everyone now hears, sees and gets the floor through the same channel, so the room no longer forms an in-group that leaves the remote three, and especially the newest member, on the margins.

title: Open-ended questions
summary: Questions that cannot be answered with "yes", "no" or a single fact - typically starting with "what" or "how" - asked to let the other person explain in their own words, so you learn what they know, think and need rather than what you assumed.
selfCheck: Could the other person have answered my question with one word, and was that what I really wanted?
Did my next question build on their answer, or did I jump to my own agenda?
Did I ask a "why" question where a "what" or "how" would have felt less like a demand for justification?
When I needed a firm answer on a specific risk, did I ask a direct, specific question instead of a vague one?
steps: Decide what you actually need to learn - their view, the obstacles, the options - before you ask anything.
Open with "what" or "how" ("What's getting in the way?", "How did the client react?") instead of "Is", "Do" or "Did".
Stop talking and let them answer fully; resist offering a suggested answer if they pause.
Build your next question on what they just said ("You mentioned the handover - what happened there?") rather than switching topic.
Reflect back what you heard before asking another question, so the exchange does not become an interrogation.
Switch to a closed or specific question when you need a commitment, a number, or a straight answer to a known risk ("Will this slip past the 30th?").

example.situation: A team lead checks in with an engineer on a database migration that has gone quiet for a week.
example.before: Is the migration still on track for the end of the month?
example.after: What's the part of the migration you're least confident about right now?
example.why: The closed question invites a reflexive "yes"; the open one asks for an explanation and presumes there is some uncertainty, which makes it easier to surface a problem early.

title: Organizational communication
summary: The academic field that studies how people in organizations create shared meaning through verbal, nonverbal and mediated messages, and how that communication coordinates work, shapes culture and, in some views, constitutes the organization itself; it supplies the research behind much workplace advice on channels, upward communication, supervisor talk and information flow.

title: Paralanguage
summary: The meaning carried by how something is said rather than which words are used: pitch, volume, rate, pauses, emphasis and voice quality. At work it shapes how competent, confident and sincere a speaker seems, though the effects in controlled studies are usually modest and depend on context.

title: Paramedic method for revising prose
summary: Richard Lanham's step-by-step editing routine for wordy sentences: mark prepositions and forms of "to be", find the buried action, turn it into a simple verb with the doer as subject, then cut slow openings and redundancies.
selfCheck: In each key sentence, can I point to who does what, as a subject followed by a verb?
Which nouns ending in -tion, -ment or -ance am I using where a verb would carry the action?
Does my first sentence start with its subject, or with a wind-up I could delete?
After cutting, does the message still carry the context and tone this particular reader needs?
steps: Finish the draft first, then pick one long or important sentence to revise at a time.
Circle the prepositions (of, in, about, for, by, on) and box every form of "to be" (is, are, was, be, been).
Ask where the action is; look for it hidden in a noun such as decision, recommendation or review.
Turn that action into a simple verb and make the person or team doing it the subject.
Delete slow wind-ups ("It is important to note that", "The purpose of this email is to") so the sentence starts with its subject.
Remove redundancies and leftover words, then count words removed divided by the original count (the lard factor).
Read the revised passage aloud and restore any context, courtesy or emphasis the reader still needs.

example.situation: A project lead's status email asks the steering committee to choose a vendor.
example.before: It is the recommendation of the project team that a decision on the selection of a vendor be made by the steering committee by the end of the month.
example.after: The project team recommends that the steering committee choose a vendor by month-end.
example.why: The actions buried in "recommendation", "decision" and "selection" become two verbs with named actors, the wind-up disappears, and 29 words drop to 13 (a lard factor of about 55%) without losing the request or deadline.

title: Paraphrasing
summary: Restating, in your own words, the substance of what someone has just said - and, where it matters, the feeling and priority behind it - then checking whether you have understood them correctly before you respond with your own view.
selfCheck: Did I restate their point in my own words, or did I just repeat their phrases back like a parrot?
Did I capture what mattered to them and how they felt, not only the facts?
Did I end with a genuine check ("Have I got that right?") and accept a correction without defending myself?
Did I hold back my own view until they agreed I had understood them?
steps: Listen to the whole point without planning your reply; note the facts, what the speaker seems to feel and what seems most important to them.
Wait for a natural pause, then restate the core of their message in one or two sentences, using your own words rather than echoing theirs.
Where feelings are clearly present, name the feeling and its cause tentatively ("it sounds like the late change left you frustrated").
End with a check question such as "Have I got that right?" or "What did I miss?" and accept corrections without arguing.
If they correct you, paraphrase the corrected version; follow up with an open question if something is still unclear.
Only once they confirm you have understood, give your own perspective, answer or proposal.

example.situation: An operations lead tells a project manager that the new vendor's delivery schedule will not work for the warehouse, and the PM's instinct is to defend the schedule.
example.before: The schedule was signed off by procurement last month, so we really can't change it now. Let's just make it work.
example.after: So if I've understood you, the Tuesday deliveries land on the same morning as the weekly stock count, which means your team either delays the count or leaves trucks waiting - and you're worried we'll start paying demurrage. Is that the main problem, or is there more to it?
example.why: The rewrite restates the specific facts and the concern behind them in the PM's own words and invites correction, so the operations lead can confirm or fix the picture before anyone argues for a solution.

title: Penance and restitution after a breach
aliases: compensating for a breach of trust
summary: Backing an acknowledgement of a breach with something concrete and costly to you that puts the other person's loss right, such as giving back time, covering their extra work or honouring the broken commitment, so that your words of regret become a credible signal and trust can recover.
selfCheck: Have I named what this cost them, not just that I am sorry?
Does my offer actually restore their position, and does it cost me something real?
Am I offering this alongside a clear acknowledgement, or using it to avoid one?
If my intent is ambiguous to them, have I made clear the breach was not deliberate, and if it was deliberate, have I accepted that money or favours alone will not fix it?
Will I keep my next few commitments to this person visibly, so the amends is not a one-off gesture?
steps: Work out what the breach actually cost the other person (hours, money, a missed opportunity, an awkward moment with their own boss) before you decide what to offer.
Acknowledge the breach in the first person and name that cost, so the amends reads as repair rather than a bribe to move on.
Offer something concrete that at least restores their position - honour the original commitment, return the time, take on the rework - and make it cost you something real.
Ask what would put things right for them, framing the question so the responsibility stays with you, and treat their answer as a guide rather than an opening bid.
Deliver the amends promptly and completely; then keep your next commitments to them visibly, because consistent behaviour is what finishes the repair.

example.situation: A team lead promised a senior analyst she would lead the client workshop she had prepared for, then gave the slot to a newer colleague without telling her.
example.before: Sorry about the workshop mix-up - things moved fast and I didn't think it through. I'll make sure you get the next one.
example.after: I promised you the Henley workshop and gave it away without telling you, and that's on me - you lost the client exposure you had worked for. I've already asked Henley's sponsor to add you as co-lead for the follow-up session on the 28th, and I'll introduce you as the owner of the analysis. Is there anything else that would make this right for you? From now on any change to a role I've promised goes to the person first.
example.why: The vague apology plus a future maybe costs the lead nothing, so it reads as cheap talk; the rewrite names the loss, restores a comparable opportunity with a date, invites her view of what is fair while keeping responsibility with the lead, and adds a change that makes a repeat less likely.

title: Perception checking
summary: A short, three-part move for testing your reading of someone's behaviour before acting on it: describe what you noticed without judging it, offer two possible interpretations, and ask the other person which (if either) is right.
selfCheck: What exactly did I see or hear, and what part of my reaction is my own interpretation of it?
Have I come up with at least two different explanations, or am I treating my first reading as fact?
Would my description sound like an observation to them, or like an accusation?
Did I actually ask, and did I let their answer replace my guess?
steps: Notice the moment you have started to explain someone's behaviour to yourself ("she's annoyed", "he doesn't buy it"), and treat that explanation as a guess.
Describe only what you saw or heard, specifically and without a verdict, e.g. "You went quiet when I mentioned the deadline."
Offer two plausible, non-accusing interpretations, e.g. "I wasn't sure if the date worries you or if something else is on your mind."
Ask an open question that hands the answer back, e.g. "Which is it, or is it something else?", then listen and accept the correction.
Act on what they tell you, not on your first guess, and paraphrase it back if the answer matters.

example.situation: In a weekly one-on-one, a team lead proposes moving a launch forward by two weeks. The engineer says "Sure, that works" but pauses, looks down and stops taking notes.
example.before: Great, glad you're on board. I'll tell the client Friday.
example.after: You said it works, but you paused and stopped writing when I said two weeks. I can't tell if the date feels tight or if something else is bothering you. Which is it?
example.why: The first version silently picks the words over the manner and commits the team to a date the engineer may not believe in. The check names the observed behaviour, offers two face-saving readings and invites the real concern before the promise is made.

title: Performance review
summary: The formal, periodic conversation - usually annual or semi-annual - in which a manager and an employee look back at the employee's performance against agreed expectations, discuss a rating or assessment of record, and agree goals and development for the next period.

title: Perspective-getting
summary: Finding out what another person thinks, wants or feels by asking them directly and listening to the answer, instead of imagining their view from your own position - the method that research finds actually improves accuracy about other minds.
selfCheck: Which of my beliefs about this person's view did I hear from them, and which did I only imagine?
Have I asked about every point my decision depends on, or only the one I was least sure of?
Did I restate their answer and let them correct it?
Would they feel safe telling me something I don't want to hear?
Am I skipping the question because I feel sure - and is that certainty based on anything they told me?
steps: Before a decision that depends on someone else's view, write down your best guess of what they think and how confident you are.
Turn each guess into a short, neutral question you can put to them directly, covering every point that matters rather than one or two.
Ask, then listen to the whole answer without arguing, and note anything that contradicts your guess.
Restate what you heard in your own words and ask whether you have it right.
Make an honest answer safe - say why you are asking, show you can hear an unwelcome reply, and never penalise one.
Where you cannot ask, get the information another way - a survey, their written priorities, or someone who has been in their position - and treat any remaining guess as a hypothesis.

example.situation: A team lead is planning next quarter's on-call rota and assumes the senior engineers want fewer weekend shifts in exchange for more weekday nights.
example.before: Team lead (to their manager) - I've redone the rota so seniors get fewer weekends. I know they'd rather take extra weeknights; they've got families.
example.after: Team lead (to each engineer, in one-on-ones) - I'm redrawing the on-call rota. Which matters more to you, fewer weekends or fewer weeknights, and is there anything about the current set-up I'm not seeing? So, if I've got it right, weekends are fine but back-to-back nights are the real problem?
example.why: The lead swaps a confident guess for a quick question about each point that matters and a check of the answer, and finds that the actual complaint (consecutive nights) is not the one they had planned to fix.

title: Perspective-taking
summary: The deliberate mental effort to understand a situation from another person's point of view - their interests, goals, constraints and likely reasoning - used as a hypothesis to test rather than a conclusion, ideally confirmed by asking.
selfCheck: Can I state what the other person is trying to achieve and what constrains them, without using my own goals?
Which of my beliefs about their view did I actually hear from them, and which did I only imagine?
What one question would confirm or overturn my best guess about their position?
Am I trying to understand their reasoning, or just feeling sorry for them in a way that will make me give ground I need?
Has imagining their side made me more suspicious or more competitive than the facts warrant?

title: Persuasion
summary: The learnable skill of changing what another person believes, feels or does through communication - credible reasons, framing and evidence - while leaving them free to say no, which separates it from pressure, coercion and manipulation.
selfCheck: Can I say, in the other person's terms, what they gain if they agree with me?
Have I earned credibility on this topic with this audience, or am I assuming it?
Am I giving reasons and evidence, or leaning on pressure, rank or urgency I have not justified?
What would change my own mind, and am I willing to adjust the proposal if I hear it?
Would I be comfortable if they saw exactly how I prepared this pitch?

title: Philip Crosby
summary: American quality-management consultant (1926-2001), ITT's corporate quality vice-president and author of Quality Is Free (1979), whose 1981 advice that managers prepare a one-minute "elevator speech" for the big boss is the earliest documented print use of the idea behind the elevator pitch.

title: Phone call
summary: A live, voice-only conversation by telephone or an audio-only internet call. It carries tone, pacing and pauses that text strips out, so it builds connection and conveys feeling well, but with no visual channel it gathers less detail and hides misunderstandings unless the caller structures the call, speaks clearly and checks understanding out loud.
selfCheck: Am I about to send a long email or chat thread only because I expect the call to feel awkward?
Does this conversation need diagrams, numbers or a careful record, so that it should be written or followed by a written summary?
Did I open the call by saying why I am calling and how long it will take?
Did I ask the other person to repeat back any number, date or decision we agreed?
When they went quiet, did I wait and ask rather than assume they agreed?

title: Plain language
summary: The principle of writing so that the intended readers can find what they need, understand it and use it the first time they read it, by writing for that audience in familiar words, clear structure and direct sentences.
selfCheck: Who exactly is reading this, and what do they already know about the subject?
Which terms here did I learn inside my team or field, and have I replaced or defined each one where it first appears?
Could a reader say in their own words what I want them to do next?

title: Politeness theory
summary: Politeness theory, set out by Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson (1978, 1987), explains polite language as a way of managing face: requests, criticism and disagreement threaten the hearer's wish to be liked (positive face) or left unimposed upon (negative face), and speakers choose more or less redressive strategies depending on social distance, relative power and the size of the imposition.

title: Power distance
summary: The degree to which people in a society, team or relationship accept that power and status are unequally distributed; it shapes whether juniors volunteer views, disagree openly or wait to be asked, but it varies as much between individuals and occupations as between countries.

title: Power posing
summary: The claim that holding an expansive, "high-power" body posture for a minute or two before a stressful event raises testosterone, lowers cortisol and makes people bolder; larger replications found no hormonal or risk-taking effect, leaving at most a small boost to how powerful people say they feel.

title: Pragmatics
summary: The study of how people mean more than their words literally say: how context, intention and shared assumptions turn a sentence into a request, a promise, a hint or an insult. Named by Charles Morris in 1938, it supplies the ideas behind implicature, speech acts and politeness that explain most everyday misreadings at work.

title: Praise and recognition
summary: Telling people, specifically and soon, what they did well and why it mattered, so that useful behaviour is repeated and people feel their contribution is valued; recognition reliably lifts performance and helping, but vague praise carries little information and popular "magic ratio" rules outrun their evidence.
selfCheck: Could the person tell from my words exactly which action I am praising and what it changed?
Am I praising effort and choices they control, or a fixed trait like talent or intelligence?
Did I slip a correction or a new request into this message, turning it into a sandwich?
Who on my team has done good work in the last couple of weeks without hearing about it?
Is this praise earned, or am I handing it out to avoid a harder conversation?
steps: Notice the specific behaviour worth repeating - an action you saw, not a trait such as "smart" or "a natural".
Say what the person did, when, and what it made possible for the team, client or project, in one or two sentences.
Deliver it soon after the work, in the channel the person values (a quiet one-to-one, a team thread, or a note copied to their manager).
Keep it clean - do not attach a correction, a "but", or a new request to the same message.
Make recognition a weekly habit across the whole team, and check who you have not recognized lately.
Thank people who help you outside their job, naming what their help changed, so they know it was wanted.

example.situation: A project manager recognizes an analyst who rebuilt a broken client data feed the night before a steering-committee meeting.
example.before: Great job everyone, thanks for all the hard work this week! You're all rock stars.
example.after: Sam - thank you for rebuilding the client data feed on Tuesday night. Because the numbers reconciled, the steering committee approved phase 2 in the meeting instead of deferring it a month. The validation checks you added are now our standard; I've told Dana how you handled it.
example.why: The rewrite names the person, the action and its concrete consequence, so Sam knows exactly what to repeat and that it mattered; the blanket message gives no information and quietly lumps a standout effort with routine work.

title: Premortem
summary: A short meeting exercise, usually run at a project kickoff, in which the leader tells the team to imagine the plan has already failed and each person writes down, then shares, the reasons why. It makes raising doubts the expected contribution instead of a disloyal one, so risks and warnings reach the decision maker before the commitment is locked in.
selfCheck: Am I running this before the decision is locked in, or only to look thorough after it is?
Did I state the failure as certain and give people time to write on their own before anyone spoke?
Did I go first with a real weakness in my own plan, and did I keep myself and other senior people from defending the plan during the round?
Which reasons changed the plan, and have I told the team what we are doing about them?
Is there someone who raised a concern quietly afterwards because the meeting still did not feel safe enough?
steps: Schedule it once the plan is clear but before anything is signed, announced or funded, and invite the people who will do the work, not only the planners.
Briefly restate the plan, then say it as a certainty - "it is a year from now and this project has failed" - rather than asking whether it might fail.
Give everyone two to three minutes to write, silently and alone, every reason they can think of for the failure.
Go around the room taking one reason per person per round until the lists are exhausted, with the leader going first and offering a real weakness of their own plan.
Record every reason where all can see it without debating or defending, and stop anyone senior from dominating the round.
Rate the reasons for likelihood and impact, assign owners to the top few, and change, test or monitor the plan accordingly.
Send a short note of what was raised and what will change, so people see that their warnings were heard and acted on.

example.situation: A team lead is kicking off a migration of the company's billing system to a new platform, with a go-live date already promised to finance.
example.before: So that's the plan - we go live on 1 March. It's tight but I'm confident. Anyone see any problems? No? Great, let's get started.
example.after: Before we start, imagine it's April and the migration has failed badly. Take three minutes and write down every reason why - on your own. Then we'll go round one at a time; I'll go first: I think I've underestimated how long finance will need to sign off the test invoices.
example.why: An open call for problems from a confident leader invites silence; declaring the failure as fact, writing alone first and having the leader model candor makes naming risks the task everyone is doing, so the doubts surface while the plan can still change.

title: Presentation
summary: A planned, mostly one-way talk in which one person (or a small team) takes the floor to inform, persuade or ask a group for something, usually with slides and a fixed time slot. It works when the speaker sets a clear goal, gives the talk a simple structure, keeps slides within what an audience can absorb, and plans for questions.

title: Presentation rehearsal
summary: Practising a talk out loud, on your feet and in conditions close to the real event - ideally in front of a few listeners who give feedback - before you deliver it. Time spent rehearsing aloud and before an audience is linked to better-rated speeches.
selfCheck: Have I said the whole talk out loud, standing, at least once from start to finish?
Do I know how long it actually runs, from a timed run-through rather than a guess?
Has anyone other than me heard it and told me what was unclear?
Did I rehearse with the same slides, notes and setup I will use on the day?
steps: Start at least several days ahead and split practice into short sessions (opening, body, close) rather than one late-night cram.
Rehearse the whole talk out loud, standing, at full volume, with the slides or notes you will actually use.
Time every full run-through and cut material until you finish comfortably inside the slot.
Record one run on your phone, watch it back, and note one or two specific delivery habits to fix.
Give at least one run-through to a small live audience - three or four colleagues - and ask each for one thing that was unclear and one thing to keep.
Do a final rehearsal in the real room or on the real video setup, then stop practising and sleep.

example.situation: A product manager has a 10-minute slot to propose a pricing change to the leadership team on Thursday.
example.before: She builds the deck on Wednesday night, clicks through it silently twice at her desk, and on Thursday runs four minutes over, loses her place on slide 6 and has no answer when the CFO asks about churn.
example.after: On Monday she talks the deck through aloud and finds it runs 14 minutes, so she cuts two slides. On Tuesday she records a run, notices she reads the slides with her back to the camera, and fixes it. On Wednesday three peers sit in; one asks about churn, so she adds a backup slide. Thursday's talk ends at nine minutes.
example.why: Rehearsing aloud exposed the timing problem, the recording exposed a delivery habit she could not feel, and a live audience surfaced the question leadership was likely to ask - none of which silent clicking would reveal.

title: Primacy and recency effects
summary: The tendency for information presented first (primacy) or last (recency) in a sequence to carry more weight in what people remember and conclude than the same information in the middle; which end wins depends on how closely people process the material and when they make their judgment.

title: Principled negotiation
summary: The four-part negotiation method from the Harvard Negotiation Project and *Getting to Yes*: separate the people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, invent options for mutual gain, and insist on objective criteria, with a BATNA as the test of any deal.

title: Proxemics
summary: The study of how people use and interpret physical space in communication, above all the distance they keep from one another; anthropologist Edward T. Hall described intimate, personal, social and public zones whose comfortable size varies by culture, relationship, gender and age.

title: Psychological safety
summary: A shared belief among members of a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks - to ask a question, admit a mistake, raise a concern or disagree - without being embarrassed, rejected or punished for it.

title: Pyramid principle
summary: Barbara Minto's framework for structuring a business document or presentation as a pyramid: one governing conclusion at the top, a small set of logically grouped supporting points beneath it, and evidence at the base, usually opened with a situation-complication-question introduction.
selfCheck: Could my reader state my conclusion after reading only the first paragraph and the headings?
Does every point under a heading actually support that heading, and are my groups free of overlaps and gaps?
Am I presenting the order in which I did the work, or the order in which my reader needs the answer?
steps: Before drafting, write the single sentence you want the reader to accept or act on - your answer, not your topic.
Write the question that sentence answers, and the situation and complication that make the reader ask it.
List every supporting point, then sort them into two to four groups that each answer "why?" or "how?" about the top sentence.
Check each group - its points should be the same kind of idea, not overlap, and together cover the claim - and put them in a deliberate order (time, structure or importance).
Turn each group into a summary sentence and a heading, place the evidence under it, and reread the top sentence and headings alone to see whether they tell the whole story.

example.situation: An operations analyst writes up a three-week investigation into rising machine-tooling costs for the plant manager.
example.before: Report on tooling costs. Week 1: we collected cost data from all six machines. Week 2: we ran tests on feed rates and coolant. Week 3: we analysed the results and found several interesting patterns, which are described below, followed by some options we considered...
example.after: Recommendation: standardise coolant pressure on all six machines; we expect tooling costs to return to last year's level within a quarter. Situation: the machines ran within budget until spring. Complication: tooling costs have since risen sharply. Question: what should we change? Three findings support the answer - 1) the cost rise tracks the machines with low coolant pressure, 2) a two-week trial at higher pressure cut tool wear, 3) the change needs no new equipment. Data for each is in the sections below.
example.why: The rewrite moves from the order the analyst worked in to the order the reader thinks in - answer, then grouped reasons, then evidence - so the manager can decide from the first paragraph and check any reason in its own section.

title: Question Formulation Technique
summary: A structured, six-part practice from the Right Question Institute in which a person or group generates questions about a short prompt without discussing them, sorts them into closed and open, rewrites some from one type to the other, picks the most important, decides how to use them and reflects on what they learned - a deliberate drill for the skill of asking good questions.
selfCheck: Did I give the group a statement to question, or did I smuggle my own hypothesis in as the prompt?
Did anyone, including me, start answering or judging questions before the production phase ended?
Which of our priority questions is open, and which is closed - and did we choose that deliberately?
Does each priority question have an owner and a place where it will actually be asked?
steps: Write a question focus - a short statement, chart or fact, not a question - that names the issue you need to understand.

Set a timer for five to ten minutes and have everyone produce as many questions as they can, writing each one exactly as said, with no discussing, judging or answering, and turning any statement into a question.
Number the list and mark each question C (closed, answerable with yes/no or a single word) or O (open).
Discuss what each type is good and bad for, then rewrite at least one closed question as open and one open question as closed.
Choose the three questions that matter most against a stated criterion (for example, the ones that would most change the decision) and note why you picked them.
Agree who will take each priority question where - a stakeholder meeting, a data request, a customer interview - and by when.
Close by asking the group what they learned about asking questions and how they will use the process next time.

example.situation: A product team's kickoff after a quarterly report shows renewals fell sharply among small-business customers.
example.before: The lead opens with 'Why are renewals down?', the most senior engineer answers 'pricing', and the rest of the hour is spent debating a pricing fix.
example.after: The lead puts up the statement 'Small-business renewals fell this quarter' and asks for ten minutes of questions only. The list of 24 includes 'Did anything change in onboarding?' and 'Which customers renewed, and how are they different?'; the team converts closed questions to open, picks three priorities and assigns each to an owner before anyone proposes a fix.
example.why: A statement instead of a question avoids anchoring everyone on one cause, the no-answering rule keeps the senior voice from closing the topic, and prioritising turns a long list into a short research plan.

title: Questioning
summary: The learnable skill of choosing, phrasing, sequencing and timing questions so that they get accurate, useful answers and strengthen the working relationship - covering what to ask, how open or pointed to make it, what to assume in the wording, and when to follow up.
selfCheck: Before this conversation, did I write down the two or three things I most need to learn, rather than only what I plan to say?
Did my questions assume the answer I wanted, or did I phrase them so a problem or a "no" was easy to say?
How many of my questions built on the other person's last answer instead of changing the subject?
Did I ask for information, or did I ask questions that were really statements, tests or criticism?
After I asked, did I stay quiet long enough for a full answer?

title: Quintilian
summary: Roman teacher of rhetoric (c. AD 35 - after 96) whose twelve-book Institutio oratoria made clarity (perspicuitas) the first virtue of style and set its classic test: speak so that the listener cannot fail to understand you, not merely so that they can.

title: RACI matrix
summary: A grid that lists a piece of work's tasks or decisions down one side and the people or roles across the top, marking for each who is Responsible for doing it, who is Accountable for it, who must be Consulted before it is done and who must be Informed after.
selfCheck: For this decision, can everyone involved name the one person who makes the final call?
Is each person I have marked Consulted someone whose input could actually change the outcome?
Do the people marked Informed know when and how they will hear the result?
steps: List the recurring tasks and decisions that cause confusion as rows, and the roles involved as columns.
For each row, name exactly one Accountable owner - the person who signs off or makes the call.
Mark who is Responsible for doing the work, keeping it to as few people as possible.
Mark Consulted only for people whose input must be heard before the work is finished, and Informed for people who need the outcome afterwards.
Scan the finished grid for rows with no A, several As, many Rs or a long list of Cs, and fix them.
Share the grid with everyone named, agree it together, and use the C and I columns as the contact list for updates.

example.situation: A product team keeps arguing about who signs off on customer-facing release notes; marketing, support and engineering all edit them and the notes ship late.
example.before: Release notes - owners: Eng, Marketing, Support (everyone please review before we publish).
example.after: Release notes - R: tech writer drafts. A: product manager approves and publishes. C: lead engineer checks accuracy by Wednesday. I: support team gets the final text on release day.
example.why: One named approver ends the circular edits, the single consulted reviewer has a deadline, and support knows it will be told rather than needing to chase or review.

title: Radical candor
summary: Kim Scott's two-axis feedback framework: good managers care personally about people while challenging them directly, avoiding three failure modes - ruinous empathy (care without challenge), obnoxious aggression (challenge without care) and manipulative insincerity (neither).
selfCheck: Am I holding back this criticism to protect the person, or to protect myself from an awkward moment?
Would the person be able to tell from how I say this that I want them to succeed?
Am I describing what they did, or judging who they are?
When did I last ask my team for criticism of me, and what did I change as a result?

title: Rapport
summary: A shared, momentary quality of an interaction in which both people are attentive to each other, feel mutual warmth and move in coordination; it belongs to the pair rather than to either person, and it makes disclosure and cooperation easier.
selfCheck: Did I give this person my full attention, or was part of me on my screen or my next point?
Did I learn one thing about them as a person before we got into the business?
Before a hard negotiation or tense thread, have we ever spoken live, even for five minutes?
Did the setting and their cues invite small talk, or did they signal they wanted to get straight to work?
Am I trying to connect, or performing techniques such as copying their posture?

title: Ray Tomlinson
summary: BBN engineer (1941-2016) who in 1971 sent the first messages between users on different ARPANET computers, chose the "@" that still separates user from host in every address, and co-wrote the 1973 header standard that made From, Subject and Date part of every message.

title: Readability formulas
summary: Equations such as Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level that estimate how hard a text is from surface counts, mainly word and sentence length; useful as a quick screen for dense drafts, but a weak guide to whether real readers will understand and act on a document.
selfCheck: Did I change any sentence only to move the score rather than to help a reader?
Which formula and tool produced this number, and did I strip headings and lists before scoring?
Has anyone from the intended audience tried to use this document, and what did they get wrong?
steps: Decide who the readers are and what they must find, understand and do before you look at any score.
Prepare the text for scoring by removing headings, bullet fragments, tables, URLs and other non-prose that calculators miscount.
Run one named formula in one tool and record which you used, so later scores are comparable.
Treat a high score only as a pointer to passages worth rereading for long sentences and unfamiliar terms; fix those for the reader, not for the number.
Never chop sentences or swap in short but vague words just to lower the score.
Check the revised draft with a few real or representative readers (ask them to find an answer or explain the next step) and let their results, not the score, decide whether it is ready.

example.situation: A policy team is told every staff notice must score at or below grade 8 before it goes out.
example.before: Leave. Approval needed. Submit form. Use portal. Manager signs. HR checks. Then booked.
example.after: To book leave, submit the leave form in the HR portal at least two weeks ahead. Your manager approves it, HR checks your balance, and you get an email when it is booked.
example.why: The choppy version scores as very easy but leaves readers guessing about order, deadline and who acts; the revised version scores slightly harder yet answers the questions readers actually have.

title: Reading lies from body language
aliases: spotting liars by their body language
summary: Judging whether a colleague, candidate or client is lying from nervous-looking behaviour such as gaze aversion, fidgeting or hesitation; meta-analyses put such judgments only slightly above chance (about 54%) because behavioural cues to deceit are faint, so the habit mainly produces confident false accusations of honest but anxious people.
selfCheck: Am I doubting this person because of how they looked or sounded, rather than because of something they said that conflicts with facts I can check?
Would an honest person under this much pressure (an interview, an investigation, a status challenge) plausibly show the same nervousness?
Have I asked open, specific questions and checked at least one detail before forming a view?
How confident am I, and is that confidence based on evidence or on a gut read of their manner?

example.situation: A hiring manager is interviewing a candidate whose CV claims she led a data-migration project; the candidate looks down often and fidgets with her pen.
example.before: Manager (thinking): 'She can't hold my gaze and keeps fidgeting - she's padding that project.' He cuts the topic short and scores her 'low credibility'.
example.after: Manager: 'Walk me through the migration from the first week. What broke, who did you escalate to, and what would the client's IT lead say your role was?' He notes the specifics and checks two of them with the reference.
example.why: Gaze and fidgeting barely track deceit and are common in nervous, honest candidates, so the first version turns interview anxiety into a verdict; open, specific questions and a factual check test the claim itself.

title: Rebecca Hincks
summary: KTH Royal Institute of Technology researcher and teacher of technical English who measured what makes presentation speech sound lively, defined the pitch variation quotient, and in 2009 with Jens Edlund tested a transient visual pitch meter for presentation practice, an early form of software-based speaking coaching.

title: Receiving feedback
summary: The learnable skill of hearing, understanding and deciding what to do with other people's input on your work, including actively asking for it, rather than rejecting it on reflex or swallowing it whole; it treats the receiver, not only the giver, as responsible for whether feedback helps.
selfCheck: Before I judged this feedback right or wrong, could I say back exactly what they observed and what they want me to do differently?
Am I reacting to what was said, to who said it, or to what it seems to say about who I am?
