Did I ask for one concrete, forward-looking suggestion instead of a general request for any feedback?
Have I separated the useful coaching from the parts I disagree with, instead of rejecting the whole message?
Did I close by saying what I will try, or that I want to think it over and come back?

title: Self-disclosure reciprocity
summary: Building a new working relationship by trading small, personal but appropriate disclosures in alternating turns - matching the other person's level of openness and deepening it gradually - rather than one person doing all the sharing or all the asking.
selfCheck: Did we take roughly equal turns, or did one of us do almost all the talking or all the asking?
When they shared something, did I answer at about the same depth before asking my next question?
Did I go deeper only after they matched the last level, or did I jump ahead to something too personal?
Given my status relative to them, was what I shared likely to build connection rather than cost me credibility?
steps: Open with a light question tied to the shared situation, then listen for what the other person chooses to reveal.
Answer their disclosure with one of your own at a similar level of personal detail - not a bigger story, not a deflection.
Hand the turn back with a question that builds on what they just said, so speaking and listening alternate in short exchanges.
Deepen one notch at a time (facts, then preferences, then experiences) only after the other person has matched the previous level.

If you are senior to the other person, share interests, experiences or lessons learned rather than current weaknesses or anxieties, and keep task-relevant shortcomings for settings that call for them.
Close the exchange while it is still balanced, and note one thing they told you to follow up on next time.

example.situation: A team lead's first coffee chat with a contractor who has just joined the project.
example.before: The lead asks eight questions in a row - background, tools, location, weekend plans - and shares nothing. Or, in the opposite version, spends fifteen minutes on their own career story and a stressful family week.
example.after: Lead: 'How's the first week landing?' Contractor: 'Good - still learning the codebase, it's huge.' Lead: 'It took me a month to stop getting lost in it; the billing module was my nemesis. Which part has been hardest so far?' The contractor names one, adds that they're new to the city, and the lead mentions a lunch spot the team likes before heading to the stand-up.
example.why: Each person shares a little and then gets the floor back, the lead matches the contractor's level of detail, and the lead's disclosure is a past struggle that is now solved rather than a current weakness.

title: Refutational two-sided messages
summary: A way of building a case in which you name the strongest objections your audience is likely to hold and then answer each one with evidence or reasoning, rather than ignoring them (one-sided) or merely mentioning them (nonrefutational two-sided).
selfCheck: Have I named the objection my toughest stakeholder would raise first, or only the ones I can easily dismiss?
For each objection I mention, have I actually answered it, or only acknowledged it?
Would the people who hold this objection agree that I stated it fairly?
Is there a point I cannot rebut, and have I said so honestly instead of hiding it?
steps: List the objections your audience is most likely to raise - ask a sceptical colleague or two which ones they would lead with, and what your proposal costs others in time and money.
Pick the two or three strongest objections, not the easiest ones to knock down, and state each one fairly in a single sentence.
Answer each objection directly with evidence, a mitigation or a changed design - do not just acknowledge it and move on.
Concede plainly any point you cannot answer, and say what you would do about it or what would change your recommendation.
Place the objections and answers where the reader will be asking them - usually right after your recommendation and main reason, not buried at the end.
Afterwards, note which objections actually came up and add any you missed to your list for next time.

example.situation: A team lead proposes moving the team's weekly status meeting to a written async update, and expects the department head to worry about losing visibility.
example.before: I propose we replace the Monday status meeting with a written update in our team channel. It will save about six person-hours a week and people prefer it. Some may feel we lose visibility, but overall the benefits outweigh that.
example.after: I propose we replace the Monday status meeting with a written update in our team channel, saving about six person-hours a week. The obvious worry is that you lose visibility into blockers. To cover that, each update has a required 'Blocked on' line, and anything blocked for more than two days triggers a 15-minute call. A second worry is that people won't write updates; we would track completion for a month and go back to the meeting if it drops below 90%.
example.why: The first version names the objection but leaves it standing, the nonrefutational pattern that tends to persuade slightly less than saying nothing. The rewrite states the two likeliest concerns and answers each with a specific safeguard and a reversal condition.

title: Register and tone
summary: Register is the variety of language a speaker or writer chooses to fit the situation - how formal, technical, warm or casual the words are - and tone is the attitude that choice conveys. Getting both right for the reader, the relationship and the channel decides whether a correct message also lands as credible and respectful.

title: Reservation value
summary: The worst deal you would still accept rather than walk away - the point of indifference between agreeing and taking your best alternative. It is calculated from your BATNA before talks begin, kept private, and used as a firm floor (or ceiling), not as the goal you aim for.

title: RFC 1855
summary: Sally Hambridge's October 1995 Internet Engineering Task Force document "Netiquette Guidelines" (RFC 1855, FYI 28), a bulleted, adaptable minimum set of courtesy rules for email, real-time one-to-one chat ("talk"), mailing lists and newsgroups that organisations were invited to tailor into their own policies.

title: Rhetorical studies
summary: The oldest discipline of communication: the study and teaching of how speakers and writers can find and use the available means of persuasion and influence for a particular audience and situation. Begun in ancient Greece and Rome, it was revived in the twentieth century as the study of all purposeful discourse, from speeches and memos to images.

title: Rhetorical appeals
summary: Aristotle's division of the persuasive means a speaker controls into three kinds: character shown in the message (ethos), the emotional state it produces in listeners (pathos) and the argument itself (logos). Used as a planning and review checklist, it helps a workplace message earn trust, show why the issue matters and prove its claim, rather than leaning on only one of the three.
selfCheck: Does my audience know why I am a credible person to make this case?
Is each main claim backed by a specific figure, test or precedent rather than an assertion?
Have I shown who is affected in a way the audience will actually feel, without overstating the stakes?
Would I be comfortable if the audience later checked every emotional claim I made?
steps: Write the one claim or request you want the audience to accept, and name the decision-maker who must accept it.
Ethos: state in one line why you are a credible person to raise this - relevant experience, what you checked, and what you stand to gain or lose.
Logos: give the strongest two or three reasons, each backed by a specific figure, test or precedent, and answer the most likely objection.
Pathos: show concretely who is affected and how, using one real case alongside the numbers, without exaggerating the stakes.
Kairos: tie the request to why now - a deadline, a budget cycle or a recent incident the audience already cares about.
Reread the draft and mark each sentence E, P or L; strengthen whichever appeal is thin and cut any emotional line the facts do not support.

example.situation: An engineering lead asks the leadership team to fund two sprints of automated regression testing.
example.before: Our test coverage is 41% and industry benchmarks suggest 70-80%. Automated regression testing would raise coverage and reduce defects. I request two sprints to build it.
example.after: I ran the last three releases and wrote the postmortems, so I have seen where our defects come from. 41% of our code is covered by tests; the March outage cost a day of support time and a refund to our largest client, and the bug sat in uncovered code. Two sprints of regression testing would cover the billing and login paths behind 8 of our last 10 incidents. Approving it now lets us finish before the Q1 renewal season.
example.why: The original is pure logos with no reason to trust the speaker or care now; the rewrite adds earned credibility, a concrete cost the audience felt, and timing, while keeping every claim factual.

title: Risk numbers as natural frequencies
summary: Restating percentages and conditional probabilities as whole-number counts drawn from one stated group ("of 10,000 orders, 20 are fraudulent and 18 of those get flagged"), so listeners can see base rates, hits and false alarms and work out what a result actually means.
selfCheck: Have I stated the reference group ("out of every 1,000 ...") before giving any count?
Can my listener see how many cases are false alarms, not just how many real cases are caught?
Am I comparing options with the same denominator and in absolute terms rather than "doubled" or "halved"?
Does every number in my sentence clearly belong to one named group?
If someone asked "so of the ones flagged, how many are real?", have I already answered it?
steps: Pick one reference group large enough that every count comes out as a whole number (1,000 or 10,000 is usual) and name it in the first sentence.
Split that group by the base rate first - how many have the condition, defect or event and how many do not.
Apply the detection or hit rate inside the first subgroup and the false-alarm rate inside the second, and write each result as a count.
Answer the decision question as "X out of Y" - for example, how many of all flagged cases are real - instead of quoting the test's accuracy.
Keep the same denominator for every option you compare, and give absolute changes ("from 20 to 10 in 1,000") rather than relative ones ("halved").
Tie every number to its group in the wording ("of the 9,980 legitimate orders, about 500 are flagged") and, for a live audience, sketch the counts as a simple frequency tree.

example.situation: A risk analyst briefs the head of operations on whether to auto-cancel every order a new fraud model flags.
example.before: The model catches 90% of fraud with only a 5% false-positive rate, so a flagged order is very likely fraudulent - I'd auto-cancel them.
example.after: Out of every 10,000 orders, about 20 are fraudulent and the model flags 18 of them. Of the other 9,980 legitimate orders it also flags about 500. So of roughly 518 flagged orders, only 18 - about 1 in 30 - are fraud. Auto-cancelling would block about 500 good customers to stop 18 bad ones; I suggest manual review instead.
example.why: The before version quotes the model's accuracy and invites the listener to ignore how rare fraud is; the counts make the base rate and the false alarms visible, so the leader can see that most flags are wrong and decide on that basis.

title: Rob Buckman
summary: British-Canadian oncologist, author and broadcaster (1948-2011) whose 1992 book How to Break Bad News turned the delivery of unwelcome news into a teachable, step-by-step skill, and who co-developed the six-step SPIKES protocol now adapted for workplace conversations about layoffs, cancellations and setbacks.

title: Role reversal
summary: A conflict and negotiation technique in which each party states, or acts out, the other side's position as accurately as they can - before arguing their own - so that misunderstandings surface and each side gets a working model of how the other sees the issue.
selfCheck: Could the other person hear my summary of their position and say "yes, that's it" without correcting me?
Did I describe their reasons and worries, or only their demand?
Are our positions actually incompatible, or have we just misunderstood each other - and has the swap made that clearer?
Am I using the swap to understand them, or to rehearse a rebuttal?
If I argued their side to someone who shares their values, would it sound persuasive or like a caricature?
steps: Agree the ground rule before the discussion starts - each person summarises the other's position, and the other confirms or corrects it, before anyone argues back.
Let each side state its own position once, briefly and without interruption.
Swap - each person presents the other's position in the first person ("As the ops lead, my concern is...") covering their goal, their reasons and what worries them.
Ask the original owner to rate the summary and fill in anything missing or distorted; repeat until they say it is fair.
Only then argue your own case, starting from the points you now know you share and naming the points that still genuinely conflict.
When preparing alone for a hard negotiation, write or rehearse the other party's brief in their voice and test which of your own arguments would actually move them.

example.situation: A product manager and an operations lead are stuck on whether to launch a feature before the quarter-end freeze.
example.before: PM - We have to ship on the 28th; sales has promised it. Ops - You always do this, and my team pays for it on call. PM - It's a small change, you're overreacting.
example.after: PM - Let me try your side first. You're worried that launching two days before the freeze leaves no window to roll back, and your on-call team absorbed the last two late launches. Is that right? Ops - Mostly; the bigger issue is we have no runbook yet. Now let me do yours: sales made a commitment to a named customer and slipping costs you credibility. PM - Yes. So can we ship to that one customer behind a flag and do the full launch after the freeze?
example.why: Each side states the other's concern until the owner agrees it is fair, which surfaces the real blocker (no runbook) and a shared fact (one customer matters most), and opens an option neither raised while they were only defending their own positions.

title: Salary negotiation
summary: The recurring workplace situation in which a candidate and an employer settle pay and other terms of a job offer (or an existing employee asks for a raise). It rewards preparation and a clear, polite ask, and it carries risks - mostly smaller than candidates fear - that depend on information, framing and who is asking.

title: Saying no
summary: Declining a request, invitation or extra assignment clearly and respectfully, so that you protect your priorities without damaging the working relationship - typically by naming what you are saying yes to, stating the no plainly, and offering a workable alternative (William Ury's "positive no").
selfCheck: If I say yes, what specific work or commitment am I saying no to instead?
Did my answer contain one sentence that a listener could not mistake for a maybe?
Am I offering an alternative I will actually deliver, or one I am inventing to escape the conversation?
Is this the kind of unrewarded task I keep being asked to do, and should it be assigned more fairly instead?
steps: Ask for time before answering ("Let me check my commitments and come back to you by 3 p.m.") instead of agreeing on the spot.
Get the details - scope, deadline, who else could do it, and whether the work counts toward anyone's goals - so you are deciding about the real request.
Name your own yes - the priority, commitment or principle that this request would crowd out.
Decide your Plan B - what you will do if the requester pushes back or escalates.
Deliver the answer in three beats - acknowledge the request and state your yes, say the no plainly in one sentence, then propose an alternative you can genuinely support.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact tone; if pressed, acknowledge their point, repeat the no calmly and do not add new excuses.

example.situation: A senior analyst is asked by a peer manager to run the quarterly offsite logistics, on top of a client deliverable due in two weeks.
example.before: Oh... I'm really swamped, but I guess I could try to fit it in? Sorry, it might be a bit late. Let me see what I can do.
example.after: Thanks for thinking of me. My priority until the 28th is the client deliverable, so I can't take on the offsite this quarter. I could send you last year's checklist and vendor list today, and I'd be glad to be considered for a rotation next quarter.
example.why: The rewrite states the competing commitment, gives an unambiguous no in one sentence and offers a concrete, smaller yes, so the requester can plan instead of waiting on a half-yes that may fail later.

title: Scheduled inbox checks
summary: Processing email and message notifications at a few planned times a day, with the inbox closed and alerts off in between, instead of reacting to each message as it arrives - a way to cut interruptions and the stress of a constant stream of incoming information.
selfCheck: Do the people who depend on me know when I will see their message and how to reach me if it cannot wait?
Did I actually close the inbox and turn off alerts between check-ins, or just check less while staying distracted?
In this check-in, did I decide what to do with each message, or did I just read and leave them?
Is my message volume high enough that batching helps, or am I adding rigidity for little gain?
Has turning alerts off made me more anxious about missing something, and if so would hourly checks suit me better?
steps: Look at how often you check messages today and what your role genuinely needs; if you are on call or in a live-support role, agree an exception path before you change anything.
Pick a small number of fixed check-in times (three a day is the most-tested dose) and block them in your calendar, sized to your usual volume.
Between check-ins, close the email tab or app and switch off desktop and phone alerts for email and non-urgent chat.
During each check-in, triage in one pass - reply, delegate, schedule or archive - rather than reading messages and leaving them for later.
Tell your team and key stakeholders when you check messages and how to reach you for anything genuinely urgent (a phone call or a named chat channel).
Review after two weeks - stress, missed items, response complaints - and adjust the number of check-ins rather than abandoning the routine.

example.situation: A finance analyst gets 120 emails and a steady flow of chat pings a day and is preparing a quarterly forecast that needs long stretches of concentration.
example.before: Outlook open all day with pop-up alerts on; the analyst answers each message within minutes and does forecast work in the gaps between replies.
example.after: Email and chat alerts off; inbox processed at 9:00, 13:00 and 16:30. The analyst's status and email signature say: 'I check messages three times a day - for anything urgent on the forecast, call my desk line.'
example.why: Fewer checks cut the interruptions that fragment the forecast work, and the stated urgent path stops colleagues guessing or escalating, which addresses the co-worker expectations the original study could not control.

title: Scott Fahlman
summary: Carnegie Mellon computer scientist who, on 19 September 1982, proposed typing ":-)" on the department's online bulletin board to mark jokes (and ":-(" for serious posts), because readers kept missing sarcasm in plain text; the convention spread into the emoticons and emoji now used to signal tone in work messages.

title: Self-affirmation before feedback
summary: A short exercise done just before hearing criticism or reviewing your own mistakes: you pick a personal value unrelated to the work being judged and spend a few minutes writing why it matters to you, so the feedback threatens less of your self-image and is easier to take in.
selfCheck: Did I affirm a value unrelated to the work being judged, rather than reassuring myself that the work is fine?
Did I do the reflection before the feedback, not as damage control afterwards?
When the hardest comment came, did I ask a question before I explained or justified?
Am I treating this as a small boost to openness, not a substitute for clear, fair feedback from the giver?
steps: Before a review, debrief or round of comments, set aside five minutes somewhere you will not be interrupted.
Pick one personal value that has nothing to do with the work being judged, such as family, friendship, craft outside work or community.
Write for about five minutes about why that value matters to you and a recent time you acted on it; do not write about the project.
Go into the conversation and, when the critical point lands, ask what they observed and what they suggest before you defend or explain.
Afterwards, list the one or two changes you will try, separating them from the points you still disagree with.

example.situation: A product manager is about to hear a director's comments on a launch that slipped two weeks.
example.before: She walks in braced, interrupts the first critical point to explain the vendor delay, and leaves having heard only that the director thinks she planned badly.
example.after: Beforehand she writes for five minutes about why mentoring two junior colleagues matters to her. When the director says the risk log was stale, she asks which risks were missed and agrees to a weekly review, noting the vendor issue separately.
example.why: Reflecting on a value outside the project keeps one critical comment from feeling like a verdict on her whole worth, so she can hear the specific fix instead of defending her identity.

title: Self-distancing strategies
summary: Stepping back from your own point of view before or after a nerve-racking moment - by talking to yourself by name or as "you", or by picturing the scene as an outside observer would - so that you judge the stakes and your own salience more like the audience does.
selfCheck: If I described this moment to myself by name, what would I tell me to do next?
From a colleague's seat, how much of this meeting is actually about me?
Am I replaying this slip in the first person, and what would an observer say mattered instead?
Have I turned the distanced view into one concrete next action?
steps: Before the meeting or talk, write or say two or three sentences of self-talk using your own name or "you" instead of "I" (for example, "Sam, you know this material; your job is to explain it").
Picture the room from the back row or from a colleague's seat, not through your own eyes, and ask what that observer would actually notice.
Notice what the observer is busy with - their own agenda, notes and next point - and adjust your estimate of how much attention you will get.
Turn the distanced view into one concrete action, such as the opening line, the one question you will ask or the one-sentence correction you will use if you slip.
Afterwards, review the moment the same way ("What did Sam do well? What would Sam change?") instead of replaying it in the first person.

example.situation: An analyst is about to raise a concern about a vendor's numbers in a cross-team review where she is the most junior person.
example.before: I'm going to sound naive. Everyone will remember that I'm the one who didn't get the model. I'll just keep quiet and email the lead later.
example.after: Priya, picture this from the back of the room: eight people focused on their own slides. You spotted a real gap. Ask one short question about the churn assumption, then let the lead answer.
example.why: Naming herself and taking an observer's view shrinks the imagined spotlight and turns vague dread into one specific, low-cost contribution, which is the pattern lab studies link to less distress and better performance.

title: Self-recording playback
summary: Filming a practice run of a talk, then watching it back against a short checklist to spot delivery habits such as fidgeting, frozen hands or lost eye contact, and fixing one or two before the next run. A meta-analysis of classroom studies links videotaped feedback to better speaking skills without a significant rise in anxiety.
selfCheck: Did I decide what to look for before I watched, or did I just react to how I looked and sounded?
Have I picked no more than two changes, each with a specific replacement behaviour?
Is my verdict on the recording closer to what a neutral colleague would say than to how nervous I felt while speaking?
Did I record a second run to check that the change actually happened?
steps: Before you record, write a three-item checklist of delivery behaviours to look for, such as hand movement, eye contact and pace.
Prop your phone at audience eye level and record one full, standing run-through with the slides or notes you will really use.
Before you press play, jot down how you think you came across, then watch as if the speaker were a colleague you are coaching.
Watch once with the sound off for gestures, posture and fidgets, and once with sound for pace, pauses and filler words.
Note what to keep and pick no more than two habits to change, writing a concrete replacement for each.
Record a second run, check whether those two habits changed, and ask a colleague to watch one clip if you can.

example.situation: A finance analyst is preparing a 15-minute budget review for department heads and has rehearsed it twice in her head.
example.before: She runs the talk silently on her laptop, feels it went fine, and on the day grips the clicker with both hands, rocks on her feet and looks at the screen for most of the talk.
example.after: She films one standing run-through, watches it muted, and sees the clicker grip and the rocking. She sets the clicker down between slides, plants her feet, uses one hand to show the three-way budget split, and records again to confirm the change.
example.why: Playback shows habits the speaker cannot feel from the inside, and checking against a short list turns a vague impression into two specific fixes.

title: Service recovery
summary: The way a person or team responds after letting a client or customer down - acknowledging the complaint, putting the outcome right, explaining what happened and treating the person with respect - so that satisfaction, trust and the relationship are restored rather than lost.
selfCheck: Have I let the client finish and restated the problem and its impact in their terms before I start explaining?
Does my reply include a tangible fix or remedy, or only sympathy?
Have I asked the client what outcome they want instead of guessing?
Have I given a specific time for the next update, and will one named person own it?
Am I explaining the cause to restore confidence, or to shift blame onto another team or the client?
Am I counting on a great recovery to make the client happier than if nothing had gone wrong?
steps: Thank the client for raising it and listen to the whole complaint before defending, explaining or offering anything; then restate the problem and its impact on them in your own words.
Apologise for the specific failure if the complaint is legitimate, without arguing about fault in the first reply.
Ask what outcome would put them right, and offer a concrete fix that at least restores their position (redo, credit, refund or extra resource) - do not rely on courtesy alone.
Give a firm time for the next update or the fix, make it easy for them to reach one named person, and meet that time.
Explain plainly what went wrong and what you are changing so it does not happen again, once you actually know.
Close the loop - confirm with the client that the fix worked and log the cause so the team can prevent a repeat.

example.situation: An agency missed a client's campaign launch date because a hand-off between two internal teams was dropped, and the client's marketing lead emails to complain.
example.before: Hi Sam, thanks for your note. Unfortunately the delay was caused by factors outside the account team's control and the creative team was dealing with resourcing issues. We are working on it and will update you when we can.
example.after: Sam, you're right - we missed the launch date we committed to, and that's on us. It left your team without the campaign for your trade-show week. The assets will be live by Thursday 10am; I'll confirm personally when they are. We won't bill this month's management fee, and if you'd prefer a different remedy, tell me what would work. The cause was a dropped hand-off between our two teams; from today every launch has a single named owner on our side, and that's me for your account. Can I call you at 3pm to walk through it?
example.why: The rewrite acknowledges the specific failure and its cost to the client, offers a concrete remedy and asks what they want, sets a firm time and a single point of contact, and explains the cause with a prevention step - covering outcome, procedure and respectful treatment rather than deflecting blame.

title: Setting reply-time expectations
summary: Telling the recipient of an email or chat message, in the message itself or in an agreed team norm, how soon you actually need a reply - a specific reply-by time for real deadlines, and an explicit "no rush" for everything else - so that receivers do not have to guess at urgency.
selfCheck: Does this message say when I need a reply, or would the reader have to guess?
Am I sending outside the recipient's working hours, and if so have I said it can wait or scheduled it?
Is the urgency I am signalling the urgency I actually have?
Would my team know our default reply window for this channel without asking?
steps: Before sending, decide when you truly need an answer - a date and time, or "no deadline" - and whether you need a reply at all or the message is for information only.
For real deadlines, state the reply-by time and the reason in the first lines or the subject line (for example "[Action by Thu 3pm]"), not only at the end.
For anything non-urgent, add one plain sentence saying so, especially when you send outside normal working hours or across time zones.
Reserve urgent labels for messages that genuinely need fast action, and use a phone call or chat ping for true emergencies instead of a late-night email.
If you work odd hours, schedule-send to the recipient's working hours or add a standing signature line saying you do not expect replies outside them.

Agree default reply windows for each channel with your team (for example chat same day, email within two working days) and write them in the team charter so individual messages only need to flag exceptions.

example.situation: A team lead reviewing a draft report on Saturday morning emails comments to an analyst; the comments are needed for a client meeting the following Thursday.
example.before: Hi Sam - a few comments on the report below. Can you take a look?
example.after: Hi Sam - comments on the report below. No need to look at this before Monday; I need the revised version by Wednesday noon for Thursday's client meeting. Enjoy your weekend.
example.why: The original leaves Sam to guess whether a Saturday email means 'reply today'; the rewrite gives the real deadline and its reason and says the weekend is free, the kind of sender-side note that removed receivers' overestimate of urgency in experiments.

title: Shannon-Weaver model
summary: The linear model of communication drawn from Claude Shannon's 1948 information theory and popularised by Warren Weaver: a source's message is encoded by a transmitter into a signal, sent over a channel where noise can corrupt it, and decoded by a receiver for a destination; it is the basis of the sender-message-channel-receiver picture used in communication textbooks.

title: Signposting
summary: Using short spoken cues - previews, transitions, internal summaries and words such as "first", "next" or "the key point is" - to tell listeners where a talk is going, where they are now and what matters most, so they can follow and remember its structure.
selfCheck: Could someone who looked at their phone for a minute tell which part of my talk I'm in when they look up?
Did I preview my main points at the start and review the same points at the end?
Does each move between points have a spoken transition, not just a new slide?
Have I explicitly flagged the one thing I most need the audience to remember or decide?
steps: Before drafting cues, write your talk's three to five main points as one-line headlines; signposts can only show a structure that already exists.
In the opening, give a one-sentence preview that names the points in order ("I'll cover the problem, two options, and what I need from you").
At every move between main points, say a full transition sentence that closes the last point and names the next one ("That's the cost; now the timeline").
Flag the one or two things the audience must remember with an explicit emphasis cue ("If you keep one number from today, it's this").
After a dense or long section, give a one-sentence internal summary before moving on.
Close by reviewing the same points you previewed, in the same words, then state the decision or action you need.
In rehearsal, check that each cue is spoken aloud and matches the slide or section it introduces.

example.situation: An operations lead has eight minutes in a weekly leadership meeting to explain why a warehouse migration slipped and what she needs.
example.before: So, the migration. We had some vendor problems in August, and the scanners came late, and then there was the labour issue, and also the cutover weekend clashed with the audit... anyway, the new date is probably mid-December, and it'd help to get some budget for temp staff.
example.after: I'll cover three things: why we slipped, the new date, and one decision I need from you. First, why we slipped: two causes - late scanners and the audit clash. That's the cause; second, the new date: 14 December, with one risk. Finally, the decision: approve temp staff for cutover week. So - two causes, a new date, and one approval.
example.why: The preview lets listeners hold a three-part map, the transitions mark when each part ends, and the closing review repeats the structure, so executives who drift for a minute can rejoin and the request is not lost at the end.

title: Silence and pauses
summary: The ability to use and read the unfilled gaps in speech: placing short silent pauses so listeners absorb key points, holding a longer silence to think before answering a hard question, and recognising that an unexpected gap from someone else can signal doubt, disagreement or exclusion.
selfCheck: After my most important sentence, did I stop for a beat before moving on, or rush straight into the next point?
When I was asked the hardest question, did I give myself a few seconds to think before answering?
Am I the more senior person here, or am I pausing in front of someone who controls the outcome and may read it badly?
When a colleague went quiet after my proposal, did I check what the silence meant instead of assuming agreement?
In this conversation, did I create silence to think, or did I let an awkward gap sit after someone else had taken a risk?

title: Situation-Behavior-Impact
summary: A three-part way to give feedback developed at the Center for Creative Leadership: name the specific situation, describe the observable behaviour, and say what impact it had on you - optionally followed by asking about the person's intent.
selfCheck: Could the other person picture the exact moment I mean, or did I say something vague like "lately"?
Is my behaviour description something a camera could record, or did I slip in a judgement or guess at a motive?
Have I said what the impact actually was, rather than assuming they already know?
Did I leave room to ask about their intent and listen before deciding what should change?
steps: Pin down the situation - the specific meeting, document or moment, with a time and place ("in Tuesday's 10 a.m. client call"), not "lately" or "last week".
Describe the behaviour as something a camera could have recorded - words said, actions taken - and strip out labels such as "rude", "lazy" or "great attitude".
State the impact the behaviour had on you, the team or the work, in your own voice, naming a concrete consequence and, if useful, your reaction (frustrated, relieved, proud).
For redirecting feedback, stop and ask about intent ("What were you aiming for there?") and listen before proposing any fix.
Agree together on what to keep doing or what to try next time, and give the feedback close to the event while it is still fresh.
Use the same three parts for positive feedback, so the person knows exactly which behaviour to repeat.

example.situation: A team lead gives feedback to an analyst who presented the quarterly numbers at a leadership review.
example.before: You came across as really unprepared today and kind of defensive. You need to step up your game before the next one.
example.after: In this morning's quarterly review with the VPs, when Priya asked where the churn figure came from, you said 'I'd have to check' and moved on. The VPs then questioned two other numbers and we lost ten minutes of the agenda, and I was worried they'd discount the whole forecast. What was going on for you at that point?
example.why: The rewrite swaps verdicts ("unprepared", "defensive") for a time-stamped situation, an observable behaviour and a concrete impact, then asks about intent - so the analyst can see exactly what to change and has room to explain instead of defending their character.

title: Small talk at work
summary: The skill of opening and sustaining brief, light, non-task conversation with colleagues, clients and acquaintances - and knowing when to deepen it, steer it back to work, or end it gracefully.
selfCheck: Did I ask at least one follow-up question that built on something they actually said?
Did I share something about myself too, or did the exchange feel like an interview?
Did I go one step deeper than the weather or the commute when the moment allowed it?
Was this a good time for them, or did I pull a focused colleague out of deep work?
Did I end the chat cleanly, with a warm close or a link back to the work?

title: Social accounts
summary: Giving the people affected by a mistake or an unwelcome decision a clear, adequate and honest explanation of why it happened and how it will be handled, so that they judge the outcome and the person behind it more fairly.
selfCheck: Could the people affected repeat the actual reason for this outcome after hearing my explanation?
Have I named only causes that are true and that I would be comfortable having checked?
Did I explain how they will be treated from here, not only why it happened?
Is my explanation a short context for an apology, or has it become an excuse that replaces one?
steps: Give the explanation at the same moment as the bad news or the admission, before people fill the silence with their own story.
State the real reason - the constraint, trade-off or goal that drove the outcome - in concrete terms rather than "business reasons".
Separate honestly what was outside your control from what was your call, and own your part; never invent a mitigating factor.
Say how the decision will be carried out and how the people affected will be treated, not only why it was made.
Make the detail proportional to the loss, then ask what still does not make sense and answer it.
If you caused the harm, put the account inside an apology - responsibility and repair first, explanation kept short.

example.situation: A team lead has to tell five analysts that the conference places she had promised them this year have been cancelled.
example.before: Hi all, due to business reasons the conference budget has been cut for this year. Thanks for understanding.
example.after: I have to take back the conference places I promised you. Q3 revenue came in 12% under plan, and finance has frozen all non-customer travel across the division until March - I argued to keep two places and lost that argument. Registrations will be refunded by Friday, so none of you are out of pocket, and I've booked 15 minutes with each of you this week to agree what we do instead for your development goals. If any part of that still doesn't add up, ask me directly.
example.why: The vague original gives no reason anyone could judge, so it invites cynicism; the rewrite names a specific, checkable cause outside the lead's control, owns the lead's own role, explains how people will be treated, and invites the questions that test whether the account was adequate.

title: Social proof
summary: The tendency to decide what to do by looking at what similar others are doing, which lets a communicator encourage a behaviour by truthfully reporting that peers already do it; field experiments show real but modest and context-dependent effects, and a norm message can backfire when it tells people the desired behaviour is rare or that they are already doing better than average.

title: Social psychology
summary: The scientific study of how people's thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and by the social situation; much of the evidence behind workplace communication advice, from source credibility to attribution errors, comes from its experiments.

title: Solution-focused coaching
summary: A coaching approach, adapted from solution-focused brief therapy, that spends less time analysing where a problem came from and more time on what the person wants instead, when the problem is already absent or smaller, and what has worked before. Experiments show its questions reliably lift mood and goal-directed motivation more than problem-focused questions, but effects on actual follow-through are less consistent.
selfCheck: Did I spend more of the conversation on what they want and what already works than on the history of the problem?
Did I let them voice the problem first, or did I push positivity on them too early?
Did the conversation end with a concrete next step and a review date, not just a better mood?
Is this problem largely within their control, or does it need a systemic fix that questions alone will not provide?
steps: Let the person describe the problem briefly and acknowledge it; do not cut off problem talk they need, but do not dig into its history either.
Ask what they want instead, in concrete terms: "If this were sorted, what would you notice on a normal Tuesday?" (a toned-down miracle question).
Ask for exceptions and past successes: "When has this gone a bit better?" and "What did you do differently that time?"
Help them turn what worked into one or two small, specific next steps they could take this week.
Close by checking commitment and agreeing when you will review progress, so the good feeling the questions create is converted into action.

example.situation: In a one-on-one, an analyst says stakeholder meetings keep running over and ending without decisions, and she is frustrated.
example.before: How long has this been happening? Why do you think they keep going off track? Who's the main culprit?
example.after: That sounds draining. Picture a meeting next month that goes well - what's different about it? ... Has any recent meeting come close? ... What did you do in that one? ... Which of those could you repeat on Thursday?
example.why: The problem-focused questions keep her rehearsing causes and blame; the solution-focused version gets her to picture the outcome, find an exception she already produced, and leave with a step she owns.

title: Public speaking anxiety
summary: Fear and physical arousal triggered by having to speak in front of others - from a team update to a conference talk - that pushes people to avoid speaking, over-script, or deliver less well than they could.
selfCheck: Am I declining this presentation because it is not my job, or because I am afraid of it?
Have I rehearsed this out loud, standing, at least once - or only read my notes silently?
Am I assuming the audience can see my nerves as clearly as I can feel them?
What is the one point I need them to leave with, if everything else goes badly?
Afterwards, am I judging the talk by how I felt or by what the audience actually did with it?

title: Spotlight effect
aliases: overestimating how much others notice us
summary: The tendency to overestimate how much other people notice, remember and judge our appearance, words and slip-ups, which makes communicators hold back, over-apologise and dwell on small mistakes that the audience barely registered.
selfCheck: Am I staying quiet because I think everyone will remember this one comment, when they are mostly thinking about their own contributions?
If a colleague had made the slip I just made, would I still be thinking about it tomorrow?
Am I about to spend the first minute of my talk apologising for something the audience has not noticed?
If I picture this meeting from the back of the room instead of through my own eyes, how big does my moment really look?

title: Stakeholder mapping
summary: A planning technique for listing everyone who can affect or is affected by a decision or change, sorting them by how much power and interest they have, and using that picture to decide whom to involve, consult or inform, and with what message.
selfCheck: Who could stop or slow this, and have I spoken to them directly rather than assuming their view?
Who will be most affected but has the least say, and how will they hear about it before it lands?
Does each group's message answer their concern, or is it the same message I would send everyone?
When did I last update this map, and has anyone's stance or influence changed since?
steps: Write down the decision or change in one sentence and set the boundary - which teams, customers, regulators and time frame are in scope.
List everyone who can affect it or will be affected by it, then ask two or three colleagues outside your team who is missing, including people with little voice.

For each stakeholder, note their main interest or concern, whether they currently support, oppose or are undecided, and what power they hold (budget, sign-off, expertise, reputation, ability to block).
Place each one on a power-versus-interest grid and pick an engagement level - partner closely, keep satisfied, consult, or keep informed.
For each group, decide who will talk to them, the one message that speaks to their interest, the channel and how often - then put that in a communication plan.
Test the map by talking to the stakeholders themselves, and revisit it at each milestone, because power, interest and stance shift.

example.situation: An operations manager is replacing the team's expense-claims tool and has a go-live date in six weeks.
example.before: Plan: send one all-staff email two weeks before go-live announcing the new tool, with a link to the user guide.
example.after: Map: Finance director (high power, high interest, undecided) - weekly check-in, co-own the cut-over date. Payroll lead (high power, low interest) - one briefing on the export file, sign-off by week 3. Frequent travellers in sales (low power, high interest, worried about slower refunds) - invite two to test in week 2, answer the refund-time question in every message. Everyone else - short email at go-live and a two-minute video.
example.why: The single email treated everyone as one audience; the map shows who can block the launch, who will feel it most and what each needs to hear, so the manager spends attention where a surprise would be costly.

title: Project status reporting
summary: The recurring written or spoken update in which a project team tells its sponsor, client or oversight body where the work stands against its agreed time, cost, scope and benefits, what has changed, which risks and issues need attention, and what decisions are needed. Research on IT projects shows such reports are often selectively optimistic, so the genre only works when the rating criteria are shared and bad news is safe to send early.
selfCheck: Would someone who knew everything I know give this project the same rating I have?
Is there a risk I am privately worried about that does not appear in this report, and why have I left it out?
Does the first line tell a busy sponsor whether they need to act, and by when?
Am I reporting change against the approved baseline, or only selecting the numbers that look good this week?
steps: Agree with the sponsor, in writing, what each status rating means (for example what turns a project amber or red) before the first report goes out.
Open with the overall rating, the one-line reason for it and any decision you need, with a date.
Report against the approved baseline for time, cost, scope and benefits, and show the change since the last report rather than only the current position.
For each significant issue, state the cause, what you have already done, the options and your recommendation.
Raise a slipping milestone in the first report where you believe it is at risk, not the one where it is missed.
After each review, ask the reader whether the report gave them what they needed and adjust the format, not the facts.

example.situation: A team lead on a six-month CRM migration sends a fortnightly status report to the steering group; a data-quality problem has put the go-live date at risk.
example.before: Status: GREEN. Good progress this sprint - 14 of 18 integration tests passing. Some data-quality items being worked through with the vendor; we remain confident about the timeline and will update next report.
example.after: Status: AMBER (was GREEN). Go-live on 2 March is at risk: 22% of migrated customer records fail validation, and at the current fix rate cleanup finishes about three weeks late. Done so far: vendor engaged, root cause traced to duplicate legacy IDs. Options: (a) add two analysts for four weeks (about $18K) and hold the date; (b) move go-live to 23 March at no extra cost. Recommendation: (a). Decision needed from the steering group by Friday.
example.why: The rewrite applies the agreed rating honestly, quantifies the problem instead of hiding it in reassurance, shows what has already been done, and turns the bad news into a decision the readers can make while there is still time to act.

title: Summarizing
summary: Pulling together several points another person has made over a stretch of conversation and stating them back as one short, organised whole - then checking it is accurate - to confirm shared understanding, mark progress and move the conversation to its next step.
selfCheck: Did my summary cover the several points they made, or only the last or loudest one?
Did I leave my own opinions and solutions out of the summary itself?
Did I ask them to correct it, and did I change it when they did?
Did the summary lead clearly into the next step of the conversation?
steps: While the other person talks, note the separate points, concerns and decisions they raise, not just the last thing they said.
At a natural transition, a long monologue or before any decision, signal the summary ("Let me pull together what I've heard so far").
Select the points that matter for the next step and group them in two to four short chunks, in their language where possible; leave out your own opinions.
Include both sides when the person is torn, and name any open questions instead of quietly dropping them.
Close with a check ("What have I missed or got wrong?") and fix the summary out loud if they correct it.
Use the confirmed summary as the bridge to what comes next - a decision, an action list, or a new topic.

example.situation: A team lead is in a one-on-one with an engineer who has spent ten minutes describing problems with a cross-team project, and the lead is about to jump to a fix.
example.before: OK, sounds rough. I'll ping the platform team and ask them to prioritise your tickets.
example.after: Let me check I've got the whole picture. Three things: the platform team's API changes keep breaking your builds, nobody told you the deadline moved to March, and you're unsure whether you or Priya owns the migration. You also said the first one is the most urgent. Is that right, and is anything missing?
example.why: The rewrite gathers scattered points into one organised statement, records the speaker's own priority and invites correction, so the lead can act on the real problem rather than the most recent one mentioned.

title: Support response
summary: A reply that keeps the conversation on the other person's topic - an acknowledgement, a paraphrase or a question about what they just said - instead of a shift response that turns the topic to yourself. Coined by the sociologist Charles Derber, it is the direct counter to conversational narcissism and the everyday form of responsive listening.
selfCheck: In my last conversation, were most of my first replies about the other person's topic or about mine?
Did I ask at least one question that built on something specific they said?
When I shared my own story, was it asked for, and did I hand the topic back afterwards?
Could the other person tell from my replies what I had understood of their point?
steps: When someone raises a topic, notice the urge to reply with your own matching story, opinion or advice, and hold it for one turn.
Make your first reply about their topic - a short acknowledgement, a paraphrase of what you heard, or an open question such as "What happened next?"
Build your next question on a specific word or detail in their answer, so it could only be asked by someone who was listening.
Share your own experience only if it is asked for or clearly useful, keep it brief, and hand the topic back with a question.
Afterwards, roughly count your shift and support replies; if shifts dominated, open the next conversation with two support replies in a row.

example.situation: At the start of a project stand-up, an analyst mentions that the data migration over the weekend took twelve hours instead of three.
example.before: Lead: 'Twelve hours is nothing - on my last programme we had a migration run for three days straight. Anyway, let's go round the board.'
example.after: Lead: 'Twelve hours - that's a long weekend. What slowed it down?' [Analyst explains a vendor API kept timing out.] 'So the timeouts are the real risk for the next run. What would you need to stop that happening?'
example.why: The first reply is a shift response that turns the analyst's report into the lead's war story and closes the topic. The second uses a support response and a follow-up question, which surfaces a risk the whole team needs to know about and shows the analyst they were heard.

title: Systematic desensitization
summary: A behavioural method for reducing fear of speaking in which a person learns a relaxation response, ranks feared speaking situations from mildest to worst, and then works up that ladder - first in imagination, then in real life - moving on only once each step can be faced calmly.
selfCheck: Have I broken the talk or meeting I dread into smaller speaking steps, or am I trying to jump straight to the hardest one?
Can I actually relax on cue yet, or am I imagining scary scenes while still tense?
Am I moving up the ladder because the last step feels manageable, or because I am impatient - or am I stalling on a step I have already mastered?
Which imagined step have I not yet taken into a real meeting this week?
Is my anxiety severe enough that I should be doing this with professional support?
steps: Learn a quick relaxation routine - for example, tensing and releasing muscle groups while breathing slowly - and practise it daily until you can relax on cue in a minute or two.
Write a ladder of eight to twelve speaking situations ranked from barely uncomfortable (asking one question in a team stand-up) to the worst you can imagine (presenting to the executive committee).
While relaxed, picture the lowest rung in detail for a few seconds; if tension rises, stop the image, relax again, and repeat until you can hold it calmly.
Move up one rung at a time, only after the current one feels manageable, and revise the ladder if a step turns out too big.
Take each mastered rung into real life - say the one comment in the stand-up, then lead one agenda item - before tackling the next.
Keep doing the real-world steps regularly; repeated speaking without a bad outcome is what keeps the fear from creeping back.
If the fear is severe or spills into everyday life, work through the ladder with a qualified therapist or a structured programme rather than alone.

example.situation: A data engineer avoids speaking in the weekly cross-team review and has just been asked to present the quarterly pipeline results to directors in six weeks.
example.before: I'll just keep my head down in the reviews and cram the night before. Maybe I can get my lead to present the deck instead.
example.after: This week I'll relax and picture asking one question in the review, then actually ask it on Thursday. Next week I'll give the two-minute data-quality update, then present one slide to my own team, and do a full run-through with two directors' staff before the real thing.
example.why: The first plan avoids every speaking step, so the fear never gets a chance to shrink and the big talk arrives as a cliff. The second turns it into a graded ladder, pairs each step with calm rehearsal and real practice, and only climbs once the lower step is manageable - the core of desensitization.

title: Teach-back
summary: Checking whether an explanation landed by asking the other person to explain it back, or show it, in their own words - framed as a test of how clearly you explained rather than of what they know - and re-explaining until their version is right.
selfCheck: Did I ask them to say it in their own words, or did I accept a nod or a "makes sense"?
Did I frame the check as testing my explanation, not their competence?
Which one or two points would cause real damage if misunderstood, and did I check those?
When their restatement was off, did I re-explain differently rather than repeat myself louder?
steps: Pick the one to three points the other person must get right to act - a deadline, a decision, a sequence of steps - rather than checking everything.
Explain each point in plain, specific language, one point at a time.
Take ownership of the check out loud, for example "I want to make sure I explained that clearly."
Ask an open request to restate or demonstrate ("How will you walk the client through this?"), never a yes/no question such as "Does that make sense?"
Listen for gaps or errors; if you hear one, re-explain that part differently and ask again until their version is accurate.
Close by confirming the agreed version in writing where it matters (a recap message or ticket).

example.situation: A team lead hands over an urgent client escalation to a colleague before going on leave.
example.before: So that's the background - escalate to Priya's team if the patch fails, and keep the client posted. Does that all make sense?
example.after: I've thrown a lot at you, so let me check I explained it well. If the patch fails on Thursday, what are your next two moves, and who hears from you first?
example.why: The yes/no check invites a polite "yes"; the open request surfaces the missing piece (who to call first) while the lead can still fix it, and frames any gap as the explainer's problem.

title: The Culture Map
aliases: Breaking Through the Invisible Boundaries of Global Business
summary: Erin Meyer's 2014 business book and framework that compares national cultures on eight workplace scales - communicating, evaluating, persuading, leading, deciding, trusting, disagreeing and scheduling - and asks managers to read differences relative to their own position rather than in absolute terms.

title: The Physician as Teacher
aliases: Whitman and Schwenk (The Physician as Teacher)
summary: A short 1987 handbook by family physician Thomas L. Schwenk and educator Neal A. Whitman that treats clinical teaching as a form of interpersonal communication. It is the source that Anne Dohrenwend's widely read 2002 article cites for the term "sandwiching" - placing one criticism between two praises - which later spread far beyond medicine as the feedback sandwich.

title: Thomas Gilovich
summary: Cornell social psychologist who, with Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Medvec, named and tested the illusion of transparency (1998) and the spotlight effect (2000), the two egocentric biases that make speakers think their nerves, slips and intentions are far more visible than they are.

title: Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument
summary: Kenneth Thomas and Ralph Kilmann's model and 30-item self-assessment that maps how a person handles conflict on two dimensions - assertiveness (pursuing your own concerns) and cooperativeness (pursuing the other person's) - giving five modes: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating, each useful in some situations and costly when overused.
selfCheck: Which mode am I about to use, and is it the one this issue calls for or just my habit?
How much do I care about my own outcome here, and how much about theirs or the relationship?
If I am about to avoid or accommodate, is the issue truly minor, or am I sidestepping a concern that will come back?
Have I found out what the other person actually needs before choosing to compete or compromise?

example.situation: A product manager and an engineering lead disagree about whether to ship a feature on Friday with a known minor bug.
example.before: We're shipping Friday. Marketing has already announced it, so I need you to make it work.
example.after: I need Friday because of the announcement; you need to avoid a bug that floods support. Can we look for an option that covers both - say, ship Friday with the feature flagged off for the affected accounts - and if we can't find one by Wednesday, we split the difference on scope?
example.why: The original competes by habit on an issue where the engineer holds information the PM lacks. The rewrite names both sides' concerns (collaborating) on a high-stakes issue, and keeps compromising as an explicit time-boxed fallback instead of defaulting to one habitual mode.

title: Thought groups
summary: Speaking in short, meaningful chunks of words - a phrase or clause each - and marking the end of every chunk with a brief silent pause and a small pitch drop, so listeners can hear which words belong together and have time to process each idea.
selfCheck: Did I pause at the end of each idea, or did I run several figures together in one breath?
Were my pauses silent, or did I fill the gaps between chunks with "um" or "so"?
Did any pause fall in the middle of a phrase, splitting words that belong together?
In each chunk, was it clear which single word mattered most?
Would a listener who joined on a weak connection or in a second language be able to follow where one idea ended and the next began?
steps: Take the script or notes for the part of the talk that matters most, such as the opening, the recommendation or the key numbers.
Mark a slash after each meaningful chunk - a short sentence, a clause or a phrase - keeping grammatical units such as "in the third quarter" intact.
Underline the one focus word in each chunk, usually the new or most important information.
Read the passage aloud, linking the words inside each chunk smoothly, letting your pitch fall slightly on the last stressed word, and pausing silently at every slash.
Where a chunk ends in a number, a name or a decision, lengthen the pause to a full breath so the listener can take it in.
Record one run-through, listen back, and move any slash that splits a phrase or any pause you filled with "um".
Once the chunking feels natural, drop the marks and practise speaking from bullet points with the same rhythm.

example.situation: A finance analyst reports quarterly results to a leadership team on a video call.
example.before: So revenue in Q3 was um four point two million which is up eight percent and costs were flat um so margin improved to eighteen percent and we expect Q4 to be similar.
example.after: Revenue in Q3 / was four point two million / [pause] up eight percent. / Costs were flat, / so margin improved / to eighteen percent. / [pause] For Q4, / we expect the same.
example.why: Each figure now sits in its own chunk with a silent pause after it instead of a filler, so listeners can hear which number goes with which measure and hold each one before the next arrives.

title: Trust repair
summary: The situation after you, your team or your organization has let someone down, where the goal is to restore their willingness to rely on you. It combines what you say (acknowledgement, apology, explanation, promises), what you give back (compensation or penance) and what you change (controls, monitoring, follow-through), and it works best when words and actions match the kind of breach.

title: Trusted advisor
summary: A framework from David Maister, Charles Green and Robert Galford for earning a client's or senior stakeholder's trust: trustworthiness rises with credibility, reliability and intimacy and falls with self-orientation (the "trust equation"), and is built through five steps - engage, listen, frame, envision and commit.
selfCheck: Before this meeting, can I state the client's real worry in their words rather than my summary of the scope?
Have I delivered every small promise I made since we last spoke, and told them early about any I will miss?
Is any part of what I plan to say mainly about my firm's revenue, my reputation or being right?
Have I listened long enough to earn the right to frame the problem, or am I jumping to my solution?

example.situation: A consultant opens a steering-committee call with a client sponsor whose project is behind schedule.
example.before: Thanks for the time. Let me walk you through our 30-slide progress deck, and at the end I'd like to talk about extending our team for phase two.
example.after: Before the deck: last week you said the board is worried about the March date. Is that still the main concern? I'll focus on what protects March, including one option that needs less of our time, not more.
example.why: The rewrite shows reliability (it remembers what the sponsor said), intimacy (it names the real worry) and low self-orientation (it puts the client's problem ahead of selling more work).

title: Tsedal Neeley
summary: Harvard Business School organizational-behaviour scholar whose field studies of English-only mandates at a French high-tech firm and at Rakuten showed how a shared working language redistributes status and trust, and who turned that work into practical advice on corporate language strategy, communicating across languages and leading remote teams.

title: Unequal participation
summary: The common pattern in group discussions where a few people take most of the speaking turns while others say little or nothing, so the group hears a narrow slice of what its members know. It is driven by status, confidence, group composition and meeting format, and is reduced by changing the format rather than by asking quiet people to try harder.
selfCheck: Who in this meeting has not spoken yet, and is that because they have nothing to add or because the format never gave them an opening?
If I counted turns, would two or three people, including me, account for most of the talking?
Did we collect everyone's view in writing or in pairs before the most senior or most confident person spoke?
Am I judging whose idea is best by its merit, or by who said it most often and most fluently?

title: Upward dissent
summary: The learnable skill of voicing disagreement with a decision, policy or practice directly to the manager or leader who can act on it - in a way that is heard as constructive rather than as a threat - studied by communication scholar Jeffrey W. Kassing, who found that presenting solutions and facts is judged far more competent than going around the boss or threatening to quit.
selfCheck: Am I taking this disagreement to the person who can actually change it, or am I venting it to colleagues instead?
Have I brought evidence and at least one workable alternative, not only my objection?
Have I framed the issue in terms of a goal my manager already cares about?
Is this issue important enough to spend credibility on, and is now a moment when it can be heard?
If I have raised it before without a response, am I about to jump to going around my manager or hinting I might leave - and is there a constructive step left first?
After the conversation, have I followed up and repaired anything that felt like a personal attack, whatever the outcome?

example.situation: A senior analyst disagrees with her director's decision to cut the user-testing phase from a product launch to save three weeks.
example.before: Honestly, cutting testing is a mistake and everyone on the team thinks so. If this goes ahead I'm not sure I want my name on it.
example.after: Before we lock the plan, can I raise one risk on the testing cut? Last release, the two issues we skipped testing on cost us about four weeks of fixes. One option: test only the checkout flow, which keeps most of the time saving. Could we decide that together by Thursday?
example.why: The rewrite raises the disagreement privately and early, ties it to the director's goal (the launch date), brings evidence and a workable alternative, and drops the veiled resignation threat and the appeal to an unnamed group - the moves Kassing's respondents rated least competent.

title: Video call communication
summary: Live conversation over a camera-and-microphone link such as Zoom or Teams; it keeps the speed and back-and-forth of a meeting without travel, but transmission lag, a screen-bound field of view and filtered nonverbal cues change turn-taking, idea generation and how people come across, so it works best when the purpose, audio and turn order are managed deliberately.
selfCheck: Does this conversation need faces and live back-and-forth, or would a phone call, a shared document or a short written update do?
If the goal is to generate ideas, have I given people a way to think away from the screen, or should we meet in person?
Is my audio clear enough that a stranger would take me seriously, and have I fixed it before worrying about my background?
Did I tell people at the start how to ask to speak and in what order I will take contributions?
After I asked a question, did I leave enough pause for the lag before filling the silence or moving on?

title: Vocal delivery
summary: The learnable skill of controlling rate, volume, pitch, pausing and articulation while speaking to a group, so that listeners can follow the talk, hear what matters most and judge the speaker as engaged and confident. Lab studies link moderate vocal variation and audible volume to liveliness and persuasion, but effects are modest and most evidence comes from short, controlled recordings.
selfCheck: In my last recording, could I hear my voice rise and fall on the key words, or did whole sentences sit on one note?
Did I slow down and pause before the number, decision or request I most needed people to remember?
Could the person farthest from me, or on the worst audio connection, hear every sentence without straining?
Was my vocal emphasis saved for the two or three points that matter, rather than spread over everything?
Did I sound sure about the claims I am in fact sure of, and plainly flag the ones I am not?

title: Wait time
summary: Deliberately leaving a pause of a few seconds after you ask a question (wait time 1) and again after the other person finishes answering (wait time 2), so people have time to think and to add to what they said, instead of the conversation snapping to the fastest or loudest reply.
selfCheck: After my last question, did I actually stay silent for at least three seconds, or did I rephrase, add options or answer it myself?
When someone finished speaking, did I pause before replying, or did I jump straight to my next point?
Did the answers I got come mostly from the fastest speakers, and would more think time have widened who spoke?
When I was asked something difficult, did I take a moment to think, or did I answer to escape the silence?
steps: Ask one question, then stop talking - do not rephrase it, add a second question or offer a sample answer.
Count silently to at least three (longer for a hard or open question, or when a group is involved) before saying anything else.
If the silence runs on, re-invite rather than rescue - "Take a moment; I'd rather hear a considered answer" - and keep waiting.
When the person finishes answering, pause again for a few seconds before you reply, so they can add the second thought that often matters most.
In a meeting, say up front that you will wait before taking answers, so the first fast voice does not set the direction.
When you are asked a hard question, give yourself the same pause - say you want a moment to think - instead of filling the gap with the first answer that comes to mind.

example.situation: A product manager runs a project retrospective with six engineers and wants to hear what really slowed the release.
example.before: So, what slowed us down? ... Was it the test environment? Or maybe the late spec changes? OK, Priya, the environment, right? Great - next item.
example.after: What slowed us down most on this release? I'll give everyone a few seconds to think before we start. [silent count to five] ... [after Priya answers, another three-second pause] ... Anything else behind that?
example.why: In the first version the manager fills the silence with guesses and accepts the first answer, so the group responds to his options; the pauses in the second version give quieter people time to form a view and give the first speaker room to add the underlying cause.

title: Wall of text
summary: Presenting a message as long, dense, unbroken paragraphs with no headings, lists, emphasis or white space, so busy readers who scan rather than read word by word miss key points and requests.
selfCheck: If a colleague only read my first two lines and the bold text, would they know what changed and what I need from them?
Does any paragraph run longer than about five lines or cover more than one idea?
Is each request or deadline on its own line, with a named owner, instead of hidden in a sentence?
Have I used bold or headings sparingly enough that they still mark what matters most?

example.situation: A project lead emails six stakeholders about a delayed data migration and needs two of them to act by Thursday.
example.before: Hi all, following up on last week's steering call where we talked through the migration timeline and some of the issues the vendor raised about the legacy schema, which as you know has been a recurring theme since phase one, the team has now completed the mapping for most tables but we discovered that the customer-history table has about 40,000 records with inconsistent date formats, so the cutover will move from the 14th to the 21st, and to keep that date we will need Finance to confirm the archive cut-off and IT Security to approve the temporary service account by Thursday, otherwise we lose the weekend window...
example.after:
Subject: Migration moves to the 21st - 2 approvals needed by Thu

Cutover moves from the 14th to the 21st. To hold that date we need two things by Thursday:

- **Finance (Priya):** confirm the archive cut-off date.
- **IT Security (Marco):** approve the temporary service account.

**Why the delay:** 40,000 customer-history records have inconsistent date formats and need cleaning.

**If we miss Thursday:** we lose the weekend window and the next slot is the 4th.
example.why: The original buries the new date and both requests mid-paragraph, so a scanning reader sees only the opening background; the rewrite front-loads the change, gives each request its own line with an owner, and uses short labelled chunks so every reader can find their part in seconds.

title: The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions
summary: A 2014 International Journal of Listening experiment in which 115 students talked with trained partners who either paraphrased and asked follow-up questions, gave advice, or simply acknowledged; active listening made speakers feel more understood, but it was not liked more than advice.

title: William Strunk Jr.
summary: Cornell English professor (1869-1946) whose 1918 classroom handbook, The Elements of Style, set out short imperative rules such as using the active voice and omitting needless words; revised by his former student E. B. White in 1959, it became the best-known American writing guide.

title: Wise feedback
summary: Delivering critical feedback together with an explicit reason for it: you hold high standards and you believe the person can meet them. The framing helps people read criticism as investment rather than bias, especially when they have reason to doubt the giver's intentions.
selfCheck: Did I say why I am giving this feedback, not just what is wrong?
Is the high standard I mentioned one I actually apply to everyone on the team?
Do I have real evidence that this person can meet it, and did I name it?
Did I offer a specific chance to revise and a time to review it?
steps: Make sure the standard is real and the work actually falls short of it; wise framing cannot rescue vague or unfair criticism.
Write specific, rigorous comments that say where the work misses the mark and what would fix it.
Add one or two sentences saying why you are giving this feedback - the bar is high because the work matters - and that you are confident this person can reach it.
Give a concrete chance to act on it, such as a revision, a second draft or a follow-up review date.
When the improved version arrives, review it against the same standard and say what changed, so your stated belief is backed by follow-through.

example.situation: A team lead returns a junior analyst's first client-facing forecast deck with many corrections.
example.before: Lots of issues here - see my comments. The assumptions slide is weak and the charts don't support the conclusion. Please fix before Thursday.
example.after: I've marked this up heavily because this deck goes to the client's CFO and I hold client work to a high bar. I've seen your modelling on the pricing project, so I know you can get this there. The two biggest fixes are sourcing each assumption and making the chart show the gap you name in the headline. Can we look at the revision Wednesday morning?
example.why: The same criticism now comes with a reason the analyst can believe - a high standard and confidence in them - plus a concrete chance to improve, so the markup reads as investment rather than a verdict on their ability.

title: The Power of Feedback Revisited
summary: Benedikt Wisniewski, Klaus Zierer and John Hattie's 2020 Frontiers in Psychology meta-analysis of 435 studies (994 effects, about 61,000 learners), which found a medium average effect of feedback (d = 0.48) with very large variation, and much stronger effects for feedback rich in information.

title: Words of estimative probability
summary: Stating how likely something is with an agreed set of likelihood words, each tied to a numeric range that is shown next to the word, so that "likely" means the same thing to the writer and every reader.
selfCheck: If three readers each wrote down the percentage they think my likelihood word means, would their numbers land in the same range as mine?
Have I put the number next to the word, or am I relying on readers to look up a key they will probably skip?
Am I using "could", "may" or "possible" to hedge when I actually have an estimate I am reluctant to commit to?
Have I kept my confidence in the evidence separate from the likelihood of the event?
steps: Agree a short likelihood scale with your team or client before you need it - for example remote (under 5%), unlikely (20-45%), roughly even (45-55%), likely (55-80%), very likely (80-95%) - with ranges that do not overlap.
Before writing a forecast, decide your own number or range first, then pick the one word on the scale whose range contains it.
Put the numeric range in brackets right after the word in the text itself ("likely (55-80%)"), not in a footnote, appendix or hover text.
Keep likelihood (how probable the event is) separate from confidence (how solid your evidence is), and say each in its own sentence.
Reserve "possible", "could" and "may" for cases where you genuinely cannot estimate the odds, and say so rather than using them as softeners.
Use the same words with the same meanings in every report, and add a short key whenever a new reader joins the distribution.

example.situation: A consultant updates a client steering committee on whether a system migration will hit its go-live date.
example.before: There is a real possibility we could miss the March 1 go-live, although the team is working hard and it may well still be achievable.
example.after: We judge it unlikely (20-45%) that we hit the March 1 go-live; very likely (80-95%) by March 22. We have moderate confidence: the estimate rests on two weeks of test-defect data. Decision needed by Friday: hold the date with reduced scope, or move it.
example.why: The before version could be read anywhere from a small risk to a probable slip; the after version gives one shared range, separates odds from confidence, and turns the forecast into a decision the committee can make.

title: Workplace meetings
summary: Planned gatherings of two or more colleagues, in person or online, held to share information, solve problems or make decisions together; the recurring situation that meeting science studies and that agendas, facilitation and recaps are designed for.

title: Zone of possible agreement
summary: The range of deals that both sides would prefer to walking away - the overlap between each party's reservation point. If the ranges overlap a deal is possible; if they do not, no amount of haggling will produce one and both sides should turn to their alternatives.

title: Zoom fatigue
summary: The tiredness and depletion people report after video meetings, linked to sustained close-up eye contact, the extra effort of sending and reading nonverbal cues on screen, watching a self-view and being kept still in front of a camera; it drains the energy people bring to later meetings and makes them less likely to speak up.
selfCheck: Does this conversation need video at all, or would a phone call, a shared document or a written update do the job?
Have I booked video meetings back to back with no break to stand up, move or look away from the screen?
Am I watching my own tile more than the people I am talking to, and could I hide self-view?
Did I make it clear that cameras are optional for this meeting, especially for newer team members?
Did people have a moment to connect as a group, or did we go straight into a wall of faces and slides?
